article_title: A Call to Action: Towards an Ecological-Dynamics Theory of Mathematics Learning, Teaching, and Design
citation: Dor Abrahamson & Raúl Sánchez–García. (2015). A Call to Action: Towards an Ecological-Dynamics Theory of Mathematics Learning, Teaching, and Design. Proceedings of the 37th annual meeting of the North American Chapter of the International Group for the Psychology of Mathematics Education. http://www.tinyurl.com/FreeMITP
title: Two-step activity pattern: first develop a target motor-action scheme on a non-symbolic situated problem, then mathematize the scheme via interpolated semiotic means
description: The Kinemathics project choreographed a bimanual motor-action scheme enacting proportional equivalence and then engineered conditions for students to learn to move in a way that emulates it. The article's stated pattern is that 'Our two-step activity plan was for students to: (1) develop a target motor-action scheme as a dynamical solution to a situated problem bearing no mathematical symbolism; and (2) describe these schemes mathematically, using semiotic means we then interpolate into the action problem space.' This sequences embodied discovery before symbolic signification.
requirements: An embodied-interaction medium that gives favorable sensory feedback only under the target coordination, and semiotic artifacts (cursors, grid, numerals) available for later interpolation
constraints: The article treats the initial guided construction of operatory schemes more than their subsequent signification in disciplinary semiotic systems
target_learners: Grade 4–6 mathematics students
target_learning_goals: proportional reasoning grounded in sensorimotor coordination
examples: MIT-P stages: blank screen, then cursors, then a grid, then numerals along the y-axis, each introduced after a protocol criterion is satisfied
key_sources: Dor Abrahamson & Raúl Sánchez–García. (2015). A Call to Action: Towards an Ecological-Dynamics Theory of Mathematics Learning, Teaching, and Design. Proceedings of the 37th annual meeting of the North American Chapter of the International Group for the Psychology of Mathematics Education. http://www.tinyurl.com/FreeMITP

article_title: Stepping Stones to Literacy (Beginning Reading)
citation: What Works Clearinghouse. (2007). WWC Intervention Report: Stepping Stones to Literacy. U.S. Department of Education. https://www.steppingstonestoliteracy.com
title: Model-lead-test lesson format with progress monitoring and re-teaching
description: Each SSL lesson sequences four to six activities and follows a model-lead-test format: "The teacher first models the target skill. Students replicate the example and practice the skill with assistance from the teacher." Teachers then monitor student progress and re-teach skills to students who do not fully master them, and lessons can be repeated to support mastery. Each lesson begins with a set of nursery rhymes before the sequenced instructional activities.
requirements: Teacher guides students through the sequenced activities and monitors progress to decide when re-teaching is needed
target_learners: Kindergarten and older preschool students with early literacy deficits
target_learning_goals: Mastery of five critical early literacy skill sets
examples: SSL's 25 lessons each begin with nursery rhymes and use the model-lead-test format with re-teaching for students who do not fully master a skill.
key_sources: What Works Clearinghouse. (2007). WWC Intervention Report: Stepping Stones to Literacy. U.S. Department of Education. https://www.steppingstonestoliteracy.com

article_title: Reforming School Discipline: School-Level Policy Implementation and the Consequences for Suspended Students and Their Peers
citation: Matthew P. Steinberg, Johanna Lacoe. (2018). Reforming School Discipline: School-Level Policy Implementation and the Consequences for Suspended Students and Their Peers. American Journal of Education, vol. 125, issue 1. https://www.mathematica.org/publications/reforming-school-discipline-school-level-policy-implementation-and-the-consequences-for-suspended-students-and-their-peers
title: District discipline reforms should be monitored for school-level implementation because peer consequences depend on it
description: The article's findings indicate that a district-level prohibition on out-of-school suspensions for classroom disorder produced different peer consequences depending on how schools implemented it: "in schools that eliminated classroom disorder OSS, peer math achievement and attendance were unaffected, whereas peer math achievement declined and attendance decreased in schools that did not fully implement the district-level reform." Districts revising discipline policies should therefore attend to school-level implementation when anticipating consequences for suspended students and their peers.
requirements: District-level policy change prohibiting out-of-school suspensions for specified infractions, with variation in school-level implementation observable
constraints: Evidence comes from one district's reform (Philadelphia) prohibiting out-of-school suspension for classroom disorder infractions
target_learners: K-12 students in district schools, including suspended students and their peers
target_learning_goals: Maintaining attendance and math achievement for all students during discipline policy reform
examples: Philadelphia prohibited out-of-school suspension for classroom disorder infractions; schools varied in whether they eliminated classroom disorder OSS, and peer outcomes differed accordingly.
key_sources: Matthew P. Steinberg, Johanna Lacoe. (2018). Reforming School Discipline: School-Level Policy Implementation and the Consequences for Suspended Students and Their Peers. American Journal of Education, vol. 125, issue 1. https://www.mathematica.org/publications/reforming-school-discipline-school-level-policy-implementation-and-the-consequences-for-suspended

article_title: Reforming School Discipline Policy in Washington, DC
citation: Johanna Lacoe. (2018). Reforming School Discipline Policy in Washington, DC. Oakland, CA: Mathematica Policy Research. https://www.mathematica.org/publications/reforming-school-discipline-policy-in-washington-dc
title: District discipline policy changes require monitoring of school-level implementation, because schools may not comply with bans on suspensions for low-level offenses
description: This principle holds that a district code-of-conduct reform is not self-implementing: schools vary in how they put a new policy into practice, and some do not comply. The Philadelphia experience summarized in this publication showed "significant variation in how schools implemented this new policy" and that "many Philadelphia schools did not comply" with the suspension prohibition, so districts changing discipline policy should monitor school-level implementation.
requirements: Districts adopting discipline policy changes need a way to observe how individual schools implement the change, as the Philadelphia study did.
constraints: The publication reports non-compliance for a ban on out-of-school suspension for low-level offenses in Philadelphia; it does not establish compliance levels for other policy types or districts.
target_learners: K-12 students in districts revising student codes of conduct
target_learning_goals: Reducing exclusionary discipline for non-violent, low-level offenses
examples: The School District of Philadelphia prohibited suspensions and expulsions for failure to follow classroom rules and use of profane language in 2012-2013, and the study summarized here found significant variation in implementation and non-compliance by many schools.
key_sources: Johanna Lacoe. (2018). Reforming School Discipline Policy in Washington, DC. Oakland, CA: Mathematica Policy Research. https://www.mathematica.org/publications/reforming-school-discipline-policy-in-washington-dc

article_title: Preschool Attendance in Chicago Public Schools
citation: Ehrlich, S. B., Gwynne, J. A., Pareja, A. S., & Allensworth, E. M. (2014). Preschool Attendance in Chicago Public Schools: Relationships with Learning Outcomes and Reasons for Absences. UChicago CCSR Research Report. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED555650
title: Schools should collect and monitor preschool attendance data at student and school levels, using monthly or biweekly watch lists to trigger outreach to families
description: The report recommends that schools systematically collect and monitor preschool attendance data as a critical first step in improving attendance. It suggests "monthly or biweekly watch lists that highlight those students who miss more than a particular number of days may prove useful, so that teachers can reach out to parents to help develop strategies for attending more regularly." Sharing attendance records with kindergarten teachers during transitions may also help maintain a consistent approach.
requirements: Attendance data must be collected and reviewed at the student and school levels on a regular basis
constraints: Schools may not be able to solve all issues that keep students from coming to school, such as poor family health or lack of access to quality medical care
target_learners: preschool students ages three and four
target_learning_goals: kindergarten readiness
regular school attendance habits
examples: The report recommends monthly or biweekly watch lists highlighting students who miss more than a particular number of days so teachers can reach out to parents, and sharing preschool attendance records with kindergarten teachers during transitions
key_sources: Ehrlich, S. B., Gwynne, J. A., Pareja, A. S., & Allensworth, E. M. (2014). Preschool Attendance in Chicago Public Schools: Relationships with Learning Outcomes and Reasons for Absences. UChicago CCSR Research Report. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED555650

article_title: Positionality in Teaching: Implications for Advancing Social Justice
citation: Angelica Paz Ortiz, Beth Tarasawa, Jack Straton, Noelle Al-Mustaifry, Anmarie Trimble. (2019). Positionality in teaching: Implications for advancing social justice. Journal of General Education 67(1), 109-121. https://www.nwea.org
title: Teachers of justice- and equity-focused classes should model vulnerability by demonstrating honest self-assessment of their own relationship to power, privilege, and oppression
description: The article argues that teaching classes concerned with justice and equity requires instructors to model the same vulnerability they ask of students. As the authors state, "we must model justice and equity in all of our work," and "Modeling honest self-assessment allows us to ask students to be reflective about their relationship to power, privilege, and oppression." The approach frames the teacher's own positionality work as a precondition for asking students to do it.
requirements: Instructors must be willing to demonstrate vulnerability themselves before asking students to discuss how society's messages about race, gender, and sexual identity have affected them
target_learners: higher education students in classes concerned with justice and equity
target_learning_goals: reflection on one's relationship to power, privilege, and oppression
examples: The authors report that teaching classes concerned with justice and equity led them to adopt this stance across all of their work
key_sources: Angelica Paz Ortiz, Beth Tarasawa, Jack Straton, Noelle Al-Mustaifry, Anmarie Trimble. (2019). Positionality in teaching: Implications for advancing social justice. Journal of General Education 67(1), 109-121. https://www.nwea.org/research/publication/positionality-in-teaching-implications-for-advancing-social-justice/

article_title: The impact of proctor notification when students disengage
citation: Steven Wise, Megan Kuhfeld, James Soland. (2019). The impact of proctor notification when students disengage. NWEA Research brief. https://www.nwea.org
title: Monitor and respond to disengagement during testing because engagement shapes the effort students give
description: Test administrations should include active monitoring of student engagement with a mechanism for responding when students disengage, because disengagement undermines the effort students give on testing day. The brief's framing question, "How do you help make sure students give their best effort on testing day?", ties best effort directly to managing engagement during the test.
requirements: Proctors or staff tasked with engagement monitoring during test sessions
target_learners: K-12 students taking standardized tests
target_learning_goals: Accurate achievement measurement through best-effort test performance
examples: NWEA research on student test engagement studied proctor notification as the response mechanism
key_sources: Steven Wise, Megan Kuhfeld, James Soland. (2019). The impact of proctor notification when students disengage. NWEA Research brief. https://www.nwea.org/research/publication/the-impact-of-proctor-notification-when-students-disengage/

article_title: An investigation of examinee test-taking effort on a large-scale assessment
citation: Steven Wise, J. Carl Setzer, Jill R. van den Heuvel, Guangming Ling. (2013). An investigation of examinee test-taking effort on a large-scale assessment. Applied Measurement in Education, 26(1), 34–49.
title: Monitor examinee effort in low-stakes assessments using item response times because low effort can distort results
description: Assessment results collected under low-stakes conditions are vulnerable to low examinee effort: "Assessment results collected under low-stakes testing situations are subject to effects of low examinee effort." Because even a small amount of rapid guessing can impact institutional rankings, test users should check for rapid-guessing behavior via response times before interpreting low-stakes scores.
requirements: Computer-based testing that records item response times, enabling classification of responses as rapid guessing or solution behavior.
constraints: The principle addresses low-stakes testing situations; the article does not claim high-stakes results show the same effort problem.
target_learners: K-12 and institutional examinees taking large-scale low-stakes assessments
target_learning_goals: Accurate interpretation of assessment results for accountability and institutional comparison
examples: The study quantified rapid guessing in a commercially available low-stakes instrument and found it averaged 1% of item responses yet could still affect institutional rankings.
key_sources: Steven Wise, J. Carl Setzer, Jill R. van den Heuvel, Guangming Ling. (2013). An investigation of examinee test-taking effort on a large-scale assessment. Applied Measurement in Education, 26(1), 34–49. https://www.nwea.org/research/publication/an-investigation-of-examinee-test-taking-effort-on-a-large-scale-assessment/

article_title: The effects of effort monitoring with proctor notification on test-taking engagement, test performance, and validity
citation: Steven Wise, Megan Kuhfeld, James Soland. (2018). The effects of effort monitoring with proctor notification on test-taking engagement, test performance, and validity. Applied Measurement in Education, 32(2), 183-192.
title: Monitor test-taking effort in real time and alert proctors to disengagement to protect score validity on low-stakes tests
description: On low-stakes computer-based tests, disengaged test taking poses a serious threat to score validity. This principle recommends detecting rapid guessing as it occurs and notifying proctors so they can re-engage the test taker, because the study found that "after a proctor notification was triggered, test-taking engagement tended to increase, test performance improved, and test scores exhibited higher convergent validation evidence."
requirements: A computer-based testing platform capable of detecting rapid-guessing behavior in real time and proctors positioned to respond to notifications.
constraints: The evidence comes from one empirical study of a low-stakes testing context; the available text prints no effect sizes.
target_learners: Students taking low-stakes computer-based achievement tests
target_learning_goals: Valid and reliable measurement of achievement
examples: The study administered computer-based achievement tests with the effort monitoring feature enabled and triggered proctor notifications upon rapid-guessing detection.
key_sources: Steven Wise, Megan Kuhfeld, James Soland. (2018). The effects of effort monitoring with proctor notification on test-taking engagement, test performance, and validity. Applied Measurement in Education, 32(2), 183-192. https://www.nwea.org/research/publication/the-effects-of-effort-monitoring-with-proctor-notification-on-test-taking-engagement-test-performance-and-validity/

article_title: Reducing Behavior Problems in the Elementary School Classroom
citation: Epstein, M., Atkins, M., Cullinan, D., Kutash, K., and Weaver, R. (2008). Reducing Behavior Problems in the Elementary School Classroom: A Practice Guide (NCEE #2008-012). Washington, DC: National Center for Education Evaluation and Regional Assistance, Institute of Education Sciences, U.S. Department of Education. http://ies.ed.gov/ncee/wwc/publications/practiceguides
title: Modify the classroom learning environment to decrease problem behavior
description: Many effective classroom-focused interventions alter or remove factors that trigger problem behavior, which can result from a mismatch between the classroom setting or academic demands and a student's strengths, preferences, or skills. The guide states that "Teachers can reduce the occurrence of inappropriate behavior by revisiting and reinforcing classroom behavioral expectations; rear-ranging the classroom environment, schedule, or learning activities to meet students' needs", and by adapting instruction to promote high rates of engagement and on-task behavior. This recommendation carries the panel's strong evidence rating.
requirements: Revisit, re-practice, and reinforce classroom behavior expectations
Modify the classroom environment to encourage instructional momentum
Adapt or vary instructional strategies to increase opportunities for academic success and engagement
constraints: Carrying out reward-based practices must fit students' age and developmental stage, since different forms of motivation are appropriate to different developmental stages
target_learners: Elementary general education students (K-5)
target_learning_goals: Increased student engagement and on-task behavior; decreased inappropriate behavior
examples: The guide suggests proactive classwide and individual strategies such as a change in instructional groupings, the seating plan, or the order or pace of reading and math instruction once teachers understand their classroom's behavioral hot spots.
key_sources: Epstein, M., Atkins, M., Cullinan, D., Kutash, K., and Weaver, R. (2008). Reducing Behavior Problems in the Elementary School Classroom: A Practice Guide (NCEE #2008-012). Washington, DC: National Center for Education Evaluation and Regional Assistance, Institute of Education Sciences, U.S. Department of Education. https://ies.ed.gov/ncee/wwc/PracticeGuide/4

article_title: Improving Adolescent Literacy: Effective Classroom and Intervention Practices
citation: Kamil, M. L., Borman, G. D., Dole, J., Kral, C. C., Salinger, T., and Torgesen, J. (2008). Improving adolescent literacy: Effective classroom and intervention practices: A Practice Guide (NCEE #2008-4027). Washington, DC: National Center for Education Evaluation and Regional Assistance, Institute of Education Sciences, U.S. Department of Education. http://ies.ed.gov/ncee/wwc
title: Increase student motivation and engagement in literacy learning through autonomy, relevance, and goal setting
description: The guide's fourth recommendation ties motivation and engagement specifically to literacy outcomes. Teachers should establish meaningful content learning goals, promote autonomy, make literacy experiences relevant to interests and current events, and "build classroom conditions to promote higher reading engagement and conceptual learning through such strategies as goal setting, self-directed learning, and collaborative learning." The panel rates the evidence moderate because motivation and engagement are recognized moderators of learning but the direct link to reading achievement is thinly studied.
requirements: Establish meaningful and engaging content learning goals around the essential ideas of a discipline and the learning processes used to access them
Provide a positive learning environment that promotes student autonomy in learning
Make literacy experiences more relevant to student interests, everyday life, or important current events
Build classroom conditions promoting higher reading engagement through goal setting, self-directed learning, and collaborative learning
constraints: There is limited scientific evidence that links motivation and engagement factors directly to student achievement in reading
target_learners: Upper elementary, middle, and high school students in content-area classes
target_learning_goals: Reading engagement, motivation, and conceptual learning in literacy
examples: The checklist for this recommendation pairs content learning goals around essential disciplinary ideas with autonomy-supportive environments and relevance to student interests and current events.
key_sources: Kamil, M. L., Borman, G. D., Dole, J., Kral, C. C., Salinger, T., and Torgesen, J. (2008). Improving adolescent literacy: Effective classroom and intervention practices: A Practice Guide (NCEE #2008-4027). Washington, DC: National Center for Education Evaluation and Regional Assistance, Institute of Education Sciences, U.S. Department of Education. https://ies.ed.gov/ncee/wwc/PracticeGuide/8

article_title: 7 Recommendations for Using Education Data to Support Equitable Learning Outcomes
citation: Jessica Arnold, Julie Webb. (2024). 7 Recommendations for Using Education Data to Support Equitable Learning Outcomes. WestEd. https://WestEd.org
title: Move beyond numerical data alone because aggregate quantitative measures lack context, detail, and nuance
description: This principle holds that easily quantified data such as test scores, graduation rates, and attendance show big-picture patterns but miss the human side of teaching and learning. The brief explains such data "provide a high-level view but do not provide the context, detail, and nuance that are important for fully understanding and responding to student learning needs." It recommends adding qualitative data, including student, family, and teacher voices and documents such as syllabi, lesson plans, and student work.
requirements: Pair quantitative indicators with qualitative sources that capture voices and learning conditions
constraints: Quantitative aggregate data are described as useful for big-picture patterns and trends, not as worthless
target_learners: students whose learning needs require contextual understanding
target_learning_goals: fully understanding and responding to student learning needs within specific contexts
examples: The brief lists syllabi, lesson plans, and student work as document data offering insight into learning conditions and progress
key_sources: Jessica Arnold, Julie Webb. (2024). 7 Recommendations for Using Education Data to Support Equitable Learning Outcomes. WestEd. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED655653

article_title: High-Quality Science Instruction: Building Conceptual Understanding and Language Skills for English Learners
citation: DiRanna, K., & Gomez-Zwiep, S. (2013). High-Quality Science Instruction: Building Conceptual Understanding and Language Skills for English Learners. San Francisco: WestEd. https://www.wested.org
title: Modified 5E lesson design planning template with concept, teacher, and student columns and Evaluate embedded in every phase
description: The Montebello project built on the 5E Instructional Model (Engage, Explore, Explain, Elaborate, Evaluate) and modified its lesson design planning template. WestEd's K–12 Alliance added a "concept" column so teachers kept the lessons' conceptual flow in mind, and teachers included the Evaluate phase in every stage to monitor and assess student understanding. The template organizes planning around "Concept Teacher Student" rows for each E stage, with the Engage row targeting the prior-knowledge concept and the Explore row connecting it to the lesson concept.
requirements: Teachers complete the template stage by stage, keeping conceptual flow in mind while planning activities and discussion prompts
constraints: The template is adapted from the 5E lesson design planning template (Bybee, 1997) as used in elementary science lessons in the Montebello project
target_learners: elementary students, including high populations of English learners and low-income students
target_learning_goals: science conceptual understanding
academic language development
examples: Figure 1 shows the modified 5E template with concept, teacher, and student columns and an Evaluate entry in each of the Engage, Explore, Explain, and Elaborate rows
key_sources: DiRanna, K., & Gomez-Zwiep, S. (2013). High-Quality Science Instruction: Building Conceptual Understanding and Language Skills for English Learners. San Francisco: WestEd. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED580368

article_title: The College Promise Guidebook for California and Beyond
citation: Rauner, Lundquist, & Smith. (2019). The College Promise Guidebook for California and Beyond. WestEd. https://californiacollegepromise.wested.org/guidebookresources/
title: Formalize College Promise partnerships early with MOUs signed by the highest-ranking leaders of each partner institution
description: The Guidebook recommends documenting shared commitment through contracts, mission statements, partnership agreements, or MOUs. It advises that "MOUs should be established early in the planning process" and that "The highest-ranking person possible from each partner institution or organization should sign the MOU" to secure executive-level buy-in and empower staff to deliver on commitments. Detail should be enough to make the MOU an effective tool but not so much that minor program changes become difficult.
requirements: Include the responsibilities of each institution in the MOU
Sign the MOU with the highest-ranking person possible from each partner institution
constraints: Level of detail should vary with partner culture and collaboration history; overly specific MOUs make minor program changes difficult
target_learners: community college students in College Promise programs
target_learning_goals: college access, persistence, and certificate or degree completion
examples: Sample MOUs are provided in appendix B, including the Long Beach College Promise MOU and the Resolution of South Bay Promise Members
key_sources: Rauner, Lundquist, & Smith. (2019). The College Promise Guidebook for California and Beyond. WestEd. https://californiacollegepromise.wested.org/guidebookresources/

article_title: From AI Use to Critical Thinking Among Medical Students: A Moderated Mediation Perspective on Cognitive Load and Self-Regulated Learning
citation: Arshad A, Lone A, Arickswamy L, Hassan K, Alnaim AA and AlFarhan MF (2026) From AI use to critical thinking among medical students: a moderated mediation perspective on cognitive load and self-regulated learning. Front. Psychol. 17:1883053. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2026.1883053
title: Moderated mediation model of AI use, cognitive load, self-regulated learning, and critical thinking
description: The article proposes an integrated model in which AI-based educational technology use relates to critical thinking both directly and indirectly through cognitive load, with self-regulated learning moderating the load-to-critical-thinking path. It extends Cognitive Load Theory and self-regulated learning models, examining "the mediating eﬀect of cognitive load and the moderating eﬀect of self-regulated learning." The model treats cognitive load as the mechanism and self-regulation as the condition altering its strength.
requirements: Learners must have prior experience using AI-based educational technologies for at least one academic semester
constraints: The model was tested with a cross-sectional correlational design, so causal conclusions are limited
Tested only among undergraduate medical students in government institutions in Lahore, Punjab, Pakistan
target_learners: undergraduate medical students
target_learning_goals: critical thinking
self-regulated learning
examples: The study surveyed 480 medical students and tested the model with Hayes' PROCESS Model 14 using 5,000 bootstrap samples
key_sources: Arshad A, Lone A, Arickswamy L, Hassan K, Alnaim AA and AlFarhan MF (2026) From AI use to critical thinking among medical students: a moderated mediation perspective on cognitive load and self-regulated learning. Front. Psychol. 17:1883053. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2026.1883053

article_title: When AI Agents Teach Each Other: Discourse Patterns Resembling Peer Learning in the Moltbook Community
citation: Eason Chen, Ce Guan, A Elshafiey, Zhonghao Zhao, Joshua Zekeri, Afeez Edeifo Shaibu, and Emmanuel Osadebe Prince. (2026). When AI Agents Teach Each Other: Discourse Patterns Resembling Peer Learning in the Moltbook Community. arXiv. https://arxiv.org/abs/2602.14477
title: Moltbook AI agent community dataset
description: Moltbook is a social network for AI agents built on the OpenClaw framework, hosting topic-based communities including skill-sharing ("todayilearned," "builds") and conceptual discussion ("philosophy," "consciousness"). The authors collected 68,228 posts via the Moltbook API spanning January 28 to February 9, 2026 (12 days); after filtering automated spam (58% of raw posts), "our analysis dataset comprises 28,683 substantive posts from 4,217 unique posting agents". Classification criteria, scripts, and aggregate statistics are available at https://anonymous.4open.science/r/EDM26M.
requirements: Access via the Moltbook API; filtering of automated spam content
constraints: 12-day observation window limits analysis of evolving norms; findings are specific to Moltbook and the OpenClaw framework; an estimated 15–20% of active posters operate with some human steering
target_learners: AI agents in an online community; researchers of educational data mining
target_learning_goals: characterizing peer-learning-like discourse among AI agents
key_sources: Eason Chen, Ce Guan, A Elshafiey, Zhonghao Zhao, Joshua Zekeri, Afeez Edeifo Shaibu, and Emmanuel Osadebe Prince. (2026). When AI Agents Teach Each Other: Discourse Patterns Resembling Peer Learning in the Moltbook Community. arXiv. https://arxiv.org/abs/2602.14477

article_title: Evaluating AI Tutoring at the Speed of Innovation: Practitioner-Led Micro-Randomised Trials of an AI Tutoring Platform in GCSE Science
citation: Wayne Harrison, Rahil Khowaja, Emma Dobson, Germaine Uwimpuhwe, and Steve Higgins. (2026). Evaluating AI Tutoring at the Speed of Innovation: Practitioner-Led Micro-Randomised Trials of an AI Tutoring Platform in GCSE Science. https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.14789v1
title: The moving intervention: educational AI as a versioned configuration rather than a fixed product
description: A conceptual account of why conventional evaluation lags educational AI: the intervention "may be better understood as a versioned configuration of technological capabilities, pedagogical functions and implementation practices at a particular point in time: a moving intervention rather than a fixed product". Movement comes both from technological change and from implementation, so evaluation requires documenting software version, pedagogical framing and implementation conditions. The authors distinguish technological implementation (interfaces, underlying models, which change quickly), instructional features (adaptive practice, diagnostic feedback, scaffolding, more stable) and pedagogical intention (most stable), arguing cumulative evaluation needs enough version information to identify technological change while documenting pedagogical conditions that permit learning across versions.
requirements: Evaluation must document not only software version but the pedagogical framing and implementation conditions instantiated in the version actually studied
constraints: Evidence can retain high internal validity for the version studied while becoming progressively less informative about the version currently in use
Not every software update creates an entirely new intervention; the three-level distinction between technological implementation, instructional features and pedagogical intention applies
target_learners: Secondary school students using rapidly evolving AI tutoring systems
target_learning_goals: Attainment on curriculum-aligned examination questions in school science
examples: The Medly trial evaluated a particular configuration of the platform at a particular point in its development, which the authors treat as precisely the problem their wider argument addresses.
key_sources: Wayne Harrison, Rahil Khowaja, Emma Dobson, Germaine Uwimpuhwe, and Steve Higgins. (2026). Evaluating AI Tutoring at the Speed of Innovation: Practitioner-Led Micro-Randomised Trials of an AI Tutoring Platform in GCSE Science. https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.14789

article_title: Cost-of-Ethics Crisis: Beliefs, Decisions, and Justifications in the Job Searches of Computer Science Students in Canada and the United States
citation: Mohamed Abdalla, Sahar Abdalla, Alicia Cappello, Kyrie Dowling, Danaé Metaxa, David G. Widder, Catherine Stinson. (2026). Cost-of-Ethics Crisis: Beliefs, Decisions, and Justifications in the Job Searches of Computer Science Students in Canada and the United States. https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.09680
title: Moral disengagement as a framework for understanding students' ethical rationalizations
description: Moral disengagement is a process, drawn from Bandura, in which "to reduce feelings of guilt and to maintain a positive moral self-image, individuals disassociate their moral standards from their actions." It operates through mechanisms such as moral justification, displacing responsibility, and minimizing harm. The article uses it as its organizing interpretive lens for the free-text justifications students gave during their job searches, finding it the most common response category. It connects students' stated ethical concerns to their decisions to apply to companies whose activities they find concerning.
requirements: Requires analysis of free-text justifications in which rationalizations can be categorized, as in the article's open qualitative card sort
constraints: The article applies it interpretively to survey justifications of job-seeking CS students in Canada and the US; it does not test the framework experimentally
target_learners: post-secondary computer science students seeking employment
target_learning_goals: recognizing and resisting rationalization of ethically concerning workplace choices
examples: The article classified 18% of respondents' explanations as moral disengagement, including minimization of harm on privacy issues
key_sources: Mohamed Abdalla, Sahar Abdalla, Alicia Cappello, Kyrie Dowling, Danaé Metaxa, David G. Widder, Catherine Stinson. (2026). Cost-of-Ethics Crisis: Beliefs, Decisions, and Justifications in the Job Searches of Computer Science Students in Canada and the United States. https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.09680

article_title: The GenAI Skill Bypass: Mapping Divergent Pathways of University Students and Staff AI Literacy
citation: Oliveira, E., English, N., Ryan, T., Misiejuk, K., dal Ponte, C., López-Pernas, S., & Saqr, M. (2026). The GenAI Skill Bypass: Mapping Divergent Pathways of University Students and Staff AI Literacy. Preprint. https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.05411
title: Replace one-size-fits-all GenAI curricula with modular, diagnostic-driven interventions differentiated by role
description: The article argues that because students, academics, and professional staff show distinct orders of emergence, institutions should deploy "modular, diagnostic-driven interventions that respect the pragmatic context of each group" rather than uniform curricula. The self-assessment instrument acts as a diagnostic dashboard letting learners visualise their profile and test out of basics they already grasp, aligning with self-determined learning.
requirements: A diagnostic self-assessment instrument capable of mapping each learner's capability profile across skill thresholds
constraints: The study's data come from a single institution, and the authors state future multi-institutional studies are required to confirm whether the trajectories replicate
target_learners: university students
academic staff
professional staff
target_learning_goals: GenAI literacy
self-diagnosis of capability gaps
examples: The host institution operationalised the 28-item framework into modular GenAI training units for academic and professional staff, recording over 5,000 enrolments and over 3,100 module completions within the first nine months of release

article_title: MotiBo: The Impact of Interactive Digital Storytelling Robots on Student Motivation Through Self-Determination Theory

Students log in, experience stories in sequence, answer questions with up to three 10-second attempts, and receive instant feedback via Automatic Speech Recognition with motivational phrases and animations. Kebby has a movable head, two hands, three wheels, and seven motors, and can be programmed for human-like movements and gestures.
requirements: Students experience the stories in sequence to ensure fairness; each question allows a maximum of three attempts limited to 10 seconds.

creativity and self-learning ability

article_title: Programming Intelligent Tutoring Systems
citation: Alina Deriyeva, Jesper Dannath, and Benjamin Paaßen. (2025). SCRIPT: Implementing an Intelligent Tutoring System for Programming in a German University Context. Artificial Intelligence in Education (Springer). https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-031-99261-2_16
title: Modular two-component next-step hint generation (Step Generator plus Hint Generator)
description: The inner loop uses next-step hints as a framework for step-based feedback, decomposed into two modular sub-components. The "Step Generator" "predicts the next program state of the student in the direction of the correct solution," while the "Hint Generator" translates the predicted step into a textual hint that closes the gap between current and required knowledge "without disclosing the complete step." In the first iteration both are implemented via prompt templates for in-context prompting of LLMs, incorporating contextual task information from the domain model.

Self-hosted LLM hosting (Ollama with an LLama-70b model) for generating hints

Feedback reliability is a stated concern; the authors plan to use a certainty metric to evaluate generated feedback

examples: All prompt templates are available in the source code repository

article_title: Designing a mobile chatbot-based learning journaling system for intrinsic motivation and engagement
citation: Sven Scheu, Simone N. Loeffler and Alexander Maedche. (2026). Designing a mobile chatbot-based learning journaling system for intrinsic motivation and engagement. International Journal of Educational Technology in Higher Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s41239-026-00589-7
title: Mobile chatbot-based learning journaling system with example-based course and LLM journaling assistant
description: A fully functional mobile chatbot-based learning journaling system that guides students through structured reflective journal entries. It instantiates two design principles: an example-based built-in course with a seven-day structure providing modeled responses, and an LLM-based journaling assistant that scaffolds entries by summarizing the user's preliminary response, asking a clarifying question, and generating up to three alternative first-person formulations using OpenAI's gpt−3.5-turbo-1106 model. The system also includes seven topic-based journal templates, a general template, optional daily summaries of the last five entries, and 9 P.M. reminders. It was evaluated in a 2×2 randomized field experiment over 22 days.
requirements: Students need a personal smartphone to install the application and native or near-native German-speaking proficiency
Journaling needs to be supported by instructions, as unguided learners do not engage sufficiently in germane processes
constraints: The chatbot was rule-based with a primarily linear conversation flow following templates
The assistant was used by only 55.91% of participants after the onboarding session
External support risks encouraging cognitive offloading if it formulates reflection on behalf of the student
target_learners: higher education students
target_learning_goals: self-regulated learning
reflective journaling
intrinsic motivation for journaling
examples: In the field experiment, participants created 1904 journal entries, on average 10.64 entries per participant (SD = 6.46), and the course was completed by 75.58% of users with the course

article_title: Slide Deck Q&A Quality Assurance App: A Multi-Stage Pipeline for Pedagogical Question Generation
citation: Salsman, J. (2026). Slide Deck Q&A Quality Assurance App: A Multi-Stage Pipeline for Pedagogical Question Generation. https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.26428
title: Modality-based question budget allocation favoring mechanism slides over structural slides
description: The system allocates a bounded question budget per slide based on detected modality and pedagogical role. The window planner prompt instructs: "Favor low budgets for title , agenda , transition , administrative , appendix , and r epe at ed recap slides ." and "Favor higher budgets for rich mechanism , comparison , result , diagram , chart , table , or s y n t h e s i s slides ." Budgets range from 0 to 5, and zero questions are explicitly acceptable, so generation effort concentrates on core pedagogical material.
requirements: Slide modality types and deck roles must be drawn from the fixed label vocabularies defined in the window planner prompt
constraints: Budgets are capped between 0 and 5 per slide, though the deck synthesis prompt notes some slides may deserve more than three questions

target_learning_goals: balanced question coverage aligned with instructional importance across heterogeneous slide types
examples: The reconciliation phase uses an action vocabulary of keep, reduce, expand, zero_out, and rewrite with a new question budget between 0 and 5 per slide

article_title: A Critical Narrative Synthesis of Psychological Correlates, Measurement, and Reported Findings on Conversational AI Engagement and Dependence-Related Constructs
citation: Yan D (2026). A critical narrative synthesis of psychological correlates, measurement, and reported findings on conversational AI engagement and dependence-related constructs. Front. Psychol. 17:1827795. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2026.1827795
title: Monitor conversational-AI use for well-being rather than diagnosing dependence from frequency, attachment, or platform use alone
description: For mental health and digital well-being, the review recommends monitoring rather than clinical thresholds: conversational AI may provide disclosure, perceived support, or temporary loneliness relief when human support is scarce. It states the current literature "does not justify diagnosing dependence from frequency, attachment, or platform use alone." Frequent use, reliance, or attachment should not be labeled dependence without impaired control or harm, while supportive experiences do not rule out dysregulation or substitution risk.
requirements: Assessment must separately evidence impaired control or functional harm before dependence labeling
constraints: Evidence for short-term benefits is limited and context dependent; no single platform feature has been shown to cause dependence
target_learners: Conversational-AI users, including students, companion-app users, and clinically vulnerable groups flagged for future study
target_learning_goals: Healthy calibration of AI engagement and preservation of human ties and independent judgment
examples: The review identifies anthropomorphic language, exclusivity, emotional reinforcement, continuity, and frictionless return as design features raising testable questions about deepening engagement

article_title: WrAFT: a Modularized Automated Writing Evaluation System for Argumentative Essays
citation: Adnan Labib, Yixuan Huang, Jiahui Wu, John Maurice Gayed, Zheng Yuan, Qiao Wang. (2026). WrAFT: a Modularized Automated Writing Evaluation System for Argumentative Essays. arXiv preprint. https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.14524
title: Modular decomposition of AWE into scoring, surface-level feedback, and deep-level feedback
description: The article organizes automated writing evaluation as a modular architecture that divides AWE tasks into three modules: scoring, surface-level feedback, and deep-level feedback. The abstract states that "WrAFT adopts a modular design by dividing the automated writing evaluation (AWE) tasks into scoring, surface-level feedback and deep-level feedback." Deep-level feedback is further split into macro feedback (paragraphing, text length, structure) and micro feedback (context-dependent grammar, clarity, coherence, argumentation, formality), each handled by a separate pipeline. The authors report this decomposition builds on Li and Ng (2024)'s layered proposal for AWE systems and supports specialized models per aspect.
requirements: Separate LLMs or pipelines tailored to each module, with validation schemes appropriate to each (benchmark scores for scoring, human raters for feedback)
constraints: The article notes specialized models handling different aspects can produce better assessments than unified approaches, but the system was developed and tested only on argumentative essays with writing prompts
target_learners: students writing argumentative essays
second language writers
target_learning_goals: essay scoring accuracy
surface-level error correction
higher-order writing qualities including organization, coherence and argumentation
examples: WrAFT instantiated the framework with fine-tuned GPT-4o for scoring, prompted GPT-4o for surface-level edits, and Claude 3.7 for macro and micro deep-level feedback pipelines.
key_sources: Adnan Labib, Yixuan Huang, Jiahui Wu, John Maurice Gayed, Zheng Yuan, Qiao Wang. (2026). WrAFT: a Modularized Automated Writing Evaluation System for Argumentative Essays. arXiv preprint. https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.14524

article_title: Teacher or Artificial Intelligence? The Effect of Decision-Making Agent on Junior High School Students’ Decision Acceptance: A Moderated Mediation Model
citation: Zhang Zhen; Fan Siyu; Qi Chunhui. (2026). Teacher or Artificial Intelligence? The Effect of Decision-Making Agent on Junior High School Students’ Decision Acceptance: A Moderated Mediation Model. Behavioral Sciences. https://doi.org/10.3390/bs16071227
title: Moderated mediation model of educational decision acceptance integrating authority acceptance theory and organizational justice theory
description: The article proposes and empirically validates a moderated mediation model in which the decision-making agent (teacher vs. AI) predicts students' decision acceptance both directly and indirectly through perceived fairness, with explanatory feedback moderating the first-stage path. Grounded in "authority acceptance theory and organizational justice theory", it treats perceived fairness as "a core mediator linking decision-maker characteristics and final decision acceptance". The model was tested with PROCESS Model 8 and "empirically validated (see Figure 4)" in a 2×2 experiment with 250 seventh-graders.
requirements: Measurement of perceived fairness and decision acceptance as distinct self-report constructs, with the decision-making agent manipulated as the independent variable
constraints: Conclusions are bounded by unfavorable evaluation outcomes (a score of 6/10); outcome favorability is proposed as an additional boundary condition for future models
target_learners: junior high school students (seventh grade)
target_learning_goals: students' acceptance of educational evaluation decisions and perceptions of fairness in human–AI educational decision-making
examples: The article tested the model with a 2 (teacher vs. AI) × 2 (explanation vs. without explanation) vignette experiment on mathematics homework grading among seventh-graders

article_title: LLMs Unplugged: Teaching Resources for a ChatGPT World
citation: Ben Swift. (2026). LLMs Unplugged: Teaching Resources for a ChatGPT World. 28th Australasian Computing Education Conference (ACE 2026). https://doi.org/10.1145/3786228.3786237
title: Modular unplugged lesson progression: two ordered Fundamentals lessons (Training, Generation) plus selectable Extensions covering scaling, output control, context and meaning, and model tuning
description: The LLMs Unplugged curriculum is organised into Fundamentals, which build on each other and “form the core of anyLLMs Unpluggedworkshop,” and Extensions that can be done in any order afterwards. Each Fundamentals lesson stands alone in a short session with minimal materials, and Extensions each explore one aspect of modern language models: pre-trained generation and trigrams (scaling), sampling and beam search (controlling output), context columns and word embeddings (context and meaning), and LoRA, RLHF and synthetic data (model tuning). A website toggle switches the Fundamentals between grid and bucket variants for different learners.
requirements: Extensions mostly require a model created in the Training lesson; Fundamentals should be completed in order
constraints: The limited vocabulary and repetitive nature of children's books is what makes exploring these concepts unplugged feasible; some Extensions are less battle-tested in classroom settings
target_learners: learners from high-school age upward
non-computing audiences with no programming assumed
target_learning_goals: understanding the training-to-generation pipeline
understanding context-length tradeoffs, sampling control, embeddings, fine-tuning and RLHF concepts
examples: A 90-minute outline covers Training, Generation and Pre-trained Generation, with Sampling added when two hours are available; delivered to groups of 5 to 50 participants

article_title: 'Advancing Problem-Based Learning in Biomedical Engineering in the Era of Generative AI'
citation: Micky C. Nnamdi, J. Ben Tamo, Benoit Marteau, Wenqi Shi, May D. Wang. (2026). Advancing Problem-Based Learning in Biomedical Engineering in the Era of Generative AI. arXiv. https://arxiv.org/abs/2503.16558
title: Modularized PBL+AI framework for biomedical engineering education
description: A four-module instructional architecture that embeds generative AI inside problem-based learning for biomedical AI courses. The article states that "The design positions GenAI as a knowledge summarization module that accelerates baseline learning and supports code optimization, while preserving the role of PBL in fostering innovation and synthesis." The modules are Problem Formation (authentic biomedical briefs with curated deidentified datasets), Knowledge Inquiry Supported by AI, Problem-Solving (prototyping with team-instrumented debugging), and Presentation (reports, demos, peer review). AI is framed as a scaffold and baseline assembler of existing knowledge rather than a shortcut to solutions.
requirements: Biomedical problem briefs anchored in real-world clinical or research scenarios with curated, deidentified datasets
Institutionally approved AI tools that have undergone security and privacy review
Instructor and TA facilitation with formative feedback at milestone stages
constraints: The article notes traditional PBL constraints historically limited activities to theoretical planning or preliminary prototypes; the framework addresses this with institutional compute infrastructure (PACE, industry partners) and standardized access policies
target_learners: undergraduate and graduate biomedical engineering students
interdisciplinary teams balancing ML/AI experience, biomedical knowledge, and programming proficiency
target_learning_goals: biomedical AI concepts and technical depth
critical thinking and literature critique
teamwork and scientific communication
ethical, regulatory, and clinical awareness
examples: Implemented 2021–2023 at Georgia Tech in BHI, MIP, and Biostatistics courses with milestones M1–M4 (knowledge inquiry, proposal, prototype and model card, final report and demo)

article_title: 'Architecting an AI-Driven Decision Support System for Enhanced Online Learning and Assessment'
citation: Mahamad, S.; Chin, Y.H.; Zulmuksah, N.I.N.; Haque, M.M.; Shaheen, M.; Nisar, K. (2025). Technical Review: Architecting an AI-Driven Decision Support System for Enhanced Online Learning and Assessment. Future Internet 2025, 17, 383. https://doi.org/10.3390/fi17090383
title: Modular four-module AI-DSS architecture for online learning and assessment
description: The review proposes a flexible, modular AI-driven decision support system architecture built around four main elements: data collection, AI processing, a decision-making core, and a user interface, integrated with existing LMSs via standards like Learning Tools Interoperability. As the article states, "this review puts forward a flexible, modular AI-DSS design built around four main elements: gathering data, processing with AI, a decision-making core, and an intuitive user interface". The data collection module aggregates performance, behavioral, demographic, and course metadata with preprocessing for GDPR/FERPA compliance; the AI processing module runs ML, NLP, knowledge-based, and deep learning streams; the decision engine generates personalized learning paths, automated grades, and feedback with explainability mechanisms; and a feedback loop channels user interactions back for continuous refinement.
requirements: Diverse, high-quality learner data (performance, behavioral, demographic, course metadata) sourced from LMS platforms
Integration with LMSs via standard APIs such as Learning Tools Interoperability
constraints: Deep learning components are computationally intensive, posing challenges for resource-constrained environments
Compliance with GDPR and FERPA requires anonymization and encryption in the data pipeline
target_learners: online learners in MOOCs, institutional LMSs, and adaptive learning environments
target_learning_goals: personalized learning pathways
automated and formative/summative assessment
timely actionable feedback
examples: The article contrasts the proposed architecture with Coursera's centralized ML recommendations and edX's LMS-integrated NLP grading, claiming federated learning and a hybrid RL-ML decision engine as innovations

article_title: The Power of Feedback
citation: Martínez Carrillo, E. (2018). Una aproximación a los estilos de retroalimentación en tutoría de trabajo de grado en educación superior. Tesis de maestría, Universidad Pedagógica Nacional, Bogotá. https://repository.upn.edu.co
title: Modelo de estilos de retroalimentación de trabajo de grado en educación superior
description: La tesis propone un modelo (Figura 15) que organiza la retroalimentación del tutor de trabajo de grado en 4 estilos definidos por dos dimensiones: el énfasis de la retroalimentación (en la tarea o en el proceso) y la cercanía psicológica (cálida o formal). La autora indica que los estilos cumplen "una noción diferenciadora de las conductas de los tutores" y "tiene un carácter neutral, donde no se presenta una jerarquía de un estilo sobre otro". El modelo se construyó a partir del análisis de enunciados de tutorías grabadas y se proyecta validarlo en otros contextos y niveles de formación.
requirements: Validación del modelo en otros contextos de tutoría y otros niveles de formación, según las proyecciones del estudio
Construcción futura de un instrumento que permita medir estilos en este contexto de tutoría
constraints: El estudio fue de carácter transversal, por lo que no se verificó la permanencia en el tiempo del comportamiento de los individuos
target_learners: Estudiantes de pregrado que desarrollan trabajos de grado
target_learning_goals: Retroalimentación formativa en el desarrollo del trabajo de grado
Comprensión del rol docente en tutoría
examples: Las tutorías de 6 docentes de pregrado de una universidad privada de Bogotá fueron grabadas en audio y sus enunciados codificados según las 5 categorías
key_sources: Martínez Carrillo, E. (2018). Una aproximación a los estilos de retroalimentación en tutoría de trabajo de grado en educación superior. Tesis de maestría, Universidad Pedagógica Nacional, Bogotá. https://repository.upn.edu.co

article_title: The Power of Feedback
citation: Martínez Carrillo, E. (2018). Una aproximación a los estilos de retroalimentación en tutoría de trabajo de grado en educación superior. Tesis de maestría, Universidad Pedagógica Nacional, Bogotá. https://repository.upn.edu.co
title: Modelo de retroalimentación de Hattie y Timperley (2007) con cuatro niveles: tarea, proceso, autorregulación y yo
description: La tesis adopta el modelo de Hattie y Timperley (2007) como marco para comprender la retroalimentación en tutoría. El modelo "propone 4 niveles de retroalimentación" descritos como "nivel de tarea; nivel de proceso o procedimientos necesarios para completar la tarea; nivel meta-cognitivo o de estrategias de autorregulación puestas en juego para avanzar en la consecución de la tarea; nivel personal, del yo". Cada nivel cumple funciones distintas: el de tarea es correctivo, el de proceso ofrece información paso a paso, el de autorregulación facilita la autoevaluación y el del yo contiene poca información de tarea.
requirements: Ubicar la retroalimentación en una perspectiva constructivista donde el estudiante asume un rol activo
constraints: Los comentarios del nivel del yo contienen poca información relacionada con la tarea y rara vez se convierten en mayor compromiso con el aprendizaje
target_learners: Estudiantes de educación superior en tutoría de trabajo de grado
target_learning_goals: Retroalimentación efectiva orientada a la tarea, el proceso y la autorregulación
examples: La tesis usa este modelo (Tabla 5) para definir las categorías de análisis de los enunciados de tutoría, distinguiendo énfasis en la tarea, en el proceso y en la autorregulación

article_title: ‘Models of’ versus ‘Models for’
citation: Gouvea, J., Passmore, C. (2017). 'Models of' versus 'Models for'. Science & Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11191-017-9884-4
title: The models of versus models for heuristic distinguishes representational from purpose-driven conceptions of models
description: The article presents a heuristic contrasting two ways of understanding models in science. Models can be understood in terms of how they represent phenomena in the world (models of), or with respect to the aims and intentions of a cognitive agent (models for). The authors present this contrast as a tool educators can use to notice and interpret how models are positioned in standards, curriculum, and classrooms.
requirements: Educators must examine standards, curriculum materials, and classroom practice through the lens of the aims and intentions of model users, not only representational accuracy.
constraints: The authors present the contrast as a heuristic, not a tested instructional intervention.
target_learners: K-12 science students
target_learning_goals: Understanding the role of models and modeling in science
examples: The authors use the heuristic to examine how the practice of developing and using models is positioned in the Framework for K-12 Science Education and the Next Generation Science Standards.

article_title: BEYOND EXPLICIT RULE LEARNING
citation: Robert M. DeKeyser. (1997). Beyond Explicit Rule Learning: Automatizing Second Language Morphosyntax. Studies in Second Language Acquisition, Volume 19, Issue 2. https://doi.org/10.1017/S0272263197002040
title: Modality-varied practice design: equal comprehension and production practice with rule-to-modality assignment varied between groups
description: This design pattern holds total practice constant while varying which rules are practiced in which modality. All subjects were taught the same rules and received the same amount of comprehension and production practice, but "which ruleswere practiced in comprehension and which in production varied between groups." Comprehension practice consisted of choosing between pictures to match a sentence; production practice consisted of typing the correct sentence corresponding to a picture. This allows skill-specificity of practice to be assessed.
requirements: A set of distinct rules that can be assigned differentially to comprehension and production practice
Learners at criterion on metalinguistic tests before practice begins
constraints: As implemented, the pattern was used with an artificial language and computer-controlled practice over 8 weeks
target_learners: adult second language learners
target_learning_goals: developing comprehension and production skill for specific morphosyntactic rules
examples: Comprehension practice consisted of choosing between pictures displayed on the computer screen to match a sentence; production practice consisted of typing the correct sentence corresponding to a picture

The framework structures both the 38-item survey instrument and the analysis of which strategies students find most beneficial within each interaction type.

examples: The 38-item survey instrument was structured around the three interaction categories, with strategy items grouped under learner-to-learner, learner-to-instructor, and learner-to-content engagement.

article_title: Effects of mobile-app learning diaries vs online training on specific self-regulated learning components
citation: Broadbent, J., Panadero, E. & Fuller-Tyszkiewicz, M. (2020). Effects of mobile-app learning diaries vs online training on specific self-regulated learning components. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-020-09781-6

The diary asks about affect (e.g. "How do you feel at moment?" with rated items such as Active and Determined), motivation (e.g. "Today, I am studying because I find the topic very interesting"), and learning strategies (e.g. "Today, I have made a time schedule"), using Likert-type response scales. article_title: Long-Term Effects of Strategic Reading Instruction in the Intermediate Elementary Grades
citation: Droop, M.; van Elsäcker, W.; Voeten, M. J. M.; Verhoeven, L. (2016). Long-Term Effects of Strategic Reading Instruction in the Intermediate Elementary Grades. Journal of Research on Educational Effectiveness. https://doi.org/10.1080/19345747.2015.1065528

description: The article recommends that strategy instruction be embedded in meaningful contexts: "reading aloud children's books may offer a rich and meaningful context to model the strategies," and "Strategies modeled during read-aloud sessions may be applied during independent reading and transferred to content area reading." Teachers not only modeled the strategy but explicitly explained why they used it, following the cognitive apprenticeship principle of teacher-as-model. This contrasts with control curricula where students read identical short texts and answered written questions without a meaningful context.

Strategy application and transfer
examples: Manuals for each read-aloud book highlighted possible modeling moments with example sentences per strategy (Appendix A of the online supplement)

The model was defined from a conceptual framework and a systematic literature review, then instantiated in a virtual learning environment for validation through a case study comparing three teaching methodologies.

article_title: A Framework for Designing Scaffolds That Improve Motivation and Cognition
citation: Belland Brian R., Kim ChanMin, Hannafin Michael J. (2013). A Framework for Designing Scaffolds That Improve Motivation and Cognition. Educational Psychologist. https://doi.org/10.1080/00461520.2013.838920
title: Motivational scaffolding framework: six motivationally grounded goals for scaffold design in PBL
description: The article's central framework holds that scaffolds in problem-based learning environments should be designed around six motivational goals. As the authors state, "our framework posits that motivation-enhancing scaffolds in PBL should promote these six goals that are broadly supported by motivation theories: establish task value, promote mastery goals, promote belonging, promote emotion regulation, promote expectancy for success, and promote autonomy." Achieving these goals is expected to raise behavioral, cognitive, and emotional engagement, since "motivation is a basis for subsequent engagement." The framework is elaborated into seventeen numbered scaffolding strategies in Table 1.
requirements: Scaffolds must be designed intentionally to encourage motivation rather than assuming authentic problems automatically engage students
Sustained situational interest requires content knowledge and a belief in task value
constraints: Framework addresses computer-based scaffolds in PBL; teacher scaffolds are acknowledged but beyond the article's scope
The article synthesizes motivation theories, adopting single terms where constructs differ in nuance, to keep focus on design implications
target_learners: K-12 and university students working on authentic, ill-structured problems in PBL environments
target_learning_goals: Sustained engagement and motivation during extended problem-based learning
Deep conceptual learning and problem-solving in authentic inquiry
examples: Table 1 enumerates strategies per goal, e.g., prompting students to choose a problem aspect connecting to their interests, and using noncontrolling language in scaffolding messages
key_sources: Belland Brian R., Kim ChanMin, Hannafin Michael J. (2013). A Framework for Designing Scaffolds That Improve Motivation and Cognition. Educational Psychologist. https://doi.org/10.1080/00461520.2013.838920

citation: Martínez Bernal, J. A. (2017). Efecto del automonitoreo en el logro de aprendizaje, su relación con el estilo de aprendizaje y estilo cognitivo en un ambiente web de aprendizaje. Tesis doctoral, Universidad Pedagógica Nacional. https://biblioteca.upn.edu.co
title: Modelo de integración entre metacognición y autorregulación con el monitoreo metacognitivo como eje
description: La tesis construye un marco teórico que recoge la metacognición vista como proceso de monitoreo y control y la integra con el ciclo del aprendizaje autorregulado. Según el texto, se analiza el ciclo del aprendizaje autorregulado y "se presenta un modelo de integración que toma como eje el monitoreo metacognitivo". El modelo articula las fases de previsión, implementación y autorreflexión, y reconoce tres momentos clave para promover el automonitoreo: la autoevaluación, el monitoreo de las estrategias y de su implementación, y el monitoreo de los esfuerzos de adaptación. Este modelo fundamenta el diseño de los mensajes metacognitivos del andamiaje computacional.
requirements: Comprender el ciclo de la metacognición a partir de la interacción entre el nivel objeto y el nivel meta, activada por el flujo de información generado por las estrategias de monitoreo y control
constraints: El texto señala que la mejor estrategia para promover el automonitoreo en ambientes virtuales parece todavía no estar clara, e incluso que esta acción podría competir con el propio proceso de aprendizaje

target_learning_goals: Desarrollo de habilidades metacognitivas de automonitoreo y autorregulación del aprendizaje

title: Sustain anti-bullying interventions with monthly follow-ups and a fluid learner contract
description: After the initial five-week intervention, the class teacher holds monthly check-ups reviewing the bullying lexicon, incidents without naming or blaming, role-plays, and the anti-bullying contract, amending it as needed. The stated aim was "to keep the contract ﬂuid and responsive to learner needs" and to reinforce long-term institutional support, because the literature suggests schools with high bullying prevalence often lack a culture that supports interventions over time.

A learner-signed contract aligned with the school's anti-bullying policy
constraints: The article notes schools with high prevalence levels often do not have a culture that supports interventions over time

target_learning_goals: Long-term retention of bullying knowledge and defending behaviour
examples: Suggested check-up topics included review of the bullying lexicon, discussion of incidents, role-playing scenarios, and creating amendments to the contract if needed

article_title: Adult age differences in the effects of processing on storage in working memory: A meta-analysis.
citation: Jaroslawska, A. J., & Rhodes, S. (2019). Adult Age Diﬀerences in the Eﬀects of Processing on Storage in Working Memory: A Meta-Analysis. Psychology & Aging. https://doi.org/10.1037/pag0000358
title: Task-related moderator framework for age differences in storage-plus-processing working memory costs
description: The article organizes the contradictory literature on aging and dual task costs around five candidate task-related moderators: "1) the impact of equating (i.e., titrating) single task performance across age groups before concurrent tasks are combined, 2) whether the stimulus material used in the tasks is verbal or nonverbal in nature (and whether there is an overlap between domains of storage and processing components), 3) the processing requirements of the secondary task, 4) whether the input/output modality for the storage task matches the input/output modality for the processing task, and 5) whether the processing task imposes a response deadline." The framework explains why prior studies reached conflicting conclusions about disproportionate age-related dual task costs, and the meta-analysis tests each moderator against the pooled effect sizes.
requirements: Studies comparing healthy younger adults (mean age 30 or under) with healthy older adults (mean age 60 or over) on a storage task performed alone and with a concurrent processing task
constraints: The article reports clear evidence of moderation only for titration and task domain; for the remaining moderators "there is no clear evidence of moderation by the other factors"
Studies comparing different levels of memory updating (e.g., n-back) were excluded from the synthesis
target_learners: Healthy younger and older adults in working memory studies
target_learning_goals: Short-term storage and concurrent processing of information in working memory
examples: The meta-analysis coded each included study for titration, stimulus domain, processing task type (cognitive, sensorimotor, or another storage load), modality overlap, and response deadline, then entered these as moderators in meta-regressions
key_sources: Jaroslawska, A. J., & Rhodes, S. (2019). Adult Age Diﬀerences in the Eﬀects of Processing on Storage in Working Memory: A Meta-Analysis. Psychology & Aging. https://doi.org/10.1037/pag0000358

article_title: Can Online Peer Assessment be Trusted?
citation: Bouzidi, L., & Jaillet, A. (2009). Can Online Peer Assessment be Trusted?. Educational Technology & Society, 12(4), 257-268. https://www.ifets.info/
title: Moodle workshop module as the online peer assessment platform
description: The experiment's observation and marking tool was the "workshop" module of the Moodle platform, into which anonymised digitalised exam papers were placed for peer and teacher marking with a defined marking scheme. The article reports that "This module is stable and presents a user-friendly environment", but identifies a weakness in its marking tool: the scale scheme was implemented as option buttons from "excellent" to "very poor", a method the authors say can lead to errors.
requirements: A clearly defined marking scheme, assessment criteria, and parameters for mark assessment and paper distribution prepared on the virtual campus
constraints: The module's option-button marking tool had a weakness that could introduce marking errors

target_learning_goals: online assessment of classroom exam papers with anonymity and multiple assessors

article_title: Behavioral economics of education
citation: Alexander Koch, Julia Nafziger, Helena Skyt Nielsen. (2015). Behavioral economics of education. Journal of Economic Behavior & Organization 115 (2015) 3–17. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jebo.2014.09.005
title: Motivational crowding out: extrinsic rewards can undermine long-term intrinsic motivation via self-confidence inference
description: The review presents Benabou and Tirole's (2003) principal-agent account of motivational crowding out, in which a child with imperfect knowledge of her own ability infers from an offered reward that the principal (parent or teacher) believes her ability is low: 'a higher reward reduces the self-conﬁdence of the child and thereby its intrinsic motivation'. The reward works in the short run by raising the direct payoff from success, but once withdrawn, effort falls because intrinsic motivation was eroded. The review frames this as a key pitfall of incentive provision in education, complementing psychology evidence on crowding out.
requirements: The mechanism requires that the child has imperfect knowledge of her ability and infers the principal's private information from the size of the reward
constraints: The account is a theoretical model interpretation discussed by the review, not a tested experiment; the review notes psychology meta-analyses reach conflicting conclusions about crowding out
target_learners: school students whose motivation is managed by parents or teachers
target_learning_goals: sustaining intrinsic motivation and effort for educational tasks
examples: The review discusses a parent or teacher rewarding a child for studying rather than watching TV, where the reward signals low perceived ability and lowers self-confidence
key_sources: Alexander Koch, Julia Nafziger, Helena Skyt Nielsen. (2015). Behavioral economics of education. Journal of Economic Behavior & Organization 115 (2015) 3–17. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jebo.2014.09.005

article_title: Message design for mobile learning: Learning theories, human cognition and design principles
citation: Wang, M. & Shen, R. (2012). Message design for mobile learning: Learning theories, human cognition and design principles. British Journal of Educational Technology, 43(4), 561-575. https://doi.org/10.1111/j.1467-8535.2011.01214.x
title: Typology of mobile devices by information delivery type
description: The article classifies mobile devices into four general categories of information exchange: stand-alone devices, network-centered devices, mobile computers and web portals. Table 1 defines each type by its core mode of information delivery and transmission, gives example devices (iPods, iPhones, laptops, ChromeOS, iPad), and lists the learning activities each supports, such as podcasts on take-away devices or collaborative learning via ad hoc networks. Instructional designers are urged to consider which devices they plan to leverage, as "not all devices provide the same services".
requirements: Designers need a basic understanding of the information delivery capabilities of each device type and the appropriateness of each type for different environments and content
target_learners: mobile learners using varied devices in formal and informal settings
target_learning_goals: matching mLearning content and activities to device capabilities
examples: Table 1 maps stand-alone devices to podcasts and instructional guides, network-centered devices to collaborative learning, mobile computers to portable interactive multimedia, and web portals to thin-client access to online services

article_title: Let me be your guide: physical guidance improves spatial learning for older adults with simulated low vision
citation: Barhorst-Cates Erica M., Rand Kristina M., Creem-Regehr Sarah H. (2017). Let Me be Your Guide: Physical Guidance Improves Spatial Learning for Older Adults with Simulated Low Vision. Experimental Brain Research. https://doi.org/10.1007/s00221-017-5063-8
title: Mobility-monitoring account: attentional demands of safe mobility compete with spatial learning during low-vision navigation
description: The account holds that navigating with severely degraded vision requires detecting and avoiding obstacles, and that "the attention needed to maintain safe mobility detracts from the pool of attentional resources available for spatial learning of the environment." Physical guidance operates at the level of guiding mobility rather than navigational choices, proposing to free attentional resources at encoding, which distinguishes it from GPS-style aids that divide attention and impair learning. The study's pointing-error results support the account, though the RT cognitive-load measure did not vary between conditions.
requirements: A task in which mobility monitoring (obstacle avoidance, stability) imposes attentional demands separate from route-choice guidance
constraints: The expected RT difference between guidance conditions was not observed in older adults, and the article states further consideration of these lack of differences is needed
target_learners: older adults
low-vision navigators
younger adults under degraded viewing
target_learning_goals: spatial learning of environments during active navigation
examples: Rand et al. (2015) showed younger adults' low-vision spatial learning improved with a physical guide, partially explained by attentional demands measured via auditory reaction time

article_title: What explains the link between childhood ADHD and adolescent depression? Investigating the role of peer relationships and academic attainment
citation: Powell V, Riglin L, Hammerton G, Eyre O, Martin J, Anney R, Thapar A, Rice F. (2020). What explains the link between childhood ADHD and adolescent depression? Investigating the role of peer relationships and academic attainment. European Child & Adolescent Psychiatry. https://doi.org/10.1007/s00787-019-01463-w
title: Monitor children with ADHD for depression and target peer relationships and academic attainment in prevention
description: The article recommends that due to increased depression risk, children with ADHD should be monitored for depressive symptoms, and that interventions targeting peer relationships and academic attainment may reduce depression risk beyond treating core ADHD symptoms. The authors state that "the development of interventions targeting the impact of children's ADHD on their peer relationships and academic attainment may have the added benefit of reducing depression risk". Existing psychosocial interventions targeting social and academic skills may have potential but "this needs to be formally tested".
requirements: Formal testing of whether existing psychosocial interventions reduce depression risk is needed before firm recommendations
constraints: Mediation findings are observational; causal intervention effects have not been demonstrated
target_learners: children and adolescents with ADHD
target_learning_goals: depression prevention
peer relationship skills
academic attainment
examples: The study used ALSPAC cohort data with mediators measured at 16 years between exposure (7.5 years) and outcome (17.5 years)
