article_title: Use of Audiovisual Information in Speech Perception by Prelingually Deaf Children with Cochlear Implants: A First Report
citation: Lorin Lachs, David B. Pisoni, and Karen Iler Kirk. (2001). Use of Audiovisual Information in Speech Perception by Prelingually Deaf Children with Cochlear Implants. Ear Hear. 2001 June ; 22(3): 236–251. https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/
title: Modality-neutral articulatory information account of audiovisual speech perception and its development through perceptual learning
description: The article frames audiovisual integration as the recovery of the talker's underlying articulations: "the sensory and perceptual information relevant for speech perception is said to be modality-neutral, because it can be carried by more than one sensory modality." Because acoustic and optic specifications arise from the same articulatory gestures, they are lawfully related, and perceptual learning exploits these co-occurrences to build multimodal representations of speech. For prelingually deaf children with implants, these learning processes begin only after implantation, and the article interprets individual differences in audiovisual gain as reflecting the degree to which children have internalized the commonalities between auditory and visual information about speech.
requirements: Perception of information about the articulations of the vocal tract in at least one sensory modality
constraints: For prelingually deafened children with cochlear implants, audiovisual learning processes only begin to develop after they receive their implant and begin to experience lawful relationships between vision and sound
target_learners: Prelingually deafened children with cochlear implants
target_learning_goals: Spoken language comprehension and spoken word recognition through combined auditory and visual speech perception

article_title: Teacher Scaffolding in Small-Group Work: An Intervention Study
citation: J. van de Pol, M. Volman, F. Oort, J. Beishuizen. (2014). Teacher scaffolding in small-group work: an intervention study. Journal of the Learning Sciences. https://doi.org/10.1080/10508406.2013.805300
title: Model of Contingent Teaching (MCT): a four-step model for contingent scaffolding in small-group work
description: The model of contingent teaching (MCT) operationalizes scaffolding as adapting support contingently to student needs by first diagnosing their current understanding. The article describes it as "a model of contingent teaching (MCT) with the following 4 steps: diagnostic strategies, checking of diagnoses, giving contingent support, and checking of student learning." The professional development program evaluated in the study was based on this model, and teachers' frequency and quality of use of the 4 steps were compared between participants and non-participants.
requirements: Teachers must use the four steps in sequence: diagnostic strategies, checking of diagnoses, giving contingent support, and checking of student learning.
constraints: The article notes that future use of the MCT works "provided that teachers' understanding of scaffolding is closely monitored."
target_learners: Students in prevocational education working in small groups
target_learning_goals: Social studies content understanding, here the European Union project
examples: Seventeen of 30 teachers participated in a professional development program based on the MCT while teaching the same 5-lesson project on the European Union.

article_title: Defensive and Expansive Cycles of Learning: A Study of Home Care Encounters
citation: Nummijoki, J., Engeström, Y., & Sannino, A. (2018). Defensive and expansive cycles of learning: A study of home care encounters. Journal of the Learning Sciences, 27(2), 224-264. https://doi.org/10.1080/10508406.2017.1412970
title: Mobility Agreement practice for embedding physical exercises in home care visits
description: The Mobility Agreement is a plan negotiated and prepared jointly by the home care worker and the elderly client, with the objective of promoting daily exercises such as stand-ups from a chair, balancing exercises and taking the stairs. It is "primarily an embodied agreement that is re-enacted within regular encounters, in joint physical actions and accompanying verbal and gestural exchanges." It is supported by an illustrated booklet graphically describing typical exercises, recorded in the client's care plan, and designed to break the vicious cycle of fear-of-falling by integrating mobility work into daily chores at home.
requirements: Joint preparation and negotiation between client and home care worker
Integration into regular recurring home care visits
Support of an illustrated exercise booklet
Recording in the client's care plan
constraints: Its potentials and benefits are only disclosed when the dominant script of home care encounters is qualitatively transformed
Each client's life situation is different and the practice must be creatively adapted
Embedding and anchoring exercise actions into daily routines takes time and needs persistent pursuit
target_learners: Elderly home care clients with reduced physical mobility
Home care workers in municipal services
target_learning_goals: Improving muscle strength, balance and functionality
Rediscovering the potentials of one's body
Breaking the vicious cycle of fear of falling and activity restriction
examples: In Case D, the home care team had continuously assessed the client's resources and changed the Mobility Agreement depending on progress and seasons, such as more indoor exercises during winter

article_title: Identifying Representational Competence With Multi-Representational Displays
citation: Mike Stieff, Mary Hegarty, Ghislain Deslongchamps. (2011). Identifying Representational Competence with Multi-Representational Displays. Cognition and Instruction. https://doi.org/10.1080/07370008.2011.558308
title: Multi-representational molecular mechanics Flash animation with model, general equation, numerical equation, and graph
description: A set of three interactive Flash animations adapted from courseware for teaching computer-based molecular modeling to undergraduate chemistry students. Each animation displayed four synchronized representations of a molecular mechanics energy term: "a ball-and-stick model of the molecular system, the general mathematical model used to model its energy, a specific numerical example of the equation, and a graph of the equation". The representations were linked via a mouse-driven slider so users could change the molecular model and observe the resulting energy change on the graph and numerical example.

constraints: The animations were converted to 17 static frames per animation for eye tracking, interacted with via keyboard arrow keys.
target_learners: undergraduate organic chemistry students
target_learning_goals: understanding molecular mechanics energy terms and the relationship between molecular spatial conformations and energy
examples: Three animations modeled the stretch, angle bend, and dihedral energy terms of the molecular mechanics equation.

citation: Stahl, G. (2012). Traversing planes of learning. Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning, 7, 467–473. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-012-9159-7
title: Model of collaborative knowledge building across interconnected planes
description: Figure 3 presents "A model of collaborative knowledge building", adapted from Stahl 2006 Ch. 9, indicating typical processes on each primary plane and "possible paths of influence or connection, as events unfolding on the different planes interpenetrate each other". The boxes and arrows operationalize an infinitely complex matter for concrete analytic work. The article states the figure sketches constraints and flows of influence without claiming to explain or model them.

constraints: The figure is not meant to reify different levels or activities and does not claim to explain or model the processes

target_learning_goals: understanding how collaborative knowledge building takes place across individual, small-group and community planes

article_title: Leveraging mobile eye-trackers to capture joint visual attention in co-located collaborative learning groups
citation: Schneider, B., Sharma, K., Cuendet, S., Zufferey, G., Dillenbourg, P., & Pea, R. (2018). Leveraging mobile eye-trackers to capture joint visual attention in co-located collaborative learning groups. International Journal of Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning, 13(3), 241–261. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-018-9281-2
title: Mobile eye-tracking methodology for capturing joint visual attention in co-located groups

A shared task on a Tangible User Interface around which gaze can be coordinated

citation: Dina Soliman, Xueqi Feng, Marlene Scardamalia, Carol Chan. (2026). Knowledge building–modeling: Grade 5 students creating models, using discourse analytics, and advancing systems thinking. Intern. J. Comput.-Support. Collab. Learn. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-026-09493-8

A codesign process between teacher and researchers to create the markers

collective model improvement
sustained idea improvement

article_title: Development of legal expertise
citation: Glöckner, A., Towfigh, E., & Traxler, C. (2013). Development of legal expertise. Instructional Science, 41, 989–1007. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-013-9266-5
title: Investing time and money in repeated mock exam practice is worthwhile, yielding roughly 0.5% improvement per exam in general and per area-specific exam
description: The authors conclude that "the money and time they invest in repeatedly solving mock exams is worthwhile." They report "an (area-of-law) unspeciﬁc practice effect, in that each exam increases the performance score by roughly 0.5 %" plus an area-specific repetition effect of also roughly 0.5 % per practice exam, while noting that "incremental improvements are relatively small."
requirements: Practice must be combined with normal studying, as the predicted effects apply to students combining mock exam participation with normal studying
constraints: The per-exam improvement amount decreases somewhat over time, particularly for persons with low initial performance
target_learners: advanced law students entering the practice exam phase
target_learning_goals: improving performance in solving complex legal cases
examples: The University of Münster's Written Examination Course offers unpublished exams from earlier state exams, corrected by senior teaching assistants and discussed in a 2-hour class

article_title: Fifth graders study videos faster than illustrated texts: Studying rate, review strategies, and learning implications
citation: Mikko Haavisto, Tomi Jaakkola. (2026). Fifth graders study videos faster than illustrated texts: Studying rate, review strategies, and learning implications. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-026-09817-z
title: The modality effect grounded in cognitive load theory, with hybrid learner control as a dual-advantage design
description: The article frames its study within the modality effect: "learning from multiple sensory modalities (e.g., viewing pictures while listening to narration) produces better learning than learning from a single modality (e.g., viewing pictures and written text)". It grounds this in cognitive load theory, since speech comprehension is innate while reading requires recalling learned letter and word patterns, and in split-attention and dual working-memory capacity accounts. It also describes hybrid learner control, in which videos continue in a system-controlled manner while providing flexible navigation, as a dual advantage over pure system or pure learner control.
requirements: Materials must offer hybrid learner control, combining automatic progression with navigation options such as pause, play, rewind, and skip
constraints: The article notes meta-analyses indicate no evidence for narration outperforming written text in studies with learner-controlled narrations that did not automatically progress
target_learners: Primary school children, specifically fifth graders
target_learning_goals: Science learning from multimedia materials, including retention and transfer
examples: The experiment used learner-controlled video and illustrated text materials with identical word and picture content (1383 words, 40 pictures) segmented into slides, studied during two 45-minute science lessons with 12 minutes of learning time
key_sources: Mikko Haavisto, Tomi Jaakkola. (2026). Fifth graders study videos faster than illustrated texts: Studying rate, review strategies, and learning implications. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-026-09817-z

article_title: How does monitoring set the stage for adaptive regulation or maladaptive behavior in collaborative learning?
citation: Sobocinski, M., Järvelä, S., Malmberg, J., Dindar, M., Isosalo, A., & Noponen, K. (2020). How does monitoring set the stage for adaptive regulation or maladaptive behavior in collaborative learning? Metacognition and Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-020-09224-w
title: Three-dimensional coding framework for monitoring events (target, valence, phase) to identify adaptive regulation and maladaptive behavior in collaborative learning
description: The study contributes an empirical framework, built on the socially shared regulation of learning (SSRL) framework, for identifying adaptive regulation and maladaptive behavior from process data. Monitoring events are coded on "target (cognition, motivation, emotion, behavior), valence (positive or negative), and phase in which monitoring occurs (task definition, goals and planning, task enactment, or reflection)". Combining valence with the group's reaction or lack of reaction defines on-track, adaptive, and maladaptive sequences: negative-valence monitoring followed by a reaction is adaptive, and without a reaction is maladaptive.
requirements: Monitoring events must be verbalized and observable in video data, so groups' monitoring can be identified and coded from utterances
constraints: No off-task behavior was found in the data because the task was an exam situation with a time limit
Monitoring behavior was not coded for valence due to the hands-on nature of the task
target_learners: high school students in advanced physics courses working in collaborative groups
target_learning_goals: effective socially shared regulation of learning during collaborative tasks
examples: In the coded example of an adaptive sequence, a student asked "Should we evaluate the correctness of the result?" and group members responded, keeping the group in the task enactment phase

article_title: Motivating Motivation Regulation Research—An Evidence and Gap Map Approach
citation: Maike Trautner, Carola Grunschel, Malte Schwinger. (2025). Motivating Motivation Regulation Research—An Evidence and Gap Map Approach. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-025-10019-1
title: Motivation regulation as conscious, deliberate control of one's motivation, distinguished from motivational monitoring and from automatic underlying motivational processes
description: The review organizes the field around Wolters' (2003) definition of motivation regulation as "activities through which individuals purposefully act to initiate, maintain, or supplement their willingness to start, to provide work toward, or to complete a particular activity or goal". It distinguishes motivation(al) control (maintaining or changing motivation) from motivational monitoring (observing and becoming aware of one's motivational states and needs), and separates deliberate regulation from underlying processes such as causal attributions and value appraisals that occur more or less automatically. Recent definitions add a qualitative dimension: learners may lack not enough motivation but the right type of motivation, where task-motivation misfit can produce less efficient approaches and poorer performance.
requirements: Applies to learners' consciously and deliberately implemented thoughts and behaviors targeting underlying motivational processes, not automatic motivational states themselves.
constraints: The review notes the term is often used for the full monitoring-plus-control sequence but sometimes synonymously with motivational control only.
target_learners: school and university students studying in formal and informal learning contexts
target_learning_goals: initiating, maintaining, and supplementing motivation for studying and goal completion
examples: The review includes studies on interest regulation when defined as conscious action or thought to change one's own motivation, and excludes studies of motivation regulation styles from self-determination theory's organismic integration theory.
key_sources: Maike Trautner, Carola Grunschel, Malte Schwinger. (2025). Motivating Motivation Regulation Research—An Evidence and Gap Map Approach. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-025-10019-1

article_title: Motivating Motivation Regulation Research—An Evidence and Gap Map Approach
citation: Maike Trautner, Carola Grunschel, Malte Schwinger. (2025). Motivating Motivation Regulation Research—An Evidence and Gap Map Approach. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-025-10019-1
title: Motivation regulation strategies span interest enhancement, goal-based self-talk, proximal goal setting, self-consequating, environmental control, and use of social resources
description: The review enumerates the families of motivation regulation strategies documented in the literature: enhancing situational interest or personal significance (e.g., turning a task into a game), goal-based self-talk (mastery, performance-approach, and performance-avoidance self-talk), proximal goal setting (splitting large tasks into smaller, more easily reachable tasks), self-consequating (promising oneself rewards), environmental control (excluding distractions), and using social resources (joining fellow students for group studying). Strategies target different motivational experiences such as task value or success expectancy; for example, self-consequating targets extrinsic aspects of task completion while situational interest enhancement aims at intrinsic motivation.
requirements: Effective use requires procedural and conditional strategy knowledge about how strategies work and when they apply, and strategies must match the respective motivational problem.
constraints: Strategies need to be applied thoroughly in a qualitatively good manner, not merely frequently.
target_learners: school and university students regulating their own motivation for studying
target_learning_goals: enhancing, maintaining, or changing motivation for tedious or difficult learning tasks
examples: The review cites Schwinger et al. (2009) reporting correlations with effort expenditure for eight different motivational strategies, with a positive relationship for six strategies and no significant relationship for two.
key_sources: Maike Trautner, Carola Grunschel, Malte Schwinger. (2025). Motivating Motivation Regulation Research—An Evidence and Gap Map Approach. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-025-10019-1

article_title: Motivating Motivation Regulation Research—An Evidence and Gap Map Approach
citation: Maike Trautner, Carola Grunschel, Malte Schwinger. (2025). Motivating Motivation Regulation Research—An Evidence and Gap Map Approach. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-025-10019-1
title: Five research traditions overlap conceptually with motivation regulation: self-regulated learning, metacognition, emotion regulation, resource management, and volitional control
description: The review maps the conceptual neighborhood of motivation regulation, stating that "several broader research areas share conceptual overlap with motivation regulation—namely self-regulated learning, emotion regulation, volitional control, resource management, and metacognition". Within self-regulated learning, motivation regulation is one regulated domain alongside cognition, behavior, and context; metacognition covers motivation regulation when the object of monitoring and control is motivation; emotion regulation operates in parallel and in service of motivation regulation, with metamotivational feelings such as boredom or frustration linking the two; resource management includes motivation as an internal resource; and volitional control shields set intentions from competing desires. The review includes studies from these traditions when they explicitly reference motivational processes.
requirements: Inclusion requires an explicit reference to motivational processes when studies come from the intersecting traditions.
constraints: The review explicitly does not draw clear theoretical boundaries between motivation and emotion regulation, noting research has mainly been conducted in a siloed fashion.
target_learners: learners in formal and informal academic settings studied across these traditions
target_learning_goals: regulating motivation, emotion, cognition, resources, and intentions during learning
examples: The review excludes volitional strategies such as implementation intentions unless they clearly aim at building and maintaining intentions and goals for studying rather than shielding them.
key_sources: Maike Trautner, Carola Grunschel, Malte Schwinger. (2025). Motivating Motivation Regulation Research—An Evidence and Gap Map Approach. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-025-10019-1

article_title: Motivating Motivation Regulation Research—An Evidence and Gap Map Approach
citation: Maike Trautner, Carola Grunschel, Malte Schwinger. (2025). Motivating Motivation Regulation Research—An Evidence and Gap Map Approach. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-025-10019-1
title: Interactive evidence and gap maps of motivation regulation research, built with EPPI-Mapper, with the underlying dataset released on OSF
description: The review's central artifact is a pair of interactive evidence and gap maps built with the EPPI-Mapper tool. The maps are matrices in which "Larger 'bubbles' in cells represent larger numbers of studies available, while smaller or non-existent bubbles indicate absence of evidence", with bubble color indicating how motivation regulation was operationalized and clickable cells exporting the references of the studies concerned. One map plots educational settings, study designs, and motivation regulation contexts against variables examined, split by reported relation direction; the second maps the sources of knowledge (settings, designs, operationalizations) against contexts. Maps can be filtered by analogue versus digital settings, questionnaire type, and level of analysis.
requirements: The dataset for creating the maps is obtainable from the project's OSF page together with a tutorial on how to create one's own map.
constraints: Relation directions in the maps are summaries of relations reported in studies, not statistical aggregations of effect sizes.
target_learners: researchers, university and school teachers seeking overviews of motivation regulation evidence
target_learning_goals: rapid identification of existing evidence, gaps, and studies relevant to specific samples, methods, or contexts
examples: The preregistered search covered EBSCO, PubPsych, BASE, Web of Science, ProQuest, Scopus, Science Direct, Google Scholar, ERIC, dissertation databases, conference programs, and manual reference searches, yielding N = 289 included studies.

article_title: Teacher Emotional Competence: A Conceptual Model
citation: Elena Savina, Caroline Fulton, Christina Beaton. (2025). Teacher Emotional Competence: A Conceptual Model. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-025-10018-2
title: Use the teacher emotional competence model as a springboard for developing emotional training programs and guiding assessment of teachers' emotional skills
description: The article's forward-looking recommendation is that its conceptual model should drive the design of teacher emotional training and assessment. Because existing training targeted generic emotional skills without delineating how they meet the profession's emotional demands, the authors argue training should be calibrated to the eight profession-specific competencies and their discrete skills. As the abstract states, "The proposed model of teacher emotional competence can be used as a springboard to develop emotional training programs and guide assessment practices aimed at the evaluation of teachers' emotional skills." The model can inform teacher preparation, professional development, and evaluation of teachers' preparedness for the emotional demands of teaching.
requirements: Training should target the specific emotional skills pertinent to the teaching profession rather than generic emotional skills
constraints: The model itself has not been empirically validated as a training framework in this article
target_learners: pre-service teachers in teacher education programs
in-service teachers in professional development
target_learning_goals: developing teachers' emotional competence for instruction, classroom management, and well-being
examples: The review documents existing training studies of emotion identification, empathy, regulation, coping, and mindfulness as the evidence base the model would refine
key_sources: Elena Savina, Caroline Fulton, Christina Beaton. (2025). Teacher Emotional Competence: A Conceptual Model. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-025-10018-2

article_title: Shunned and Admired: Montessori, Self-Determination, and a Case for Radical School Reform
citation: Angeline S. Lillard. (2019). Shunned and Admired: Montessori, Self-Determination, and a Case for Radical School Reform. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-019-09483-3
title: Self-determination as Montessori's central premise, with evidence-based corollaries
description: This framework holds that Montessori's central premise is independence or self-determination, from which several research-aligned features follow as natural corollaries: free choice, interesting work (aided by embodied cognition and interconnection), deep concentrated attention developing executive function, intrinsic rather than extrinsic rewards, warm teacher–child relationships, and natural peer engagement in an orderly environment. The article states that "self-determination requires that children choose their own activities" and maps these prerequisites and consequences in Fig. 2, arguing each is supported by educational psychology research.
requirements: Children must be able to choose their own activities in a prepared environment for self-determined learning to occur
constraints: The article presents this as an interpretive alignment framework, not a directly tested causal model
target_learners: children from birth to 18
target_learning_goals: intrinsic motivation
executive function
academic and social–emotional development
examples: The article maps the corollaries in Fig. 2: interesting work, embodied cognition, interconnected work, intrinsic rewards, work with peers in 3-year age groups, teacher warmth and direction, and order and organization
key_sources: Angeline S. Lillard. (2019). Shunned and Admired: Montessori, Self-Determination, and a Case for Radical School Reform. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-019-09483-3

article_title: Shunned and Admired: Montessori, Self-Determination, and a Case for Radical School Reform
citation: Angeline S. Lillard. (2019). Shunned and Admired: Montessori, Self-Determination, and a Case for Radical School Reform. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-019-09483-3
title: The Montessori education system (birth to 18)
description: Montessori is a system of education for children from birth to 18, developed by an Italian physician through observations between 1890 and 1952. It involves "3-year age groupings (0 –3, 3 –6, and so on)" with carefully developed apparatus for each age group, an interconnected network of materials across all curriculum areas, and a teacher whose role is not to impart information but to connect children to an environment where self-guided learning occurs. Its central premise is that children are active learners with intrinsic motivation who develop themselves when adults do not interfere and they can concentrate on meaningful work.
requirements: AMI-recognized implementations require AMI-trained teachers, a full set of approved materials, specific age divisions, 3-hour morning and 2–3-hour afternoon work periods, and one trained teacher with 24–35 children per class
constraints: Implementation quality varies significantly (Daoust 2004), particularly outside stricter AMI-recognized implementations
target_learners: children from birth to age 18, including atypically developing children and children of low-income families
target_learning_goals: independence and self-determination
academic achievement across language, math, geometry, science, geography, music, art, and practical life skills
social–emotional development
examples: The article describes the system's 3-year age groupings, interconnected apparatus across curriculum areas, and teachers presenting individual lessons meeting successive developmental needs

article_title: Embodied Learning Environments for Graphing Motion: a Systematic Literature Review
citation: Carolien Duijzer, Marja Van den Heuvel-Panhuizen, Michiel Veldhuis, Michiel Doorman, & Paul Leseman. (2019). Embodied Learning Environments for Graphing Motion: a Systematic Literature Review. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-019-09471-7
title: Moderate embodiment view: bodily experiences constitute the fundament of knowledge while allowing off-line simulation and links to a-modal conceptual knowledge
description: The review frames embodied learning environments within a moderate view of embodied cognition, positioned between simple and radical readings. It acknowledges "the critical importance of bodily experiences as part of the meaning of both concrete and abstract concepts, thus as constituting the fundament of all human knowledge, but allows for two additional resources": off-line grounding through mental simulation re-using sensorimotor circuits, and Hebbian-associative connection of multimodal sensorimotor cognition to a-modal verbal conceptual knowledge. Under this view, both making one's own movements and observing others' or objects' movements (via mirroring mechanisms) count as embodied, and embodied simulation supplies previously acquired sensorimotor experiences when immediate interaction is unavailable.
requirements: Perceptual-motor experiences must be task-relevant for the learning content for embodiment to support learning
constraints: The radical view is noted to have difficulty explaining cognition in the absence of direct environmental stimuli, such as symbolic language and mental arithmetic
target_learners: Learners across education levels, from primary education to higher education
target_learning_goals: Grounding abstract formal mathematical and scientific concepts in concrete bodily experiences
examples: The review cites studies where task-relevant whole bodily motion conditions outperformed non-motion conditions in learning two-digit numbers, and where observing a teacher demonstrating a geometry concept improved understanding

article_title: Time Management and Achievement Motivation: A Review of What We Know and Directions for Where to Go
citation: Christopher A. Wolters, Anna C. Brady, Hyun Ji Lee. (2025). Time Management and Achievement Motivation: A Review of What We Know and Directions for Where to Go. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-025-10032-4
title: Research and practice on time management should treat motivation and time management as reciprocally related within SRL
description: The review argues that within SRL, motivation and time management are "expected to be reciprocally and dynamically related processes": motivation energizes strategic time management, while managing time may in turn shape confidence and values. It recommends that future research move beyond cross-sectional bivariate correlations toward longitudinal and experimental designs that can test these reciprocal causal pathways. Practitioners should therefore attend to both motivational beliefs and time management skills rather than treating either in isolation.
requirements: Testing reciprocal pathways requires longitudinal and/or experimental designs rather than cross-sectional correlations
constraints: The review notes only a small proportion of motivation-strategy research has focused on time management, and evidence for each causal path is limited
target_learners: students across academic levels, from secondary school through post-secondary education
target_learning_goals: self-regulated learning, effective time management, and adaptive academic motivation
examples: The review highlights cross-lagged findings such as self-efficacy predicting later time management but not vice versa, and time management predicting later intrinsic motivation
key_sources: Christopher A. Wolters, Anna C. Brady, Hyun Ji Lee. (2025). Time Management and Achievement Motivation: A Review of What We Know and Directions for Where to Go. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-025-10032-4

article_title: Integrating Motivation and Instruction: Towards a Unified Approach in Educational Psychology
citation: Andrew J. Martin. (2023). Integrating Motivation and Instruction: Towards a Unified Approach in Educational Psychology. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-023-09774-w
title: Motivation and Engagement Wheel: four higher-order dimensions subsuming eleven lower-order factors
description: The Motivation and Engagement Wheel is an integrative framework organizing multidimensional motivation and engagement. It comprises four higher-order dimensions—positive motivation, positive engagement, negative motivation, and negative engagement—each subsuming convergent lower-order factors such as self-efficacy, valuing, mastery orientation, planning, task management, persistence, anxiety, failure avoidance, uncertain control, self-handicapping, and disengagement. The article states "There are four higher order dimensions and eleven lower order factors in the Motivation and Engagement Wheel." It was developed to reflect multidimensionality, positive/negative demarcation, and lower-order factors under broader dimensions.
requirements: Measurement via the parallel Motivation and Engagement Scale to assess students on each part of the Wheel
constraints: The Wheel is not intended to be exhaustive, definitive, or prescriptive; factors such as intrinsic motivation, autonomy, and participation are excluded; it represents predominantly intra-personal constructs, with interpersonal factors such as relatedness beyond its composition
target_learners: elementary school students
high school students
university/college students
target_learning_goals: academic motivation and engagement
examples: Figure 2 graphically represents the synthesis of four positive and negative higher-order dimensions and the eleven specific factors subsumed under them
key_sources: Andrew J. Martin. (2023). Integrating Motivation and Instruction: Towards a Unified Approach in Educational Psychology. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-023-09774-w

article_title: Integrating Motivation and Instruction: Towards a Unified Approach in Educational Psychology
citation: Andrew J. Martin. (2023). Integrating Motivation and Instruction: Towards a Unified Approach in Educational Psychology. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-023-09774-w
title: Motivation and Engagement Scale (MES): 44-item self-report instrument with three educational-level versions
description: The Motivation and Engagement Scale is the measurement instrument accompanying the Wheel, comprising "44 items (4 items for each of the 11 factors)" for student self-report. It comes in elementary school, high school, and university/college versions. The review reports, citing Liem and Martin (2012), that responses to the MES factors are normally distributed, internally consistent, and perform well in lower-order and higher-order confirmatory factor analysis, and that MES factors are significantly associated with academic outcomes such as achievement.
requirements: Used to assess students on each part of the Wheel
constraints: A detailed account of MES psychometrics and construct validity is beyond the scope of this review

high school students
university/college students
target_learning_goals: assessment of multidimensional motivation and engagement
examples: Other multidimensional instruments noted in a footnote include PALS, MSLQ, SEI, AMS, and ISM

article_title: Embodied Learning Activities Focusing on Letter-Sound Knowledge Increase Spelling Performance in 1st Grade Children with Low and High Reading Ability
citation: Damsgaard, L., Nielsen, A.-M. V., Topor, M. K., Hansen, R. A., Jensen, S. K., Markers, R. L., Gejl, A. K., Malling, A. S. B., & Wienecke, J. (2023). Embodied Learning Activities Focusing on Letter-Sound Knowledge Increase Spelling Performance in 1st Grade Children with Low and High Reading Ability. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-023-09791-9
title: Movement-phoneme activity program: paired whole-body letter-sound exercises over 4 weeks
description: A 4-week intervention of three 25-minute weekly sessions in which children "were taught to make specific whole-body movements to letter-sounds (movement phonemes)" across 25 letters, working in pairs under a trained instructor with a 1:2 teacher-student fraction. Activities included letter-sound relay, alphabet chaos, become-a-letter, miming, letter salad, sound duel, rime-twister, and hidden-word games, built on the Danish teaching material Fandango Mini.

article_title: A Framework for Motivating Teacher-Student Relationships
citation: Robinson, C. D. (2022). A Framework for Motivating Teacher-Student Relationships. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-022-09706-0
title: The Motivating Teacher-Student Relationships framework: three motivational beliefs drive teachers' relationship-building behaviors
description: The Motivating TSRs framework is an explanatory model integrating multiple motivation theories to explain why some teachers invest more in building relationships with students. It hypothesizes that teachers' beliefs about roles, values, and self-efficacy determine whether they "direct (and sustain) energy and effort toward building relationships with their students," which in turn shapes TSR quality. The beliefs are interdependent, reciprocal with experiences, and underpinned by sociocultural contexts. The article states it "does not elevate one theory of motivation over another" but integrates aspects of each.
requirements: Teachers must attend to all three beliefs with high salience and a favorable overall valence for relationship-building behaviors to occur at a given moment
constraints: The framework addresses teachers' motivations only; students' motivational beliefs about TSRs are explicitly outside the article's scope
The association between beliefs and TSR quality is hypothesized, not experimentally tested in this article
target_learners: K-12 teachers
target_learning_goals: Building positive teacher-student relationships that support student achievement and engagement
examples: Figure 1 presents the hypothesized pathway from motivational beliefs through relationship-building behaviors to TSR quality, with sociocultural contexts as the foundation

article_title: Motivational Apprenticeship: An Apprenticeship Framework for Developing Students’ Motivational Competencies
citation: Shan Li, Juan Zheng. (2026). Motivational Apprenticeship: An Apprenticeship Framework for Developing Students' Motivational Competencies. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-025-10114-3
title: Motivational apprenticeship: a six-component framework for developing learners' motivational self-regulation
description: The article proposes motivational apprenticeship, a conceptual framework extending cognitive apprenticeship to motivation, so learners "develop autonomous motivational regulation skills". It operationalizes six components: modeling, coaching, scaffolding, articulation, reflection, and exploration, treating motivation as "a teachable skill set rather than solely an internal state". The framework aims to make motivational processes visible and teachable through guided expert support that fades over time.
requirements: Experts who can demonstrate and articulate their own motivational strategies and processes
Authentic learning contexts in which motivational skills are practiced
constraints: The manuscript focuses on students from elementary through postsecondary education; adaptations for teachers, coaches, or other adult learners are stated to be beyond its scope
target_learners: Students at varying developmental stages, from elementary through postsecondary education
target_learning_goals: Autonomous motivational regulation skills
Metacognitive awareness of motivation
Lifelong motivational self-regulation
examples: Table 1 lists sample techniques per component, such as live demonstrations and recorded video examples for modeling, and reflective journals for reflection

article_title: Motivational Apprenticeship: An Apprenticeship Framework for Developing Students’ Motivational Competencies
citation: Shan Li, Juan Zheng. (2026). Motivational Apprenticeship: An Apprenticeship Framework for Developing Students' Motivational Competencies. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-025-10114-3
title: Four core principles underpinning motivational apprenticeship: visible, situated, guided, and metacognitive motivation
description: The framework rests on four principles. Visible motivation makes implicit motivational processes explicit, with experts "transparently sharing their struggles with motivation". Situated motivation treats motivation as context-dependent and develops it in authentic contexts. Guided experience provides structured support that gradually increases independence. Metacognitive awareness builds learners' capacity to monitor and regulate their own motivational states, extending Wolters' facets of motivational regulation.
requirements: Experts able to verbalize motivational strategies and struggles
Scaffolded practice opportunities within authentic tasks
constraints: The principles are conceptual; the article presents no empirical test of the principle set itself
target_learners: Elementary through postsecondary students
target_learning_goals: Metacognitive awareness of motivation
Application of motivational strategies in authentic contexts
examples: A teacher coaching students on an actual multi-week research project as they encounter real motivational challenges

article_title: Mental Effort, Workload, Time on Task, and Certainty: Beyond Linear Models
citation: Jimmie Leppink & Patricia Pérez-Fuster. (2019). Mental Effort, Workload, Time on Task, and Certainty: Beyond Linear Models. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-018-09460-2
title: Model-comparison approach for linear vs non-linear mental-effort relations (Models 0–4)
description: A reusable analytic procedure the article introduces: five competing two-level mixed-effects models (random participant intercepts) ordered by complexity — no relation, linear, quadratic, cubic, and more complex than cubic (mental effort as factor) — compared on marginal R2, AIC and BIC. Model 4 sets "the maximum possible R2M for a set of fixed effects", letting researchers quantify what is lost by simplifying. The authors state "the approach we have provided is applicable to any study that involves sufficiently large samples and/or includes multiple measurements from the same participants".
requirements: Same random-effects structure and identical data across compared models; repeated measurements per participant or large samples
constraints: Compound-symmetry (random-intercept) models were used because more flexible random-effects structures are unreliable in small samples; multiple imputation was avoided in small samples
target_learners: researchers analysing repeated-measurement cognitive load data
target_learning_goals: accurate modelling of relations between mental effort and other learning-relevant variables
examples: Analyses were run in Jamovi version 0.9.5.11, chosen because it is open source and provides marginal and conditional R2 statistics

article_title: Hybridizing Motivational Strains: How Integrative Models Are Crucial for Advancing Motivation Science
citation: Ronnel B. King, Luke K. Fryer. (2024). Hybridizing Motivational Strains: How Integrative Models Are Crucial for Advancing Motivation Science. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-024-09850-9
title: Theoretical fragmentation of motivation science as a field-level problem hindering cumulative progress
description: The essay argues that motivation research in educational psychology is divided into camps, each with its own theory, that ignore findings from other camps. It documents repeated calls for integration from leading scholars and argues that without integration the field risks 'unchecked and likely unsustainable growth in the number of theories', undermining reliable findings and the field's reputation with practitioners and policymakers.
requirements: Researchers must recognize that no single theory can fully capture the complexity of motivation and learning
constraints: The essay attributes fragmentation partly to researchers themselves and to misaligned incentives rather than to the theories' content
target_learners: educational psychology researchers
graduate students
target_learning_goals: understanding student motivation and learning through cumulative theoretical knowledge
examples: The essay quotes Murphy & Alexander (2000), Eccles & Wigfield (2002), Dweck (2017), Koenka (2020), Anderman (2020), Hattie et al. (2020), Wentzel (2021), and Greene (2022) all calling for integration

article_title: Motivation-Achievement Cycles in Learning: a Literature Review and Research Agenda
citation: Vu, T., Magis-Weinberg, L., Jansen, B. R. J., van Atteveldt, N., Jansen, T. W. P. J., Lee, N. C., van der Maas, H. L. J., Raijmakers, M. E. J., Sachisthal, M. S. M., & Meeter, M. (2021). Motivation-Achievement Cycles in Learning: a Literature Review and Research Agenda. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-021-09616-7
title: The motivation-achievement cycle: a synthesis model of reciprocal motivation-achievement interactions
description: The review proposes a summary model (Fig. 1) capturing commonalities across prominent academic motivation theories, in which motivation arises from an appraisal combining value and expectancy, which drives achievement behaviors (quantity and quality of learning) and academic emotions, and achievement feeds back through perceived performance and flow. As the authors state, "Figure 1 represents an attempt to synthesize, fo r the purposes of this paper, some of the commonalities of well-established theories". The model also marks external influences (culture, social influence, rewards, feedback form, instruction quality) that affect the cycle without being part of it.
requirements: Multiple motivation constructs and their behavioral mediators must be measured to study the cycle's reciprocal links empirically
constraints: The authors state the goal is not to comprehensively review and synthesize existing theories but to illustrate commonalities suggesting a framework
target_learners: school and college students in academic domains
target_learning_goals: academic motivation and academic achievement (knowledge, skill)
examples: The model distinguishes two routes from motivation to achievement (quantity and quality of academic behaviors) and two routes from achievement to motivation (perceived performance and flow)

citation: Kubsch, M., Strauß, S., Grimm, A., Gombert, S., Drachsler, H., Neumann, K., & Rummel, N. (2025). Self-regulated Learning in the Digitally Enhanced Science Classroom: Toward an Early Warning System. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-025-10011-9
title: Technology-enhanced digital workbook (Moodle-based) for inquiry-based physics instruction
description: A Moodle course implementing a technology-enhanced workbook that "replaced paper-based worksheets and notebooks" in an inquiry-based energy unit. It featured task formats from multiple-choice to open-ended answers, recorded student artifacts across 36 tasks, and gave each student a personal laptop or tablet. The recorded artifacts supplied the cognitive data stream (107 scores per student via evidence-centered design scoring), while self-report instruments after each of five unit parts supplied affective and metacognitive data.
requirements: Each student needs access to a laptop or tablet; teachers participate in professional learning on project-based pedagogy and the workbook
constraints: Data collection is limited by classroom affordances such as missed lessons and teacher instructions to skip tasks, which produced missing task responses
target_learners: middle school students in grades 7 and 8 in Gymnasium and Gemeinschaftsschule school types
target_learning_goals: energy concept understanding
scientific practices such as planning investigations and constructing explanations
examples: Students investigated the driving question about mounting solar cells on a house through three sub-driving questions across five unit parts

title: Moreno's summary article on nine ways to reduce cognitive load
description: This element is Moreno's summary article on nine ways to reduce cognitive load, cited by Reisslein as the work through which he first encountered her research. The editorial's reference list does not print this article's full citation, but Reisslein's tribute identifies it as a summary of methods for reducing cognitive load in multimedia learning, the research area the editorial describes as one of Moreno's primary research areas. It connects to the edited volume on cognitive load theory she later co-edited with Plass and Brünken.

target_learning_goals: reducing cognitive load during learning from multimedia instruction

citation: Holzberger, D., & Prestele, E. (2021). Teacher Self-Efficacy and Self-Reported Instructional Quality: A Multilevel Perspective on the Role of School Characteristics. Learning and Instruction, 76, 101513. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.learninstruc.2021.101513
title: When investigating teacher self-efficacy and instructional quality, model the school context rather than treating self-efficacy as purely individual
description: The article argues that research on teacher motivation and instruction should not neglect the school context: teachers' self-efficacy should be modeled both as an individual variable and as a school-level composite, and school characteristics (collective efficacy, collaboration, participation, leadership) should be tested as context predictors and moderators. The authors state the findings "indicate the differential importance of addressing the school context when investigating teacher self-efficacy and instructional quality".
requirements: Multilevel data with multiple teachers per school; separation of teacher-level and school-level variance via centering
constraints: School-level differences in self-efficacy and instructional quality were small (1–5% between-school variance), and effects were rather small and not consistent across all indicators

school leaders
education researchers
target_learning_goals: understanding how teacher motivation relates to instructional quality across organizational levels

article_title: Silver linings and storm clouds: Divergent profiles of student momentary engagement emerge in response to the same task.
citation: Symonds, J. E., Schreiber, J. B., & Torsney, B. M. (2021). Silver linings and storm clouds: Divergent profiles of momentary engagement emerge in response to the same task. Journal of Educational Psychology. https://doi.org/10.1037/edu0000605
title: Momentary task engagement as a dynamic system of emotion, cognition, agency and behavior at micro-level grain size
description: The article frames momentary task engagement as a multidimensional construct with affective-motivational, cognitive and behavioral components, occurring at the "micro-level grain size of momentary time, at the micro-level grain size of a specific task, and at the micro-level grain size of individual student experiences". It proposes that momentary engagement "is proposed to operate as a rapid, non-linear dynamic system where motivation, emotion, and mental and physical action continually shape and are shaped by the emergent property of engagement as they co-act in context". The framework motivates person-oriented latent profile analysis, since components can co-act divergently within one student during one task. Its opposite, momentary disaffection, includes inattention, negative academic emotions, and disengagement as a behavioral indicator.
requirements: Data collected at the micro-level grain size of a single task and momentary time, measuring at least two engagement dimensions
constraints: The system responds sensitively to task context and setting, so patterns and predictors are task specific rather than general across tasks
target_learners: Adolescent secondary school students
target_learning_goals: Momentary engagement and disaffection during academic classwork
examples: The study operationalized the framework with self-reported emotional and cognitive engagement and observed on-task behavior during one ten-minute literacy task

article_title: The potential of relevance interventions for scaling up: A cluster-randomized trial testing the effectiveness of a relevance intervention in math classrooms.
citation: Gaspard, H., Parrisius, C., Piesch, H., Kleinhansl, M., Wille, E., Nagengast, B., Trautwein, U., & Hulleman, C. S. (2021). The potential of relevance interventions for scaling up: A cluster-randomized trial testing the effectiveness of a relevance intervention in math classrooms. Journal of Educational Psychology. Advance online publication. https://dx.doi.org/10.1037/edu0000663
title: MoMa (Motivation in Mathematics) 90-minute classroom-based relevance intervention
description: MoMa is a 90-minute classroom-based relevance intervention for ninth-grade academic-track math students in Germany. "The 90-min intervention consists of a psychoeducational presentation for the whole class and relevance-inducing reflection tasks, on which students work individually." The presentation covers research on effort and self-concept in math achievement (targeting growth mindsets and inoculating against backfire effects for low-expectancy students) and examples of mathematics' utility across life domains; students then evaluate six interview quotations from young adults about the usefulness of mathematics for personal relevance. Materials were optimized from the efficacy trial (e.g., traffic-light cards as ice-breaker, take-home message slides, updated daily-life examples).
requirements: A trained deliverer (master's student or teacher) who received the intervention materials including a lesson plan, PowerPoint slides, and a script with detailed notes for the presentation
constraints: Developed for ninth-grade academic track students in Germany; the waitlist control had no access to materials to limit diffusion
target_learners: ninth-grade academic-track students in Germany
target_learning_goals: perceived utility value of mathematics
growth mindsets about math ability
mathematics achievement
examples: In the effectiveness trial, 28 classes received MoMa from master's students and 25 from their regular math teachers after brief training; observers noted only very few severe deviations from the standardized procedure across 15 pre-defined phases

article_title: School belonging predicts whether an emerging adult will be not in education, employment, or training (NEET) after school.
citation: Philip Parker, Kelly-Ann Allen, Rhiannon Parker, Jiesi Guo, Herbert W Marsh, Geetanjali Basarkod, and Theresa Dicke. (2021). title: Monitor school belonging as an early indicator of NEET risk and intervene while youth are still in school
description: Because low school belonging at age 15 predicts NEET status at ages 16-20 even after graduation and covariates are controlled, the article recommends that "school personnel and, at a national level, policymakers, should monitor school belonging as one of a range of indicators of NEET risk". Measures of belonging let teachers, schools, and policymakers identify at-risk students and implement interventions that may break a pattern of social exclusion before youth leave the institution.

youth at risk of social exclusion after school
target_learning_goals: reducing post-school social exclusion (NEET)
fostering school belonging
examples: The two-cohort LSAY analysis showed belonging predicted NEET among non-graduates, where five percentage points separated strong-belonging from weak-belonging youth

article_title: A longitudinal randomized trial of a sustained content literacy intervention from first to second grade: Transfer effects on students’ reading comprehension.
citation: Kim, J. S., Burkhauser, M. A., Relyea, J. E., Gilbert, J. B., Scherer, E., Fitzgerald, J., Mosher, D., & McIntyre, J. (2023). A Longitudinal Randomized Trial of a Sustained Content Literacy Intervention From First to Second Grade: Transfer Effects on Students' Reading Comprehension. Journal of Educational Psychology, 115(1), 73-98. https://doi.org/10.1037/edu0000751
title: Model of Reading Engagement (MORE): schema instantiation account of sustained content literacy transfer
description: The MORE framework holds that thematic lessons give students an intellectual framework connecting new learning to a general schema, such as how scientists study past events. The article defines sustained content literacy intervention as an approach in which "thematic lessons are designed to provide sustained and recurrent exposure to schema-building activities so that knowledge is more accessible to children as they build coherent text representations." Schema instantiation is the proposed mechanism of transfer: "schema instantiation can facilitate transfer across topics within a domain and enhance comprehension of novel material that fits the same situation." Domain-specific vocabulary networks supply retrieval cues that activate the general schema.
requirements: Sustained instruction across grades so that general schemas have time to develop
Topic-specific schemas sharing structural components that map onto the general schema
Domain-specific academic vocabulary networks embedded across topics to cue schema activation
constraints: The article notes transfer is difficult to achieve and measure in reading comprehension, and few early-grade interventions have targeted generalized schema development
target_learners: Early elementary grade students (Grades 1-2) in urban elementary schools
target_learning_goals: Reading comprehension of complex informational texts
Domain and topic knowledge in science and social studies
Academic vocabulary knowledge
examples: Grade 1 unit on animal survival laid the foundation for the Grade 2 unit on how paleontologists study prehistoric events, both instantiating the general schema of how scientists study past events.

article_title: Retrieval practice is costly and is beneficial only when working memory capacity is abundant
citation: Yicong Zheng, Pengyuan Sun and Xiaonan L. Liu. (2023). Retrieval practice is costly and is beneficial only when working memory capacity is abundant. npj Science of Learning 8:8. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-023-00159-w
title: Modified SAC dual-process account of the testing effect
description: The article adapts the source of activation confusion (SAC) model to explain when retrieval practice strengthens memory. It assumes retrieval practice involves two sequential processes, a retrieval attempt and a post-retrieval re-encoding process, both consuming resources from a limited WM pool. Its critical assumption is "trading" WM resources for memory strengthening, so that "successfully retrieving the item does not guarantee that the memory is more effectively strengthened than restudying the item" when resources are depleted. Item familiarity reduces WM consumption, explaining why lower-capacity learners benefit only from familiar stimuli.
requirements: Retrieval attempts must succeed for re-encoding to strengthen nodes, since re-encoding only strengthens the episode node when retrieval is successful (no feedback was provided)
constraints: The simulation simplified to Days 2 and 3, assuming Day 1 learning criteria equalized associations; the authors state the cognitive mechanisms underlying the two processes remain unclear
target_learners: undergraduate students learning novel cue-target associations
target_learning_goals: long-term retention of learned associations
examples: The authors fitted a weighting parameter for extra WM cost and individual-level mean and standard deviation parameters by minimizing root-mean-square error against observed accuracy

article_title: Building dementia knowledge globally through the Understanding Dementia Massive Open Online Course (MOOC)
citation: Eccleston, C., Doherty, K., Bindoff, A., Robinson, A., Vickers, J. & McInerney, F. (2019). Building dementia knowledge globally through the Understanding Dementia Massive Open Online Course (MOOC). npj Science of Learning 4:3. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-019-0042-4
title: MOOCs should include objective, validated measures of knowledge acquisition rather than relying on engagement or completion metrics
description: The article argues that evidence of MOOC educational impact is limited because, as it observes, "Few MOOCs, include objective measures of knowledge acquisition, instead choosing primary outcome measures such as engagement, retention and completion as evidence of success." Building validated knowledge measures into the course itself allowed the UDMOOC evaluation to demonstrate actual knowledge gains across a broad cohort. The principle calls for embedding reliable outcome instruments in MOOC design so learning, not participation, is the success criterion.

examples: The UDMOOC had the DKAS 2.0 built in as a pre-post measure, revealing gains from a median of 34.5 to 45

article_title: A working memory dependent dual process model of the testing effect
citation: Zheng, Y., Shi, A. & Liu, X. L. (2024). A working memory dependent dual process model of the testing effect. npj Science of Learning 9:56. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-024-00268-0
title: Modified SAC model quantifying WM resource trade-off
description: A modified Source of Activation Confusion model in which memory strength is delineated by base-level strength and activation level in a network of concept and episode nodes connected by associative edges. The article states the trade-off idea "has been quantitatively implemented in a modiﬁed Source of Activation Confusion (SAC) model". The model posits a limited pool of WM resources, consumed by node operations such as encoding and retrieval and replenished over time; individuals with higher WMC have greater WM resources available.
requirements: A limited pool of WM resources whose consumption and replenishment are modeled for encoding and retrieval operations
constraints: The model is a quantitative implementation rooted in the original SAC framework; the article notes direct validation of the shared-resource assumption is lacking
target_learners: learners with high or low working memory capacity
target_learning_goals: memory strengthening through retrieval practice
examples: Used to model how familiarity of memory nodes impacts WM resources consumed during encoding and retrieval

article_title: Faster implicit motor sequence learning of new sequences compatible in terms of movement transitions
citation: Susanne Dyck & Christian Klaes. (2025). Faster implicit motor sequence learning of new sequences compatible in terms of movement transitions. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-025-00296-4
title: Movement-transition-based associative map for implicit motor sequence learning
description: The article proposes that in implicit motor sequence learning the memory representation underlying facilitative learning of compatible sequences is an associative map built from movement transitions between consecutive responses, rather than from ordinal positions. It situates this within dual-system accounts of MSL, in which an intra-dimensional system associates representations within one dimension and supports implicit MSL. As the authors put it, "in implicit MSL movement transitions form the basis for an associative map", contrasting with the cognitive-motor schema based on ordinal positions reported for explicit MSL. The authors prefer the expression facilitative learning or schema-like memory effect.
requirements: Extensive previous training of the original sequence (three sessions in experiment 1) before switching to the new sequence
constraints: The associative map is likely based on simple associations between consecutive movements within a single dimension, so the authors prefer the term schema-like memory effect rather than schema memory
target_learners: Healthy adults aged 18-35 learning motor sequences in an implicit serial reaction time task
target_learning_goals: Implicit motor sequence learning and transfer to new, compatible motor sequences
examples: Experiment 1 trained an original sequence for three sessions before switching to new, compatible, incompatible, or same sequences in an implicit bimanual SRTT; both compatible and incompatible sequences shared the same movement-transition overlap and were learned faster than a completely new sequence

article_title: Realizing the potential of mobile interventions for education
citation: Breitwieser, J., Neubauer, A. B., Schmiedek, F. & Brod, G. (2024). Realizing the potential of mobile interventions for education. npj Science of Learning, 9, 76. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-024-00289-9

description: The article defines mobile interventions as a complement to m-learning (mobile devices as content-delivery learning tools) and mobile data collection for theory testing (research tools). Mobile interventions aim "to change students' behavior, experiences, or cognitive processes relevant to learning" across analog and digital, formal and informal contexts. Two features set them apart: "the repeated delivery of intervention prompts at shorter time intervals" and "the utilization of high-resolution data collected alongside the intervention," enabling support before or between learning sessions.

emotional and motivational states relevant to learning

article_title: Montessori education: a review of the evidence base
citation: Chloë Marshall. (2017). Montessori education: a review of the evidence base. npj Science of Learning 2:11. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-017-0012-7
title: Montessori method as a triad of child, teacher and prepared environment with self-directed engagement
description: The review describes the Montessori method as organised around "the dynamic triad of child, teacher and environment", in which the teacher guides children through a prepared environment supporting development "through active exploration, choice and independent learning". Two aspects are highlighted: manipulable learning materials for sensorial and academic concepts, and a self-directed mode of engagement during a 3-h work cycle in which children choose what, where, with whom and for how long they work, free of competition and extrinsic rewards. Montessori's underlying account holds that children pass through sensitive periods and stages of development, and that self-construction is fostered by self-directed activity in the prepared environment.
requirements: Requires trained teachers who guide children based on careful observation of the children rather than a formal timetable
Requires a specially prepared environment and class rules within which freedom operates
constraints: The name is not copyrighted and implementation varies considerably across schools, with the name frequently used without full adherence
target_learners: Children aged 3–6 and 6–12 in preschool and elementary settings
target_learning_goals: Optimal development across intellectual, physical, emotional and social domains
Sensorial concepts, mathematics, literacy, science, geography and history
examples: Children build the pink tower from ten cubes differing only in dimension, choosing when to repeat the activity and tidying it away afterwards
A 3-h external work cycle in which children move freely around the classroom and select activities while the teacher guides and gives small-group lessons

article_title: Montessori education: a review of the evidence base
citation: Chloë Marshall. (2017). Montessori education: a review of the evidence base. npj Science of Learning 2:11. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-017-0012-7
title: Montessori learning-materials design pattern: single-concept isolation, control of error, and concrete-to-abstract progression
description: The review enumerates the design principles running through Montessori's learning materials: the child learns through movement and gains a concrete foundation preparing for more abstract concepts; each material isolates just one concept, as in the pink tower where cubes "differ only in their dimensions"; and each piece contains a control of error that alerts the child to mistakes, "thereby allowing self-correction with minimal teacher support". The materials span practical life, sensorial, literacy (writing before reading, phonics), mathematics and geography, with sensorial materials such as the long rods and touchboards serving as preparation for academic materials.
requirements: Materials must isolate a single concept with no additional cues
Each material must include a control of error enabling self-correction
constraints: The review notes it offers only a brief survey of some of the most important elements, not an exhaustive treatment
target_learners: Children aged 3–6 and 6–12
target_learning_goals: Sensorial classification and naming
Literacy and mathematics foundations through concrete materials
examples: The sound boxes contain six pairs of closed cylinders varying in sound, with sound as the only usable cue for matching
Number rods divide ten rods into alternating red and blue 10 cm sections so they take the numerical values 1–10

citation: Li, M., DeMille, M. M. C., Lovett, M. W., Bosson-Heenan, J., Frijters, J. C., Gruen, J. R. & the GRaD Study Consortium. (2024). title: Moderated mediation model of gene effects on reading via phonological awareness conditioned on home environment
description: The article proposes and tests a model in which "The relationship between RU2-Short and reading outcomes was mediated by the phonological awareness. And this relationship was moderated by different values of parental education and SES." Phonological awareness (CTOPP Elision and Blending composite) transmits the effect of the DCDC2-READ1 RU2-Short risk variant to word reading accuracy, fluency, and comprehension, while parental education and SES condition the strength of the indirect effect. The model was estimated with PROCESS OLS regression with bootstrapped indirect effects.

Measures of phonological awareness and reading outcomes, and home environment indicators (parental education and SES)

Cross-sectional design; the authors state a longitudinal design would have been more appropriate to test mediation

target_learning_goals: English word reading accuracy, word reading fluency, and reading comprehension

article_title: Mapping the Montessori mathematics curriculum to Dehaene’s four pillars of learning
citation: Marshall, C., Livingston, L., & Van Herwegen, J. (2026). Mapping the Montessori Mathematics Curriculum to Dehaene's Four Pillars of Learning. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-026-00436-4
title: Four key design principles of the Montessori maths curriculum: concrete-to-abstract, simple-to-complex, repetition, and control of error
description: The article enumerates four principles underpinning the Montessori maths curriculum. Concrete representations are always the starting point, with subsequent materials becoming "increasingly less concrete"; sequences are logical with each new challenge isolated so children explore something simple before elaboration; repetition is offered in many ways, with parallel and less-concrete materials, so children can deep-mine understanding at their own pace; and most materials have in-built control of error so children find mistakes themselves and repeat as needed.
requirements: Children need controlled and coordinated hand movements, perceptual discrimination, and self-discipline from the practical life and sensorial curricula before starting the maths materials
constraints: Abstraction is the result of individual experience, so children vary in how long they take, requiring freedom to work at their own pace
target_learners: 3- to 6-year-old children in Montessori early-years settings
target_learning_goals: Abstract mathematical concepts including number, the decimal system, arithmetic operations, and fractions
examples: The Group 1 sequence moves from Number Rods embodying quantities 1-10, to Sandpaper Numerals, to the Spindle Box, to Numbers and Counters where children create the sequence themselves and recall quantities from memory.

citation: Robin Samuelsson. (2023). The two-faced process of learning and the importance of Janus-faced solutions. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-023-00210-w
title: Montessori education and Tools-of-the-Mind as exemplar active learning programmes
description: The article cites two contemporary programmes as instances of the Janus-faced balance. Montessori preschools and schools are described as 'promoting active, hands-on learning with select tools and scaffolding, which is a well-tested 33 alternative to typical classroom approaches to teaching and learning at the more constructivist side'. Tools-of-the-Mind programmes are described as using cultural tools as a major component 'in a play-based sociocultural alternative implementing a balance of play and teacher-scaffolded activity'.

constraints: The article characterises Montessori as sitting more at the constructivist side of the balance

target_learning_goals: active hands-on learning; play-based development supported by cultural tools and scaffolding
examples: The article references a cited evaluation describing Montessori education as well-tested, and describes Tools-of-the-Mind's balance of play and teacher-scaffolded activity

article_title: Semantic relatedness and the efficacy of retrieval practice
citation: Gupta, M.W., Pan, S.C., & Rickard, T.C. (2026). Semantic relatedness and the efficacy of retrieval practice. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-026-00416-8
title: Do not infer whether a factor moderates testing efficacy from an ANOVA interaction on proportion correct; use a process model plus distribution matching instead
description: When both restudy and test condition means shift in the same direction across levels of another factor, an ANOVA interaction on proportion correct is theoretically uninterpretable, because the mapping from latent memory strength to accuracy is non-linear and unknown. The article instead evaluates an empirically supported process model as a yardstick and applies a matching strategy via cumulative proportion-correct distributions. This revealed a real relatedness × testing-efficacy interaction that "a traditional ANOVA interaction" masked.
requirements: A process model whose quantitative mapping from the psychological construct to the dependent measure has empirical support for at least one level of the moderator
Sufficiently large samples to minimize sampling variability in cumulative distributions
constraints: The article limits the interpretation problem to cases where both condition means change in the same direction across factor levels, and notes special cases such as crossover interactions are interpretable
target_learners: Researchers and practitioners evaluating when retrieval practice is effective
target_learning_goals: Accurate theoretical and applied inference about the moderators of the testing effect
examples: In the present experiment the null ANOVA interaction coexisted with a significant Data Type × Relatedness interaction in the model-based comparison and with distribution-wide overprediction for the high relatedness group

title: Four-aspect analytical lens for motor skills learning systems: sensing, modelling, designing, and delivering feedback
description: The paper reviews 17 motor skills learning systems along four numbered aspects: 1) sensing the learner's corporal movement and context, 2) modelling interactions to compare learner movement against the accurate movement, 3) designing the feedback (what support, and when and how), and 4) delivering feedback "in an effective non-intrusive way to advice the learner on how the body and limbs should move". Personalization issues within each aspect are flagged as places where AIED research can contribute.
requirements: Each aspect requires its own design decision: sensor choice, comparison model, feedback design, and non-intrusive delivery channel.

examples: Applied in Table 1 to systems from karate training with accelerometers to vibrotactile violin bowing feedback (MusicJacket).
