article_title: Data-Related Ethics Issues in Technologies for Informal Professional Learning
citation: Pammer-Schindler, V. & Rosé, C. (2021). Data-Related Ethics Issues in Technologies for Informal Professional Learning. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-021-00259-x
title: MoodMap App for self-tracked mood and team awareness
description: The MoodMap App is a mood self-tracking prototype whose interface follows Russell's two-dimensional model of affect along valence and arousal, with mood captured by clicking a bi-dimensional mood map based on Itten's colour system. Users can attach free-text notes and context information; moods, notes and context are aggregated and visualized at individual and collaborative levels, including a Compare Me View and a Collaborative View showing others' current mood. It was tested in two field studies, in virtual team meetings and in call-center teams.
requirements: User-centered design iterations adapted the app to each study setting, including configuration of whether contextual information to mood was mandatory
constraints: In the virtual team meeting setting the collaborative view anonymized user names, which impacted usefulness because knowing the author of a mood entry is necessary to react ad personam
target_learners: professionals in collaborative and team-based workplace settings
target_learning_goals: reflection on salient work issues, awareness of own emotions, team communication
examples: Case 4 in four business-2-business call-center teams showed positive impact for those two of the four teams who accepted the intervention

citation: Viswanathan Kodaganallur, Rob R. Weitz, David Rosenthal. (2005). A Comparison of Model-Tracing and Constraint-Based Intelligent Tutoring Paradigms. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://telearn.hal.science/hal-00197305

description: The article contrasts two approaches to building intelligent tutoring systems: the "well-established model-tracing paradigm" and "the relatively newer constraint-based paradigm". It evaluates the proponents' claim that constraint-based tutors "afford performance at levels comparable to that of model-tracing tutors, but with significantly less development effort", and organizes the comparison around remediation quality, domain feasibility, and development effort.

article_title: Student Modeling Based on Problem Solving Times
citation: Pelánek, R., & Jarušek, P. (2015). Student Modeling Based on Problem Solving Times. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-015-0048-x
title: Use model parameters — difficulty, discrimination, and randomness — as feedback for content authors and to filter and sequence problems
description: Beyond predicting solving times, the fitted parameters give insight into pedagogical properties of problems. The article notes that "Problems with small discrimination and large randomness clearly depend more on luck than on skill and thus are probably not a very good pedagogical problems, so we may want to filter out such problems." Early in a session, when the skill estimate is weak, problems with small discrimination and variance give more reliable time estimates; later, higher-discrimination problems tune selection to the individual student. Parameter discrepancies also helped detect cheating and misbehaving problems.
requirements: Sufficient solved-problem data per problem to estimate discrimination and variance reliably
constraints: At session start, when skill estimates are weak, prefer low-discrimination, low-variance problems; the boundary guidance follows the article's recommendation, not an optimized optimum
target_learners: students in computerized adaptive practice systems
target_learning_goals: selecting problems of appropriate difficulty and discriminating power for adaptive practice
examples: In the Problem Solving Tutor, the linear scoring function for recommendations combines expected solving time, problem randomness, and prior attempts, and parameters are given as feedback to content authors

citation: Thomas Daniel Ullmann. (2019). Automated Analysis of Reflection in Writing: Validating Machine Learning Approaches. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education (2019) 29:217–257. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-019-00174-2
title: Model for reflection detection: eight categories synthesized from 24 reflective writing models
description: The article synthesizes 24 reflective writing models into a "model for reflection detection" combining depth and breadth qualities. "In total, the model consists of eight categories": the depth dimension Reflection (reflective vs. non-reflective) and seven breadth categories — Experience, Feeling, Belief, Difficulty (critical stance), Perspective, Learning (retrospective outcomes), and Intention (prospective outcomes). The synthesis deliberately used a general model rather than one specific model, so the evaluation covers categories "common to many models" used in manual content analysis of reflective writing.
requirements: Categories are operationalized as indicator questions rated by coders sentence by sentence, e.g. "The writer describes an experience he or she had in the past"
constraints: No widely agreed definition of reflection exists; the article adopts its own working definition for the purpose of the study
target_learners: higher education students writing reflective essays
target_learning_goals: reflective thinking
reflective writing
examples: Example annotated sentences per category, e.g. for Feeling: "Although I was a bit anxious about the lesson, I kept on top of the feelings."

Learners can complete courses at their own pace, and MOOCs "enable self-directed learning where learners can achieve their own learning needs and goals by applying appropriate personal learning strategies." citation: Patricia Azevedo Tedesco. (2003). MArCo: Building an Artificial Conflict Mediator to Support Group Planning Interactions. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education, 13, 117-155. https://telearn.hal.science/hal-00197314
title: Model of strategic changes describing what types of changes happen to a group plan and how changes to one strategy component impact the others
description: The article builds "a model of strategic operations, which describes what types of changes happen to a plan as well as how changes to one component of the strategy (beliefs, intentions, ordering relations, context beliefs and goals) impact the other ones." It serves to diagnose which changes are happening to the group plan during interaction. Together with a model of the group and the history of the interaction, it supplies the inputs the conflict mediator uses to detect and mediate meta-cognitive conflicts.

article_title: Implementation of Motivational Tactics in Tutoring Systems: 20 years on
citation: du Boulay, B., & del Soldato, T. (2016). Implementation of Motivational Tactics in Tutoring Systems: 20 years on. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education, 26, 170-182. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-015-0052-1
title: MORE's characterisation of motivation as effort, confidence and independence monitored on thresholded linear scales
description: MORE characterised motivation indirectly via three associated factors: "effort, confidence and independence". Each was conceived as a linear scale, seeded halfway, incremented or decremented by learner and system activities, with a threshold below which the system switched on tactics to raise the value — "the model was essentially a motivational thermostat". Confidence here meant confidence in tackling the next task, not stable self-efficacy, and the three scales interacted, e.g. providing help could raise effort but lower independence.
requirements: Continuous monitoring of learner actions such as perseverance, help requests and menu choices, rather than one-off pre-lesson measurement
constraints: The authors state this notion of motivation was a huge simplification, omitting academic emotions, engagement, goal setting and learner values
target_learners: learners in problem-solving tutoring, e.g. Prolog debugging
target_learning_goals: maintaining and improving motivation during a single lesson
examples: Effort was measured via perseverance when facing difficulties; confidence and independence via help requests and menu choices about perceived problem difficulty

article_title: Implementation of Motivational Tactics in Tutoring Systems: 20 years on
citation: du Boulay, B., & del Soldato, T. (2016). Implementation of Motivational Tactics in Tutoring Systems: 20 years on. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education, 26, 170-182. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-015-0052-1
title: MORE (Motivational Reactive Plan): a Prolog-debugging tutor with separate domain and motivational planners plus an arbitration mechanism
description: MORE was a 1990s teaching system for Prolog debugging that "incorporated two kinds of pedagogic reasoning": a domain planner sequencing problems by prerequisites and difficulty, and a production-system motivational reasoner maintaining or improving the learner's motivational state. Because the two planners could disagree about the next action, "a third mechanism (a set of rules) was implemented which arbitrated about how to deal with such disparities". Its defining feature was making micro-adaptive motivational pedagogy explicit and adjustable.
requirements: Explicit, adjustable representations of motivational strategy and tactics so rules can be revised in light of new theory or evidence
constraints: The system was not developed and maintained, so the motivational reasoning component was never integrated into a large-scale domain-based tutor
target_learners: students learning Prolog debugging
target_learning_goals: domain mastery alongside maintained motivation
examples: When the planners disagreed, e.g. offering a harder problem versus one of the same difficulty, the arbitration rules decided the action

article_title: Implementation of Motivational Tactics in Tutoring Systems: 20 years on
citation: du Boulay, B., & del Soldato, T. (2016). Implementation of Motivational Tactics in Tutoring Systems: 20 years on. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education, 26, 170-182. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-015-0052-1
title: Motivational strategy as ordered production rules mapping student state to goals and tactics
description: MORE expressed its motivational pedagogy as an ordered production system (Table 1) whose rules matched student-model and history items such as "effort-valu < medium", "help-state = rejected" or "problem-state = failed" to top-level goals (increase confidence, increase effort, respect control) and tactics (provide specific help, praise performance, stimulate challenge, avoid intervention). The first matching rule fired. The grain size is the lesson-level strategy layer sitting beside domain sequencing.
requirements: A student model with motivational, behavioural and problem-outcome variables for rules to match against
constraints: The authors note an ambiguity between goals and tactics sharing the same term, and that the rules were the same for all learners and initial values were set arbitrarily at the halfway point
target_learners: individual learners in a tutoring system
target_learning_goals: effort, confidence and independence maintenance during problem solving
examples: If problem-state = given-up, goals were increase effort and increase confidence with tactics encourage effort and facilitate success, e.g. providing help about the next step

title: MOVES-NL: a technology-enhanced inclusive embodied design for learning integer arithmetic
description: MOVES-NL is a novel, technologically enabled classroom design for learning basic arithmetic procedures through coordinating full-body and manual interactions centered on navigating the number line. It includes three activities supporting an egocentric-to-allocentric enactive progression: walking a floor-projected number line, walking with a wall-projected avatar mimicking the student's actions, and reenacting movements with a handheld figurine on a tablet. Per the SpEED framework, it employs "Both interactive projections and mirrored/tangible avatars as media; ambulatory (embodied), visual, auditory and haptic modalities; and NLs as semiotic modes."
requirements: A motion-sensing camera, projectors, and a mini-PC housed in a portable structure (MOVES), plus the SENSEi software for the avatar interaction
constraints: The current design is restricted to individual usage by the chosen media, posing challenges for scaling to full-class instruction
target_learners: middle-school students with and without cognitive disabilities
target_learning_goals: integer addition and subtraction on the number line
examples: Students stood on the number line, turned toward the positive or negative side, and took steps equal to the absolute value of the second operand, moving forward for positives and backward for negatives

article_title: Model-based support for teaching practice and self-efficacy in artificial intelligence-enhanced virtual reality teaching simulation
citation: Chih-Pu Dai · Fengfeng Ke. (2026). Model-based support for teaching practice and self-efficacy in artificial intelligence-enhanced virtual reality teaching simulation. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-026-10592-4
title: A three-stage design framework for model-based support in VR simulation-based teacher education
description: The article proposes a design framework for model-based support in simulation-based teacher education that integrates Grossman et al.'s teaching practice components, Kavanagh et al.'s pedagogical reasoning model, and Kolb's experiential learning theory. The framework structures support across three stages: "support at the pretraining stage, support during in-situ (or in-simulation) practice, and support at the post-simulation stage." Its aim is to guide preservice teachers in making pedagogical decisions when facing dilemmas while interacting with AI-powered virtual students.

Teaching self-efficacy

title: Treat motivation as a constant design factor throughout all functions of a multimedia learning application

article_title: Applying MOOCocracy learning culture themes to improve digital course design and online learner engagement
citation: Akinkuolie, B., & Shortt, M. (2021). Applying MOOCocracy learning culture themes to improve digital course design and online learner engagement. Education Tech Research Dev, 69, 369–372. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-020-09936-5
title: MOOCocracy learning culture themes as a framework for understanding MOOC learning culture
description: The MOOCocracy themes, drawn from Loizzo and Ertmer's (2016) study of "the learning culture of massive open online courses", serve as an organizing framework for thinking about MOOC design. In this response commentary, the authors use the themes as the lens through which "key ideas, value, and future research implications are addressed in relation to MOOC design". The framework treats MOOCs as having a distinctive learning culture that designers should attend to when building digital courses and seeking to engage online learners.
requirements: The framework is applied to MOOC design contexts, as in the source commentary's relation of the themes to digital course design
constraints: The framework derives from Loizzo and Ertmer's (2016) MOOCocracy study; this article is a response commentary and reports no new empirical data
target_learners: online learners in massive open online courses
target_learning_goals: engagement and learning in massive open online courses
examples: The commentary addresses key ideas, value, and future research implications of the MOOCocracy study for MOOC design using its themes

title: Modified Future Ready Schools—Librarian Self-Reflection survey instrument
description: The study used a modified version of the Future Ready Schools—School Librarian Self-Reflection survey (All4Ed, 2023), an instrument "designed to assess a librarians' professional practices alignment with the Future Ready Schools—Librarian Framework." Approximately 2–4 questions aligned with each of the nine constructs, answered on a 5-point Likert scale from "Never" (1) to "Very Frequently" (5). Wording was changed from the pronoun "I" to "library services/personnel" so the instrument could be administered to administrators, teachers, and librarians alike.

constraints: Response rate was relatively low (23%) per the article's limitations section

target_learning_goals: Measuring perceptions of librarian professional practice across pedagogy, collaboration, and systems and policies
examples: Sample items include 'I coached my colleagues on the effectiveness of digital tools and resources to support student learning'

article_title: The ever evolving MOOC
citation: Patricia A. Young. (2021). The ever evolving MOOC. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-021-09959-6
title: MOOCocracy: MOOCs as a social learning democracy comprising place and space
description: MOOCocracy is the account, proposed by Loizzo and Ertmer and discussed in this editorial, that MOOCs function as a social learning democracy with two components. The editorial states that "MOOCocracy's comprise both place and space": adult learners participate from the places where they live worldwide, while the space represents "digital learning cultures on a massive scale" (p. 1016). Interactions are asynchronous with little formal oversight or personal contact.
requirements: Adult learners participate asynchronously from their own locations, requiring little formal oversight
constraints: Interactions require little formal oversight and even less personal contact, as stated in the editorial
target_learners: adult learners worldwide taking MOOC courses
target_learning_goals: topic-driven knowledge attainment and self-directed learning in massive open online courses
examples: The special section offers four responses critiquing and examining Loizzo and Ertmer's (2016) MOOCocracy study

citation: Wong, J., Khalil, M., Suschevskiy, V., Baars, M., de Koning, B., & Paas, F. (2026). Student engagement profiles in a mobile app: Links to self-regulated learning and performance. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-026-10586-2
title: Mobile study app for retrieval practice with practice, test, compete, and battle modes
description: A mobile study app developed by a university lecturer, developer, and programmer, designed to enhance learning by facilitating SRL through retrieval practice with instructor-provided multiple-choice questions and feedback. Students could use it in "practice, test, compete, and battle" modes: practice gives immediate feedback per item, test gives feedback at the end of a set, compete is a timed competition with a leaderboard, and battle is a peer or instructor challenge. Use in the Law course was optional.
requirements: The course instructor must provide a set of multiple-choice questions along with answers and explanations for the app to be used in a course.
constraints: The app provides only MCQs, which the authors note face arguments about whether they can assess higher-order cognition.

target_learning_goals: retrieval practice and reinforcement of key course information
familiarization with multiple-choice exam questions
examples: In the nine-week Law course, 60% of final exam grades were based on MCQ scores, and app use was an optional study tool during self-study time.

title: Innovation spectrum of mobile learning pedagogies
description: The review organizes mobile learning pedagogies along an innovation spectrum ranging from low to radically innovative and disruptive practices. Illustrative examples are discussed "across this innovation spectrum", distinguishing ordinary technology-augmented practice from the radical, structurally disruptive end achieved by very few studies. This spectrum serves as the review's organizing axis for characterizing the degree to which mobile approaches disrupt traditional school structures and practices.
requirements: Classification of studies requires criteria distinguishing degrees of innovation, as instantiated in the review's content and thematic analysis
constraints: Applied to mobile learning pedagogies for school-aged students in the 2010-2017 literature

examples: The review discusses illustrative examples across the spectrum, including the 3 articles identified as radically innovative and disruptive

citation: James Wakefield & Jessica K. Frawley. (2020). How does students’ general academic achievement moderate the implications of social networking on specific levels of learning performance? Computers & Education. https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0360131519302477?via%3Dihub
title: Consider students' general academic achievement as a moderator when embedding social networking in course delivery
description: The article recommends that using social networking sites in teaching and learning interventions must be carefully considered in light of students' general academic achievement. It states efforts must ensure that "educational embedding of SNS technologies does not inadvertently disadvantage weaker students", since lower achievers are further distracted by Facebook while higher achievers are not significantly impacted.

constraints: The article states findings are unique to introductory accounting and similar equation and problem based subjects, and should not be generalised to wider student populations.

target_learning_goals: introductory accounting performance across Bloom's taxonomy learning difficulty levels
examples: The study split the sample at the median WAM and found only low achievers significantly negatively affected by Facebook use.

article_title: Using Internet videos to learn about controversies: Evaluation and integration of multiple and multimodal documents by primary school students
citation: Salmerón, L., Sampietro, A., & Delgado, P. (2020). Using Internet videos to learn about controversies: Evaluation and integration of multiple and multimodal documents by primary school students. Computers & Education. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.compedu.2020.103907
title: Mode affordance and the humanizing voice account of source evaluation in videos
description: The article draws on social semiotics to define "mode affordance" as "the ability of each mode to easily convey a particular information aspect", noting videos visually present the author and provide "additional credibility cues conveyed by particular modes". The humanizing voice hypothesis holds that voice and the author's visible presence make sources seem more human and trustworthy, so students adopt views conveyed in videos more than those in texts. The study's belief-shift results are read as supporting this account over the persuasiveness of print hypothesis.
requirements: Videos must make the source visually salient (e.g., the author on camera) for the credibility cues to operate
constraints: The article notes the humanizing effect was demonstrated for sources depicted on video, and the persuasiveness-of-print effect may fade as students gain broader reading experience
target_learners: primary school students (grades 4-6)
target_learning_goals: evaluating source credibility in multimodal documents
examples: In the video-against-bottled-water condition, students shifted toward the view expressed in the video by the expert author

citation: Vo, H. N. (2020). Understanding higher education learners' acceptance and use of mobile devices for language learning: A Rasch-based path modeling approach. Computers and Education, 146, Article 103761. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.compedu.2019.103761
title: Modified UTAUT model as a framework for examining MALL acceptance.
description: The modified UTAUT model (Dwivedi et al., 2019) adds attitude as an additional construct to the original UTAUT and drops all moderating variables. It proposes that performance expectancy, effort expectancy, social influence, and facilitating condition predict attitude and behavioral intention, which in turn predict use behavior. The study found the model fit the data well and concluded it is "an appropriate model for examining MALL acceptance" in the Vietnamese context.

constraints: Cross-sectional design; changing attitudes and behavior over time were not modeled

article_title: The Effects of Mathematical Modelling on Students' Achievement-Meta-Analysis of Research
citation: Andrzej Sokolowski. (2015). The Effects of Mathematical Modelling on Students’ Achievement-Meta-Analysis of Research. The IAFOR Journal of Education, Volume III - Issue I - Winter 2015. https://journals.iafor.org/index.php/joe
title: Modelling cycles: staged structure of mathematical modelling activity
description: The article describes mathematical modelling as an activity with a staged structure called modelling cycles, citing Blum and Leiss (2007). The stages are "understanding the problem (constructing), simplifying (structuring), mathematizing, working mathematically, interpreting, validating and exposing", with transitions involving observations, measurements, and interactions described as data. The meta-analysis uses this framing to characterize what treatment groups experienced, and notes models—the products—are simplified but accurate representations of aspects of the real world.
requirements: Learners progress through the stages with teacher guidance rather than direct solutions, consistent with the constructivist paradigm the article attributes to Hussmann (2007)
constraints: Conducting real experiments is difficult in mathematics classrooms traditionally not designed for that purpose, so supports such as computerized experiments may be needed
target_learners: high school mathematics students
college mathematics students
target_learning_goals: applying mathematics to extra-mathematical situations
constructing and validating mathematical models
examples: The 13 meta-analyzed studies all placed students in student-centered settings deriving models for given problems, using teachers' expertise only when needed

article_title: Impact of continuing professional development (CPD) on patient outcomes: a systematic scoping review.
citation: Ali Salwa, Sethi Ahsan, Soltani Abderrezzaq, Nazar Zachariah. (2025). Impact of continuing professional development (CPD) on patient outcomes: a systematic scoping review. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-025-07883-4
title: Moore's modified CPD outcome framework for evaluating CPD effectiveness across seven levels
description: Moore's modified CPD outcome framework provides a structure for evaluating CPD effectiveness across multiple levels, from participation and satisfaction (levels 1–2) through knowledge and competence acquisition (levels 3–4) to performance change, patient health improvement, and population health impact (levels 5–7). The review uses this framework to highlight that most CPD evaluations focus on lower levels, with few studies examining higher-level outcomes related to patient and population health. It serves as one of several established evaluation frameworks, alongside Kirkpatrick's Four-Level Model and Stufflebeam's CIPP Model.
requirements: Evaluation must map CPD outcomes across levels from participation and satisfaction through to population health impact
constraints: Most CPD evaluations focus primarily on the lower levels of this framework, with relatively few studies examining higher-level outcomes
target_learners: Healthcare professionals (physicians, nurses, pharmacists, dentists, allied health professionals)
target_learning_goals: Evaluating the effectiveness of continuing professional development programs in improving patient health outcomes

citation: Langan, L., Frazer, K., Darley, A., Goodman, L., Browne, F., Fulfilled, P., Halligan, P., & Redmond, C. (2025). title: Moriña's (2021) framework on inclusive pedagogy encourages educators to reflect on their underlying beliefs, knowledge, design and actions of EDI approaches to teaching and learning
description: Moriña's (2021) framework on inclusive pedagogy draws heavily from previous research evidenced in a systematic review and is particularly relevant in higher education. It "encourages educators to reflect on their underlying (1) beliefs, (2) knowledge, (3) design and (4) actions of EDI approaches to T&L". The framework is rooted in the belief that students are valuable contributors to the T&L process and are seen as an asset to the T&L environment, shifting the focus from providing learning opportunities for most students to focusing on providing opportunities for all students.
requirements: Educators need to have an in‐depth understanding of how and what students learn, and what students' individual needs are including disabilities.
target_learners: undergraduate nursing students
nurse educators
target_learning_goals: inclusive pedagogy
equality, diversity and inclusion in teaching and learning
key_sources: Langan, L., Frazer, K., Darley, A., Goodman, L., Browne, F., Fulfilled, P., Halligan, P., & Redmond, C. (2025). Inclusive pedagogy in online simulation‐based learning in undergraduate nursing education: A scoping review. Journal of Advanced Nursing, 81, 591–606. https://doi.org/10.1111/jan.16284

article_title: Healthcare research and education: actively constructed research knowledge-a model for online systematic reviews and meta-analyses courses.
citation: El Ansari Walid, El-Ansari Kareem, Hany Mohamed. (2025). Healthcare research and education: actively constructed research knowledge–a model for online systematic reviews and meta-analyses courses. BMC Research Notes. https://doi.org/10.1186/s13104-025-07111-8
title: Model online SR/MA course design framework
description: The article proposes a model online SR/MA course that integrates self-paced and self-directed learning, high interactivity, expert-guided feedback, and PRISMA alignment. It is designed for busy medical and health students and clinicians, delivered via Moodle LMS, and structured so that learners progressively build skills across modules, culminating in a real learner-performed SR/MA project within virtual research teams. The framework emphasizes the 'human' factor through synchronous and asynchronous trainer-learner and learner-learner interactions.
requirements: Utilizes Moodle LMS for content delivery, assignment submission, and communication
Requires expert trainers with discipline-specific knowledge and SR/MA skills to provide individualized feedback
constraints: Designed for SR/MA training in health, medical, surgical and related fields
target_learners: Medical and health students
Clinicians
target_learning_goals: Conducting systematic reviews and meta-analyses
Applying PRISMA principles
Critical appraisal and quality assessment
key_sources: El Ansari Walid, El-Ansari Kareem, Hany Mohamed. (2025). Healthcare research and education: actively constructed research knowledge–a model for online systematic reviews and meta-analyses courses. BMC Research Notes. https://doi.org/10.1186/s13104-025-07111-8

description: The proposed course utilizes the Moodle learning management system (LMS) platform for distributing training materials and assignments, enabling communication and feedback. The article states Moodle is recognized for its effectiveness in collaborative online learning and assessments, and enables a clear overview of course structure, supports synchronous and asynchronous communication, and provides a centralized hub for assignment submission and evaluation.

Platform must support assignment submission, resubmission, and expert evaluation

article_title: Instructional design features in ultrasound-guided regional anaesthesia simulation-based training: a systematic review.
citation: Sekhavati P, Wild T, Martinez IDPC, Dion PM, Woo M, Ramlogan R, Boet S, Shorr R, Gu Y. (2025). Instructional design features in ultrasound‐guided regional anaesthesia simulation‐based training: a systematic review. Anaesthesia. https://doi.org/10.1111/anae.16527
title: Modified Kirkpatrick model for classifying simulation training outcomes
description: The review applies a modified Kirkpatrick model with four levels to classify outcomes of ultrasound‐guided regional anaesthesia simulation training. Level 1 assesses learners' perceptions including satisfaction and confidence; level 2 evaluates "knowledge acquisition, skills and attitudes"; level 3 examines behavioural changes in the professional setting such as transfer of skills to clinical practice; and level 4 measures outcomes of learners' actions such as patient outcomes and block success. The model structures the review's synthesis of which instructional design features accompany which outcome levels.
requirements: Studies must report outcomes classifiable into one of the four modified Kirkpatrick levels
constraints: The review notes the restrictive definition of Kirkpatrick level outcomes limits identification of studies investigating process or time to perform a skill on a patient rather than patient outcomes directly
target_learners: healthcare providers including staff physicians, postgraduate trainees and medical students
target_learning_goals: ultrasound‐guided regional anaesthesia skills including sono‐anatomy knowledge and needling skills
key_sources: Sekhavati P, Wild T, Martinez IDPC, Dion PM, Woo M, Ramlogan R, Boet S, Shorr R, Gu Y. (2025). Instructional design features in ultrasound‐guided regional anaesthesia simulation‐based training: a systematic review. Anaesthesia. https://doi.org/10.1111/anae.16527

article_title: Motivation Theories and Constructs in Experimental Studies of Online Instruction: Systematic Review and Directed Content Analysis.
citation: Lesselroth Blake; Papadakis Stamatis; Lo Chung; Gavarkovs Adam PhD; Miller Erin PhD; Coleman Jaimie MPT; Gunasegaran Tharsiga HBSc; Kusurkar Rashmi A MD, PhD; Kulasegaram Kulamakan PhD; Anderson Melanie MLiS; Brydges Ryan PhD. (2025). Motivation Theories and Constructs in Experimental Studies of Online Instruction: Systematic Review and Directed Content Analysis. JMIR Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.2196/64179
title: Six-category taxonomy of motivational constructs targeted by instructional design strategies
description: The review organizes motivational constructs targeted by online design strategies into six a priori categories derived from prominent motivation theories and prior research. The authors state: "Our list included the following categories of motivational constructs: intrinsic value beliefs (eg, interest), extrinsic value beliefs (eg, instrumentality), competence and control beliefs (eg, self-efficacy), social connectedness (eg, relatedness), autonomy, and goals." Intrinsic value refers to value derived from completing an activity, whereas extrinsic value refers to value derived from outcomes external to the activity. This taxonomy served as the deductive coding scheme for the directed content analysis.
requirements: Coding requires a priori construct categories derived from established motivation theories and prior motivational research.
constraints: The categorization scheme was refined during coding from the published protocol, aggregating more constructs into fewer categories.
target_learners: Health professions learners
target_learning_goals: Learner motivation in online instruction
examples: The review used the taxonomy to code 46 experimental comparison studies of online motivational design strategies.
key_sources: Lesselroth Blake; Papadakis Stamatis; Lo Chung; Gavarkovs Adam PhD; Miller Erin PhD; Coleman Jaimie MPT; Gunasegaran Tharsiga HBSc; Kusurkar Rashmi A MD, PhD; Kulasegaram Kulamakan PhD; Anderson Melanie MLiS; Brydges Ryan PhD. article_title: Research education and training for nurses and allied health professionals: a systematic scoping review.
citation: King, O., West, E., Lee, S., Glenister, K., Quilliam, C., Wong, S. A., & Beks, H. (2022). Research education and training for nurses and allied health professionals: a systematic scoping review. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-022-03406-7
title: Modified Kirkpatrick educational outcomes typology as a multi-level framework for mapping research education outcomes
description: The review used Barr and colleagues' modified Kirkpatrick educational outcomes typology as its organising framework for classifying the outcomes that research education programs report. The typology "gives rise to the identification of outcome measures at multiple levels", reflecting that individuals, programs, organisational and other factors interact to produce various outcomes. The review mapped every included program's reported outcomes onto this typology, which exposed the concentration of evaluation at lower levels such as satisfaction and confidence.
requirements: Outcomes measured and reported in the papers must be mappable to the typology's levels or domains
constraints: The review notes complex interactions between individuals, programs, organisational and other factors make discernment between education interventions and other RCB strategy elements a fraught endeavour
target_learners: nurses
midwives
allied health professionals
pharmacists
target_learning_goals: research knowledge and skills
evidence-based practice capability
research capacity building
examples: Outcomes of the 68 included programs were mapped to the typology, revealing lower-level outcomes such as satisfaction, improved research knowledge and confidence dominated
key_sources: King, O., West, E., Lee, S., Glenister, K., Quilliam, C., Wong, S. A., & Beks, H. (2022). Research education and training for nurses and allied health professionals: a systematic scoping review. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-022-03406-7

article_title: The development and implementation of a 12-month simulation-based learning curriculum for pediatric emergency medicine fellows utilizing debriefing with good judgment and rapid cycle deliberate practice.
citation: Jeffers, J. M., & Poling, S. (2019). The development and implementation of a 12-month simulation-based learning curriculum for pediatric emergency medicine fellows utilizing debriefing with good judgment and rapid cycle deliberate practice. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-018-1417-6
title: 12-month longitudinal simulation curriculum with monthly 2–4 hour sessions pairing a good-judgment debrief scenario with an RCDP scenario
description: The curriculum ran monthly for 2–4 hours (nine 2-hour sessions and three 4-hour sessions integrating procedural skills) over 12 months, so fellows encounter the full curriculum twice across a three-year fellowship. "Each two-hour session had two scenarios. One utilized debriefing with good judgment to focus on mental models, teamwork, and thought processing to fill in performance gaps"; the second used RCDP for procedural skills and integration. Monthly core concepts allowed scenario flexibility relating to recent real patients, and seasonality shaped content scheduling.
requirements: A 12-month duration sized to an estimated attendance rate so learners are exposed to the curriculum twice during fellowship
A core educator present at all sessions
Monthly core concepts to allow flexible, real-patient-related scenarios
constraints: Attendance around 68% due to off-campus rotations, work hour rules, and conference attendance
Sessions held in the institution's Medical Simulation Center
target_learners: pediatric emergency medicine fellows (two per year, six per academic year)
target_learning_goals: procedural competence
crisis resource management and teamwork
management of complex medical and traumatic pediatric emergencies
examples: Hypothermia from cold water drowning was scheduled for winter and the first cardiac session occurred early in the academic year; airway management procedures recurred across many months rather than only in the airway skills session
key_sources: Jeffers, J. M., & Poling, S. (2019). The development and implementation of a 12-month simulation-based learning curriculum for pediatric emergency medicine fellows utilizing debriefing with good judgment and rapid cycle deliberate practice. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-018-1417-6

article_title: Is computer-assisted instruction more effective than other educational methods in achieving ECG competence amongst medical students and residents? A systematic review and meta-analysis.
citation: Viljoen Charle André, Scott Millar Rob, Engel Mark E, Shelton Mary, Burch Vanessa. (2019). Is computer-assisted instruction more effective than other educational methods in achieving ECG competence amongst medical students and residents? A systematic review and meta-analysis. BMJ Open. https://doi.org/10.1136/bmjopen-2018-028800
title: Modified Kirkpatrick framework for evaluating educational interventions in ECG training studies
description: The review applied a modified version of the Kirkpatrick framework to classify the outcomes of the included educational interventions. It appraises outcomes at levels measuring "participants' perceptions of (reactions to) the learning experience (level 1)", modification of attitudes and perceptions (level 2a), modification of knowledge and/or skills (level 2b), transfer to the workplace (level 3), change in organisational practice (level 4a) and benefits to patients (level 4b). All thirteen included studies reported level 2b outcomes; none reported level 3 or 4 outcomes.
requirements: Studies must measure an objective outcome such as acquisition or retention of ECG competence to be classified at level 2b
constraints: None of the included studies evaluated CAI at Kirkpatrick level 3, 4a or 4b, which the review calls a widely recognised ongoing shortcoming of health professions education research
target_learners: medical students
residents enrolled for specialty training
target_learning_goals: ECG analysis and interpretation competence
examples: Eight studies reported participants' reactions to CAI (level 1) and three reported changes in attitudes and perceptions (level 2a), with variable and inconsistent preferences between CAI and lectures
key_sources: Viljoen Charle André, Scott Millar Rob, Engel Mark E, Shelton Mary, Burch Vanessa. (2019). Is computer-assisted instruction more effective than other educational methods in achieving ECG competence amongst medical students and residents? A systematic review and meta-analysis. article_title: Use of theory in computer-based interventions to reduce alcohol use among adolescents and young adults: a systematic review.
citation: Tebb Kathleen P., Erenrich Rebecca K., Jasik Carolyn Bradner, Berna Mark S., Lester James C., Ozer Elizabeth M. (2016). Use of theory in computer-based interventions to reduce alcohol use among adolescents and young adults: a systematic review. BMC Public Health 16, 517. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12889-016-3183-x
title: Modified Painter classification system for theory use in interventions (mentioned, applied, measured)
description: The review applies a modified version of Painter et al.'s classification system to categorize how each CBI uses theory. A CBI is classified as "mentioned" if an established broad theory is named, "applied" if any associated article describes how the theory informed the intervention, and "measured" if any article includes at least one measure of a construct within the theoretical framework. The authors state the classification system "offers a guiding framework for reporting how theory based principles can be applied to computer based interventions".
requirements: Requires review of all articles associated with a given CBI to classify mention, application, and measurement of theory
constraints: The 'measured' category departs from Painter's 'tested' category, which required over half of a theory's constructs to be measured; the fourth Painter category, building or creating theory, was not used because it was not applicable
target_learners: adolescents and young adults aged 12-21
target_learning_goals: preventing or reducing alcohol use through computer-based interventions
examples: Applied to 42 unique CBIs, with Tables 1 and 2 listing each intervention's theories, application descriptions, and measured constructs
key_sources: Tebb Kathleen P., Erenrich Rebecca K., Jasik Carolyn Bradner, Berna Mark S., Lester James C., Ozer Elizabeth M. (2016). citation: Mohd. Jasmy Abd Rahman, Mohd. Arif. Hj. Ismail & Muhammad Nasir. (2014). Development and Evaluation of the Effectiveness of Computer-Assisted Physics Instruction. International Education Studies, 7(13). https://doi.org/10.5539/ies.v7n13p14
title: Interactive physics software "Motion and Vector Analysis" for XI-grade motion and vector topics
description: A CD-ROM-based interactive physics learning package on motion and vector analysis for XI-grade senior high school students, aligned to the KTSP curriculum and built using Delphi Seventh version. It displays learning competences and visualizations including "Parabolic motion and motion component display" and "Circular motion display", with home page, main menu and learning options screens. The software was evaluated by design, pedagogic, technical and content experts and by 31 experienced physics teachers before classroom use.
requirements: Developed using the ADDIE Model design and Life Cycle Model, built in Delphi Seventh version, considering design, technical, pedagogical and content aspects of the learning material
constraints: Developed for the KTSP curriculum context of Indonesian SMA students in Pekanbaru on the motion and vector analysis topic

target_learning_goals: conceptual understanding of motion and vector analysis
learning motivation in physics
examples: Evaluated by nine experts across technique, content and pedagogy, then by 31 experienced physics teachers, then trialled in a quasi-experiment with two XI-grade classes

title: Model Eliciting Activities as a realistic-problem learning approach for constructing mathematical concepts
description: Model Eliciting Activities (MEA) is described as "one of the mathematical learning approaches which allows students to construct mathematical concepts through realistic problems". Students are involved directly in understanding concepts, discuss with classmates, create plans, and determine appropriate steps to solve mathematical problems, which the article says helps enhance their knowledge and reasoning ability. Software integration makes the teaching and learning process more interactive.

target_learners: junior high school students
target_learning_goals: constructing mathematical concepts
reasoning ability
examples: Both study groups received Model Eliciting Activities; the MEAC group additionally used Cabri 3D during the activities.

article_title: Distributional Moderation Analysis: Unpacking Moderation Effects in Intervention Research
citation: Wiedermann, W., Reinke, W. M., & Herman, K. C. (2025). Distributional moderation analysis: Unpacking moderation effects in intervention research. Journal of School Psychology, 108. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jsp.2024.101399
title: Moderated GAMLSS: distributional moderation modeled through interaction terms in up to six distribution-parameter equations
description: Moderated GAMLSS extends the inflated GAMLSS framework by adding treatment-by-moderator product terms to the regression equations for the location, dispersion, skewness, kurtosis, and the two scale-endpoint probability parameters. As the article states, "distributional moderation effects can be modeled through including proper interaction terms in the GAMLSS regression equations." For each outcome parameter, the sum of the treatment main effect and the interaction coefficient gives the conditional treatment effect moderated by m, and mean-centering the moderator makes the main effect a simple slope at the moderator's mean. Post-hoc probing uses the pick-a-point approach with pre-selected values such as the mean, mean ± 1 SD, or quartiles. The framework accommodates continuous, discrete, and mixed outcome distributions and random effects for nested designs.
requirements: Continuous moderators assumed to be mean-centered so that main effects are interpretable as simple slopes at the moderator mean

Selection of candidate distributions and covariates based on a priori theory; model selection via generalized Akaike Information Criterion and diagnostics such as wormplots and normalized quantile residuals
constraints: In the empirical application, skewness and kurtosis could not be explicitly modeled because the best-fitting LOGITNO distribution parameterizes only location and scale
target_learners: Students in cluster-randomized school-based intervention trials
target_learning_goals: Identifying contextual effect modifiers of intervention effects across the whole outcome distribution
examples: The article specifies a zero-inflated LOGITNO model with classroom-level random effects on all three estimated equations (location, scale, and the probability of no behavior concerns) for the IY TCM re-analysis
key_sources: Wiedermann, W., Reinke, W. M., & Herman, K. C. (2025). Distributional moderation analysis: Unpacking moderation effects in intervention research. Journal of School Psychology, 108. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jsp.2024.101399

article_title: From Challenging Assumptions to Measuring Effect: Researching the Nokia Mobile Mathematics Service in South Africa
citation: Roberts N, Spencer-Smith G, Vänskä R, Eskelinen S. (2015). From challenging assumptions to measuring effect: Researching the Nokia Mobile Mathematics Service in South Africa. South African Journal of Education, 35(2). https://doi.org/10.15700/saje.v35n2a1045
title: Strigel and Pouezevara framework of mobile learning configurations, extended with access/affordability and mathematical pedagogy spectrums
description: The article uses the Strigel and Pouezevara (2012) framework of "Variations on Mobile Learning Configurations", which attends to three spectrums: a learning spectrum from formal to informal, a kinetic spectrum from stationary to mobile, and a collaborative spectrum from individual to group work. The authors situate the service as informal but school-supported, mobile, and near the individual end. They argue two dimensions are missing: an access and affordability spectrum (from free public access and free broadband data to BYOD and private data contracts) and a mathematical pedagogy spectrum attending to knowledge, attitudes and beliefs about mathematics and how it is taught.
requirements: M-learning interventions in mathematics should position themselves in relation to contrasting approaches to Mathematics teaching and learning, for particular topics and age groups
constraints: The article states the framework as applied lacks dimensions for access/affordability and mathematical pedagogy in resource-constrained contexts
target_learners: Grade 10 Mathematics learners in South African public schools
target_learning_goals: Situating and comparing m-learning interventions supporting school Mathematics
examples: The service was plotted at Point A (informal but school-related), Point B (mobile end of kinetic spectrum) and Point C (near individual end) in Figure 1
key_sources: Roberts N, Spencer-Smith G, Vänskä R, Eskelinen S. (2015). From challenging assumptions to measuring effect: Researching the Nokia Mobile Mathematics Service in South Africa. South African Journal of Education, 35(2). https://doi.org/10.15700/saje.v35n2a1045

citation: Ahmed Yousif Abdelraheem & Abdelrahman Mohammed Ahmed. (2015). Effects of Activity Based Blended Learning Strategy on Prospective Teachers' Achievement and Motivation. i-manager's Journal of School Educational Technology, Vol. 11, No. 1, June - August 2015.
title: MOODLE-based enrichment activity set for activity-based blended learning
description: The experimental condition's instructional component: a MOODLE course management environment in which both groups completed shared activities (concept maps, ASSURE model application, presentations, videos, research papers, reflection), while the experimental group additionally completed enrichment activities such as "critical thinking in an online discussion", online quizzes, creating their own ASSURE model, presentations with Prezi, PresentationTube, PowToon and Emaze, videos with Camtasia and VideoStudio, and evaluating materials using rubrics. Resources and instructions were linked into MOODLE before the course started.

Resources, instructions, learning objectives and content materials created and linked into MOODLE before the course starts

target_learning_goals: educational technology knowledge and skills
online communication and collaboration skills
