article_title: On Mobile Device Security Practices and Training Efficacy: An Empirical Study
citation: Amita Goyal Chin, Ugochukwu Etudo, Mark A. Harris. (2016). On Mobile Device Security Practices and Training Efficacy: An Empirical Study. Informatics in Education, 15(2). https://doi.org/10.15388/infedu.2016.12
title: Motivated avoidance of sociopolitical information as an explanation for security training's failure to change behavior
description: The article applies Shepherd and Kay's (2012) theory of motivated avoidance of sociopolitical information, never before used in mobile security, to explain why mandatory self-paced training did not alter behavior. The theory describes a path beginning with "psychological discomfort associated with epistemic uncertainty," leading complex activities to prompt individuals to "simply outsource personal responsibility to supposed qualified others." The authors argue that trust in device manufacturers, software vendors, and regulators tempers the effect of awareness on behavior, producing information avoidance and inaction.
requirements: The account presumes learners perceive securing their devices as a complex activity amid a deluge of available information
constraints: The authors present this as an interpretive explanation consistent with their results, not as a tested mechanism in this study
target_learners: undergraduate business students using personal mobile devices
target_learning_goals: adopting secure mobile device practices
examples: The authors invoke the theory in the discussion to explain the indifferent attitude toward mobile security even after a mandatory, self-paced training program
key_sources: Amita Goyal Chin, Ugochukwu Etudo, Mark A. Harris. (2016). On Mobile Device Security Practices and Training Efficacy: An Empirical Study. Informatics in Education, 15(2). https://doi.org/10.15388/infedu.2016.12

article_title: The Effect of Modeling Based Science Education on Critical Thinking
citation: Bati, K. & Kaptan, F. (2015). The Effect of Modeling Based Science Education on Critical Thinking. Educational Policy Analysis and Strategic Research, 10(1). https://www.inased.org/
title: Modeling-based inquiry as a classroom process running from mental models to consensus models and experimental testing
description: The article organizes model-based science education around Gilbert's (2005) categories — "mental models, expressed models, consensus models, scientific models and teaching models" — and a modeling process that moves from encountering a problem, through forming and sharing temporary models, to systematic observation, model evaluation and revision. In the study's classroom version, students form and share mental models, choose a consensus model, assess it for usefulness, predictive power, coherence and testability, then experimentally test, accept, revise or reject it. The in-class process was deliberately stopped at the consensus stage.
requirements: Problem situations drawn from the curriculum subject titles, here the phenomena of electrification and electrical current
Experimental materials attainable enough for students to test their models empirically
constraints: The in-class modeling process was designed only up to the consensus stage because the next step would require participants to act as scientists
target_learners: 7th grade lower-secondary science students
target_learning_goals: Understanding electrification and electrical current
Critical thinking skills such as weighing evidence and creating cause-and-effect relations
examples: Activities such as Faraday and Electromagnetism, I am Making Electroscope, and Current Voltage Resistance had students design, share and experimentally test models of electrification and electrical current
key_sources: Bati, K. & Kaptan, F. (2015). The Effect of Modeling Based Science Education on Critical Thinking. Educational Policy Analysis and Strategic Research, 10(1). https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1127622

article_title: Mobile Technology and CAD Technology Integration in Teaching Architectural Design Process for Producing Creative Product
citation: Isham Shah bin Hassan, Ramlee Mustafa & Mohd Arif Ismail. (2011). Mobile Technology and CAD Technology Integration in Teaching Architectural Design Process for Producing Creative Product. i-manager's Journal of Educational Technology, 8(1). http://www.kajian_senireka.param.mobi
title: Mobile real-case website for architectural design information, built on Carroll's minimalist theory
description: A researcher-built mobile website that provides design information about real buildings of the same type students are designing, reachable "without time and place limits". It was developed following Kearsley's (1994) rendering of Carroll's minimalist theory: learners start immediately on meaningful tasks, reading is minimised, and activities are self-contained and independent of sequence. Students accessed it via mobile devices to gather focused information for their kindergarten design project.
requirements: Learning system must provide information without time and place constraints and let students choose and change information according to their needs (Chen and Kinshuk 2005, as cited)
constraints: Website content is tied to the same building type as the student project, so searching stays focused on project needs
target_learners: final-semester diploma architecture students in Malaysian polytechnics
target_learning_goals: gathering design information for architectural design projects
examples: Treatment students from POLIPD and PMM used the site during a six-week kindergarten design project, recording 392 searches (M=6.53) versus 178 (M=2.97) in the control group
key_sources: Isham Shah bin Hassan, Ramlee Mustafa & Mohd Arif Ismail. (2011). Mobile Technology and CAD Technology Integration in Teaching Architectural Design Process for Producing Creative Product. i-manager's Journal of Educational Technology, 8(1). https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1102114

article_title: Mobile Technology and CAD Technology Integration in Teaching Architectural Design Process for Producing Creative Product
citation: Isham Shah bin Hassan, Ramlee Mustafa & Mohd Arif Ismail. (2011). Mobile Technology and CAD Technology Integration in Teaching Architectural Design Process for Producing Creative Product. i-manager's Journal of Educational Technology, 8(1). http://www.kajian_senireka.param.mobi
title: Conceptual framework integrating mobile information access and CAD ideation to produce creative design products
description: The study's framework combines Carroll's minimal theory (1995) for the mobile website, Brown and Campione's learning-with-technology theory (1996) for technology integration, and the Creative Product Analysis Matrix (CPAM) of Besemer and Treffinger (1981) for evaluating creativity. It posits two independent variables — use of web mobile for obtaining design information and use of CAD technology in creating new ideas — influencing one outcome, the creative product. CAD integration occurs at the synthesis stage, the simulation stage and before producing the final creative product, with stage products compared across the process.
requirements: Integration should use "the latest equipments required to get the accurate results" per Brown and Campione's theory as applied by the researcher
constraints: The study concentrates on the schematic stage of design, involving sketching and schematic design, not the whole process
target_learners: polytechnic diploma architecture students
target_learning_goals: producing creative architectural design products
examples: The framework was operationalised in a six-week quasi-experiment across four polytechnics using ACAD 2007 and 3D Studio Viz, with stage products evaluated by lecturer raters
key_sources: Isham Shah bin Hassan, Ramlee Mustafa & Mohd Arif Ismail. (2011). Mobile Technology and CAD Technology Integration in Teaching Architectural Design Process for Producing Creative Product. i-manager's Journal of Educational Technology, 8(1). https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1102114

article_title: The Effect of Using Flipped Classroom in Teaching Calculus on Students' Achievements at University of Tabuk
citation: Albalawi, A.S. (2018). The effect of using flipped classroom in teaching calculus on students‟ achievement at University of Tabuk. International Journal of Research in Education and Science (IJRES), 4(1), 198-207. https://doi.org/10.21890/ijres.383137
title: Moodle-delivered flipped Math2 course designed with the ADDIE model
description: The study's treatment artifact: the Math2 calculus course was reorganized "with the analysis, design, development, implementation, and evaluation (ADDIE model)" and launched on the Moodle platform, with recorded videos of the course content uploaded and available to the treatment group at any time. The control group had no access to the videos. The achievement instrument was validated by expert review, with correlation coefficients from 0.67-0.92, item difficulty 0.35-0.75, and Cronbach's alpha 0.902.
requirements: Recorded videos of the course topics must be available to students at any time via a platform such as Moodle
constraints: Implemented only for male preparatory-year students in three calculus topics (limits and continuity, differentiation, applications of differentiation) during fall semester 2015-2016
target_learners: preparatory-year (freshman) science-major students at University of Tabuk
target_learning_goals: calculus achievement in the Math2 course
examples: The treatment group used the flipped calculus course for a whole semester while the control group was taught without video access
key_sources: Albalawi, A.S. (2018). The effect of using flipped classroom in teaching calculus on students‟ achievement at University of Tabuk. International Journal of Research in Education and Science (IJRES), 4(1), 198-207. https://doi.org/10.21890/ijres.383137

article_title: A Randomized Control Trial on the Effects of MoBeGo, a Self-Monitoring App for Challenging Behavior
citation: Allison Bruhn, Joseph Wehby, Lesa Hoffman, Sara Estrapala, Ashley Rila, Eleanor Hancock, Alyssa Van Camp, Amanda Sheaffer, and Bailey Copeland. (2022). A Randomized Control Trial on the Effects of MoBeGo, a Self-Monitoring App for Challenging Behavior. Behavioral Disorders, 48(1), 29–43. https://doi.org/10.1177/01987429221093987
title: MoBeGo self-monitoring app with automated data-based goal adaptation
description: MoBeGo is a multicomponent mobile self-monitoring app with parallel teacher and student components in which both independently rate the student's behavior on a fixed interval schedule (e.g., every 5 min) on a 0–4 scale. The app calculates an individualized initial goal 10 percentage points above the baseline median, graphs teacher and student ratings, and its "data-based algorithm" notifies teachers and students when a goal should be increased or decreased. It was developed iteratively by the authors through an Institute of Education Sciences grant.
requirements: Teacher collects 5 days of covert baseline ratings before the student begins self-monitoring
Teachers and students are trained individually (about 2 hr for teachers, 30 min for students) to 100% proficiency
Required components include precorrection, teacher and student rating, and end-of-session feedback
constraints: The article notes fidelity was lower for precorrection (60.88%) and end-of-session feedback (69.82%) than for teacher (98.00%) and student (98.63%) ratings
Teachers may decline the app's recommended goal changes
target_learners: third- to eighth-grade students with challenging classroom behavior
target_learning_goals: increased academic engagement
reduced disruptive behavior
self-regulation of behavior
examples: In the trial, teachers selected one to four replacement behaviors from a list of 10 default behaviors (e.g., Be On-Task, Be Respectful), and 15 of 28 teachers elected to add contingent reinforcement
key_sources: Allison Bruhn, Joseph Wehby, Lesa Hoffman, Sara Estrapala, Ashley Rila, Eleanor Hancock, Alyssa Van Camp, Amanda Sheaffer, and Bailey Copeland. (2022). A Randomized Control Trial on the Effects of MoBeGo, a Self-Monitoring App for Challenging Behavior. Behavioral Disorders, 48(1), 29–43. https://doi.org/10.1177/01987429221093987

article_title: The Effects of Mosaic Based Approach on Involvement Levels of Children
citation: Akyol, T., & Erkan, S. (2018). The effects of mosaic based approach on involvement levels of children. International Journal of Educational Methodology, 4(4), 303-309. https://doi.org/10.12973/ijem.4.4.303
title: The mosaic approach: a three-stage participatory framework for listening to young children
description: The mosaic approach, developed by Peter Moss and Alison Clark, creates environments reflecting children's perspectives of their educational institutions by combining information "obtained from different methods and resources". It uses visual, physical, and oral tools such as camera use, album-map creation, and in-school tours alongside observations and interviews. It proceeds in three stages: collecting information from different sources, sharing and interpreting that information with children and teachers, and deciding with children what can change or stay the same and making adjustments.
requirements: Children and teachers should effectively participate in the second stage of sharing and interpreting information
constraints: The approach was developed based on research conducted in England between 1999-2000
target_learners: preschool children (five-year-olds in this study)
target_learning_goals: children's active participation and expression of opinions and experiences in educational institutions
examples: The authors built a 10-week education program embedding all three mosaic stages in each of three themes (learning centres, activity types, play areas)
key_sources: Akyol, T., & Erkan, S. (2018). The effects of mosaic based approach on involvement levels of children. International Journal of Educational Methodology, 4(4), 303-309. https://doi.org/10.12973/ijem.4.4.303

article_title: The Effects of Mosaic Based Approach on Involvement Levels of Children
citation: Akyol, T., & Erkan, S. (2018). The effects of mosaic based approach on involvement levels of children. International Journal of Educational Methodology, 4(4), 303-309. https://doi.org/10.12973/ijem.4.4.303
title: Mosaic Approach Based Education Programme for five-year-old children
description: A 10-week education program developed by the authors to develop the involvement level of five-year-old children, applied "3 days per week, 4 hours per day" for a total of 120 hours. It included Turkish, art, play, movement, drama, music, and science and mathematics activities, organised into three themes (learning centres, activity types, play areas) with three education plans per theme, each theme embedding the three mosaic stages. It was reviewed by 7 academicians and an experienced preschool teacher and piloted in August 2016 before application.
requirements: Expert review and pilot application were conducted, with corrections applied before full implementation
constraints: Applied within class, interior of school building, school garden, and tour areas outside school; themes lasted 9, 11, and 10 days respectively
target_learners: five-year-old children in preschool education
target_learning_goals: children's involvement levels
examples: Applied to the experimental group between 03 October 2016 and 09 December 2016 while the control group received the Ministry of National Education Pre-School Education Program (2013)
key_sources: Akyol, T., & Erkan, S. (2018). The effects of mosaic based approach on involvement levels of children. International Journal of Educational Methodology, 4(4), 303-309. https://doi.org/10.12973/ijem.4.4.303

article_title: The Influence of Blended Learning Environment on Self-Regulated and Self-Directed Learning Skills of Learners
citation: Uz, R., & Uzun, A. (2018). The influence of blended learning environment on self-regulated and self-directed learning skills of learners. European Journal of Educational Research, 7(4), 877-886. https://doi.org/10.12973/eu-jer.7.4.877
title: Moodle-based blended learning environment with SCORM learning objects, projects and forums for a Programming Languages course
description: The article designed a blended environment for a Programming Languages course combining face-to-face direct instruction and question-and-answer with a Moodle online component. Weekly materials included "presentations, videos, tests, projects and forums", and database topics were prepared as five interactive Adobe Captivate learning objects packed as compatible with SCORM, each ending with practice questions and visible scores so students "could evaluate their self -progress". A four-week text-file project and forums supported interaction.
requirements: Learners need internet access to the web-based environment so they can reach materials at their convenience and at their own learning speed
constraints: Videos could be watched repeatedly but questions could be answered only three times
target_learners: undergraduate students in Computer Education and Instructional Technologies and Electronic Engineering departments
target_learning_goals: self-regulated learning skills
self-directed learning skills
programming languages content
examples: Database topics were covered with five learning objects built in Adobe Captivate, including evaluation questions and an individual success report link named Grades
key_sources: Uz, R., & Uzun, A. (2018). The influence of blended learning environment on self-regulated and self-directed learning skills of learners. European Journal of Educational Research, 7(4), 877-886. https://doi.org/10.12973/eu-jer.7.4.877

article_title: CALL, Prewriting Strategies, and EFL Writing Quantity
citation: Sajad Shafiee, Mansour Koosha & Akbar Afghari. (2015). CALL, Prewriting Strategies, and EFL Writing Quantity. English Language Teaching, 8(2). http://dx.doi.org/10.5539/elt.v8n2p170
title: Model how to apply prewriting strategies, not just describe them
description: The article's discussion holds that strategy instruction works when learners are shown application, not merely told about strategies. It states the experimental groups succeeded "probably because the former were not merely made versed in metacognitive prewriting strategies" and that "What they were subjected to was indeed the teacher’s modeling of how to apply prewriting strategies". This aligns with the modeling step of the strategy-instruction model used.
requirements: Teacher modeling of strategy application during instruction
constraints: The article offers this as an interpretation of why its experimental groups outperformed the control group, not as a separately tested manipulation
target_learners: EFL learners, particularly novice writers
target_learning_goals: Effective use of prewriting strategies
Improved writing ability and quantity
examples: In the study's experimental conditions, teachers modeled how to apply the targeted prewriting strategies within the strategy-instruction sequence
key_sources: Sajad Shafiee, Mansour Koosha & Akbar Afghari. (2015). CALL, Prewriting Strategies, and EFL Writing Quantity. English Language Teaching, 8(2). http://dx.doi.org/10.5539/elt.v8n2p170

article_title: The Effect of a Computer Program Based on Analysis, Design, Development, Implementation and Evaluation (ADDIE) in Improving Ninth Graders' Listening and Reading Comprehension Skills in English in Jordan
citation: Talal Alodwan & Mosaab Almosa. (2018). The Effect of a Computer Program Based on Analysis, Design, Development, Implementation and Evaluation (ADDIE) in Improving Ninth Graders' Listening and Reading Comprehension Skills in English in Jordan. English Language Teaching, 11(4). https://doi.org/10.5539/elt.v11n4p43
title: Devote more concentration and time to listening and reading comprehension in basic schools
description: The article recommends that more concentration and time be devoted to listening and reading comprehension in basic schools, noting that "students at this level lack the listening and the reading comprehension proficiency". It specifically recommends lengthening the period given to each listening and reading comprehension class. This principle rests on the study's diagnosis of weak receptive skills in Jordanian schools and on its finding that a technology-based program improved both skills.
requirements: School timetabling that can accommodate longer listening and reading comprehension periods
constraints: Stated for basic schools in Jordan where English exposure is minimal
target_learners: basic-school EFL students in Jordan
target_learning_goals: listening comprehension proficiency
reading comprehension proficiency
examples: The researcher recommends that the period given to each listening and reading comprehension class should be lengthened
key_sources: Talal Alodwan & Mosaab Almosa. (2018). The Effect of a Computer Program Based on Analysis, Design, Development, Implementation and Evaluation (ADDIE) in Improving Ninth Graders' Listening and Reading Comprehension Skills in English in Jordan. English Language Teaching, 11(4). https://doi.org/10.5539/elt.v11n4p43

article_title: A Pedagogical Perspective on Promoting English as a Foreign Language Writing through Online Forum Discussions
citation: Jayaron Jose & Mohammed Jafre Zainol Abidin. (2016). A Pedagogical Perspective on Promoting English as a Foreign Language Writing through Online Forum Discussions. English Language Teaching, 9(2). https://doi.org/10.5539/elt.v9n2p84
title: Moodle-mediated synchronous forum and asynchronous blog tools for EFL writing practice
description: Moodle is an open-source Learning Management System used at Al Musanna College of Technology, Oman, as the platform for the study. It "facilitates the interaction of students through asynchronous (individual blogs) and synchronous (real-time forum discussion) communications". The Forum tool served the experimental group for synchronous discussions and its blog format served the control group for asynchronous writing over ten topics.
requirements: Well-equipped learning management system with effective infrastructures and facilities
Two weeks of training in using the OFD and blog tools
Pre-booked computer labs with technician support
constraints: Moodle does not have the option of grouping a batch of students into groups of 3 or 4, so participants could not easily locate group members' posts
target_learners: tertiary EFL students
target_learning_goals: EFL writing in the target language through online interaction
examples: Ten topics relevant to learners' social and academic context were displayed on the e-learning page for discussion or writing
key_sources: Jayaron Jose & Mohammed Jafre Zainol Abidin. (2016). A Pedagogical Perspective on Promoting English as a Foreign Language Writing through Online Forum Discussions. English Language Teaching, 9(2). https://doi.org/10.5539/elt.v9n2p84

article_title: The Effect of Mock Tests on Iranian EFL Learners' Test Scores
citation: Hossein Khodabakhshzadeh, Reza Zardkanloo, Iman Alipoor. (2017). The Effect of Mock Tests on Iranian EFL learners’ Test Scores. International Journal of Education & Literacy Studies 5(3). http://dx.doi.org/10.7575/aiac.ijels.v.5n.3p.47
title: Mock-test intervention procedure for IELTS preparation courses
description: An instructional component in which IELTS candidates sit a complete mock test every class session instead of receiving content instruction. Over 10 weekly sessions across 3 months, "The four different sections of the test were administered and the results were emailed to the learners prior to the next session." No particular teaching was done and no discussions were held after the tests. Speaking and writing were scored with CEFR rubrics and reading and listening with an answer key; the four skill scores were averaged into one overall gained score for analysis.
requirements: Two different versions of the IELTS academic module (administered by the British Council in 2016) as pretest and posttest
Consent forms administered at the beginning of the study
The same teacher conducted both groups' classes
constraints: No particular teaching was done in the mock-test group and no discussions were held after the test to discuss test issues
target_learners: Upper-intermediate and advanced IELTS candidates aged 18-29
target_learning_goals: Overall IELTS score across the four test sections
examples: Group 1 received a mock test every session with results emailed before the next session; Group 2 received deductive, rule-based instruction with role-play practice of speaking part 1
key_sources: Hossein Khodabakhshzadeh, Reza Zardkanloo, Iman Alipoor. (2017). The Effect of Mock Tests on Iranian EFL learners’ Test Scores. International Journal of Education & Literacy Studies 5(3). http://dx.doi.org/10.7575/aiac.ijels.v.5n.3p.47

article_title: Improvement of the Robotics Cross-Cutting Course for Training of Specialists in Professions of the Future
citation: Elena V. Soboleva, Nikita L. Karavaev, Nadezhda V. Shalaginova, Marina S. Perevozchikova. (2018). Improvement of the Robotics Cross-Cutting Course for Training of Specialists in Professions of the Future. European Journal of Contemporary Education, 7(4). https://doi.org/10.13187/ejced.2018.4.845
title: In robotics training, verification should rely on monitoring the results of students' cognitive activity rather than on tests and quizzes
description: The article argues that among the components of the methodical system, control deserves particular attention in robotics courses. Because learners gain fundamental theoretical knowledge through experimentation and object manipulation, the leading form of verification should be monitoring of cognitive-activity results in the form of a project, model, system or problem solution. As the authors put it, "It is impossible during the training of robotics to reduce control to evaluation through tests, quests, crosswords, since the learner gets the necessary fundamental theoretical knowledge precisely through experimentation and object manipulation." The experiment's control work operationalised this with competence-referenced criteria for excellent, good and satisfactory solutions.
requirements: Assessment criteria must correspond to the essence of the formed competences, e.g. seeing system integrity, structure and system-environment relations, and independence in choosing scope, algorithm and solution method
target_learners: school and university students in robotics courses
target_learning_goals: cross-professional competence formation in robotics and engineering
examples: The experimental control work rated students excellent when they independently saw system integrity, interpreted software error messages and searched for ways to improve the mechanism
key_sources: Elena V. Soboleva, Nikita L. Karavaev, Nadezhda V. Shalaginova, Marina S. Perevozchikova. (2018). Improvement of the Robotics Cross-Cutting Course for Training of Specialists in Professions of the Future. European Journal of Contemporary Education, 7(4). https://doi.org/10.13187/ejced.2018.4.845

article_title: Evaluating the Effects of Mother Tongue on Math and Science Instruction
citation: Behrmann, T. (2018). Evaluating the effects of mother tongue on math and science instruction. Monument, CO, USA: ISTES Organization. https://www.istes.org
title: Use students' mother tongue as the medium of instruction so they can grasp concepts and later transfer knowledge to other languages
description: The article recommends making Kreyol the language of instruction in Haitian classrooms because students can then acquire a solid grasp of concepts in the only language they know. As the introduction states, using Kreyol "would possibly ensure that students grasp concepts presented", after which students may transfer knowledge to French or another language. The principle does not call for replacing French but for building conceptual understanding first in the mother tongue, consistent with the international program evidence the review cites.
requirements: Instructional materials and teacher proficiency in the mother tongue, since the article notes teacher content proficiency affects transmission of information
constraints: The article notes Kreyol is seen as the language of the poor and that social advancement in Haiti is tied to French mastery, creating resistance to implementation
target_learners: Haitian students, primarily monolingual Kreyol speakers, in primary and secondary math and science classes
target_learning_goals: Conceptual understanding in math and science
Literacy in the mother tongue
Later transfer of knowledge to a second language
examples: The study implemented this principle by teaching designated classrooms' math and science lessons in Kreyol while a control group received the same concepts in French
key_sources: Behrmann, T. (2018). Evaluating the effects of mother tongue on math and science instruction. Monument, CO, USA: ISTES Organization. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED603513

article_title: Effects of Using Model Robots in the Education of Programming
citation: Attila PÁSZTOR, Róbert PAP-SZIGETI, Erika LAKATOS TÖRÖK. (2010). Effects of Using Model Robots in the Education of Programming. Informatics in Education, 9(1), 133–140. https://doi.org/10.15388/infedu.2010.09
title: Model Robot Programming subject: constructivist project-based lessons with LEGO NXT robots in small groups
description: A semester-long subject in which only about twenty percent of lessons use traditional teacher explanation and presentation; new material is introduced by examples, and students then "solve programming problems and tasks in groups of two-three members". The central activity is a group project to write an algorithm and program and build a robot controlled by that program, with documentation, video and slides presented to classmates and evaluated by teachers, other students and group members.
requirements: Real programmable devices (LEGO NXT robots)
group work of two-three members
teacher acting as facilitator rather than transferring knowledge
constraints: Traditional teaching methods are still retained for about twenty percent of the total lessons
target_learners: college IT students who meet programming first at higher education
target_learning_goals: basic programming structures
problem solving
collaborative knowledge building
examples: Students produced documentation, video and slides of their robot project and presented them, with evaluation by teachers, peers and project group members
key_sources: Attila PÁSZTOR, Róbert PAP-SZIGETI, Erika LAKATOS TÖRÖK. (2010). Effects of Using Model Robots in the Education of Programming. Informatics in Education, 9(1), 133–140. https://doi.org/10.15388/infedu.2010.09

article_title: Modifying a Research-Based Problem-Solving Intervention to Improve the Problem-Solving Performance of Fifth and Sixth Graders with and without Learning Disabilities
citation: Krawec, J., & Huang, J. (2017). Modifying a Research-Based Problem-Solving Intervention to Improve the Problem-Solving Performance of Fifth and Sixth Graders With and Without Learning Disabilities. Journal of Learning Disabilities, 50(4), 468–480. https://doi.org/10.1177/0022219416645565
title: Modified Solve It! problem-solving intervention: four PISA-aligned phases with seven cognitive strategies and embedded metacognitive self-regulation
description: The intervention aligns with the OECD/PISA problem-solving model, which "identifies four phases: (1) exploring and understanding, (2) representing and formulating, (3) planning and executing, and (4) monitoring and reflecting." Seven cognitive strategies (Read, Paraphrase, Visualize, Hypothesize, Estimate, Compute, Check) are embedded in Phases 1–3, while Phase 4 carries the metacognitive "say, ask, and check" self-regulation processes activated throughout. Instruction uses explicit teaching with cueing, modeling, rehearsal, and feedback. The goal is that students internalize the cognitive processes so they become automatic.
requirements: Explicit instruction methodology with structured lessons, scaffolded supports, guided and distributed practice, and immediate corrective feedback
Teacher professional development (a one and one-half day workshop) prior to implementation
constraints: Scope limited to single- and multistep problems using the four operations with whole numbers and decimals; open-ended problems were not included
target_learners: Fifth and sixth grade students of varying ability: average-achieving, low-achieving, and students with learning disabilities in inclusive math classrooms
target_learning_goals: Mathematical word problem solving: problem representation, solution planning, computation, and self-regulated monitoring
examples: General education math teachers taught six initial scripted 50-min lessons over consecutive school days, followed by weekly practice sessions (12–16 per year) with problems aligned to the district pacing guide
key_sources: Krawec, J., & Huang, J. (2017). Modifying a Research-Based Problem-Solving Intervention to Improve the Problem-Solving Performance of Fifth and Sixth Graders With and Without Learning Disabilities. Journal of Learning Disabilities, 50(4), 468–480. https://doi.org/10.1177/0022219416645565

article_title: Reducing Test Anxiety among Third Grade Students through the Implementation of Relaxation Techniques
citation: Heidi A. Larson, Mera K. El Ramahi, Steven R. Conn, Lincoln A. Estes, and Amanda B. Ghibellini. (2010). Reducing Test Anxiety Among Third Grade Students Through the Implementation of Relaxation Techniques. Eastern Illinois University. https://www.city-data.com
title: Modified Westside Test Anxiety Scale for young children
description: The Westside Test Anxiety Scale (WTAS; Driscoll, 2007) is a 10-item self-report instrument yielding a general test anxiety score, with subscales for incapacity (memory loss and poor cognitive processing) and worry/dread. For this study it was modified for young readers: "exam" was replaced with "test," "fail" was replaced with "bad job" and "mind sometimes wanders" was replaced with "daydream." The researchers used the total score, where higher scores indicate greater test anxiety.
requirements: Items must be understandable to young participants, which motivated the study's wording modifications
constraints: The article states validity had been shown only in some small samples, and reliability information was unavailable at the time of the study
target_learners: third-grade elementary students
target_learning_goals: measuring general test anxiety levels
examples: Internal consistency estimates (coefficient alphas of .88, .89, and .75 for the two experimental subgroups and control group) were calculated for this study
key_sources: Heidi A. Larson, Mera K. El Ramahi, Steven R. Conn, Lincoln A. Estes, and Amanda B. Ghibellini. (2010). Reducing Test Anxiety Among Third Grade Students Through the Implementation of Relaxation Techniques. Eastern Illinois University. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ885222

article_title: Is Case-Based Instruction Effective in Enhancing High School Students' Motivation toward Chemistry?
citation: Yalçınkaya, E., Boz, Y., & Erdur-Baker, Ö. (2012). Is case-based instruction effective in enhancing high school students' motivation toward chemistry? Science Education International, 23(2), 102-116. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ970613
title: Motivation as a goal-directed process inferred from choice, effort, and persistence
description: The article adopts Pintrich and Schunk's definition of motivation as "the process whereby goal -directed activity is instigated and sustained", treating motivation as a process rather than a product that cannot be observed directly but deduced from behaviors such as choice of tasks, effort, persistence, and verbalizations. It organizes motivation into six measurable components (intrinsic and extrinsic goal orientation, task value, control of learning beliefs, self-efficacy for learning and performance, and test anxiety), which serve as the study's dependent variables.
requirements: Measurement via self-report instruments such as the MSLQ motivation section, since motivation cannot be observed directly
constraints: The article treats this framework in the context of 10th-grade chemistry motivation; affective change is described as difficult to achieve
target_learners: 10th-grade high school chemistry students
target_learning_goals: Understanding and measuring students' motivational beliefs about chemistry
examples: The six MSLQ motivation subscales were used as dependent variables in the MANOVA on gain scores
key_sources: Yalçınkaya, E., Boz, Y., & Erdur-Baker, Ö. (2012). Is case-based instruction effective in enhancing high school students' motivation toward chemistry? Science Education International, 23(2), 102-116. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ975553

article_title: The Effects of the RAP Strategy Used in a Peer-Tutoring Setting to Foster Reading Comprehension in High-Risk Fourth Graders
citation: Leidig, T., Grünke, M., Urton, K., Knaak, T., & Hisgen, S. (2018). The Effects of the RAP Strategy Used in a Peer-tutoring Setting to Foster Reading Comprehension in High-Risk Fourth Graders. Learning Disabilities: A Contemporary Journal, 16(2), 231-253.
title: Combine strategy instruction with a multicomponent motivational system (scoring, visual feedback, attribution-based praise) rather than a token economy alone
description: The article concludes that pairing the RAP reading comprehension strategy with a motivational system comprising curriculum-based scoring, visual progress feedback, and verbal praise grounded in attribution theory is essential for effectiveness in peer-tutoring settings. The authors state that "a simple token economy did not have the same effect as the combination of monitoring progress, constant visual feedback, and frequent verbal praise" and that without such supports, "not much seems to be achieved by endeavors to boost students' comprehension skills." Tutors visualized tutee progress on graphs and gave attribution-based praise after each session.
requirements: A scoring system based on curriculum-based assessment, visual feedback displays, and verbal praise incorporating attribution theory principles must be embedded in the intervention
Tutors must be briefed on how to apply motivational tools to reduce or cope with disruptive and off-task behavior
constraints: The article's evidence comes from an explorative pilot with a small, unique sample; the authors note the explorative nature does not allow causal inferences
target_learners: low-achieving fourth-grade readers at risk for reading comprehension failure
students with learning disabilities or at risk for EBD in inclusive elementary classrooms
target_learning_goals: reading comprehension of expository texts
identifying main ideas and paraphrasing paragraph content
examples: Tutees earned a point per correct answer on five comprehension questions; tutors plotted scores on empty graphs and delivered internal attributions for success (e.g., effort) and variable attributions for setbacks
key_sources: Leidig, T., Grünke, M., Urton, K., Knaak, T., & Hisgen, S. (2018). The Effects of the RAP Strategy Used in a Peer-tutoring Setting to Foster Reading Comprehension in High-Risk Fourth Graders. Learning Disabilities: A Contemporary Journal, 16(2), 231-253. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1194573

article_title: Blended Learning Approach for Enhancing Students' Learning Experiences in a Knowledge Society
citation: Suprabha. K, & Subramonian, G. (2015). Blended learning approach for enhancing students learning experiences in a knowledge society. i-manager's Journal of Educational Technology, 11(4). http://www.eric.ed.gov
title: Model Driven Design for developing complex blended learning experiences
description: The article describes Model Driven Design (MDD), attributed to Stephen (2012), as "the concept of developing complex learning experiences through the use of a team model (how the team is staffed and empowered), a process model (how the experience is developed) and a perceptual model (how the experience is discussed and visualized)". It provides the ability to share models and learning units beyond the borders of the institution. The article presents blended learning as a process-model instructional design committing to steps from developing a curriculum concept and high-level design through detailed unit design, development of supporting digital materials, review and refinement, implementation, and ongoing assessment of program effectiveness.
requirements: A team model, a process model, and a perceptual model for developing complex learning experiences
Development of curriculum concepts, high-level and detailed unit designs, and supporting digital materials
target_learners: students in blended higher education programs
target_learning_goals: curriculum innovation
sustainable instructional design
examples: The article states that Model Driven Design provides a sustainable approach that reduces some of the cost of complex curriculum development and improves the sustainability of curriculum innovation.
key_sources: Suprabha. K, & Subramonian, G. (2015). Blended learning approach for enhancing students learning experiences in a knowledge society. i-manager's Journal of Educational Technology, 11(4). https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1098578

article_title: Advancing Diagnostic Skills for Technology and Engineering Undergraduates: A Summary of the Validation Data
citation: Foster, W. T., Shahhosseini, A. M., & Maughan, G. (2016). Advancing Diagnostic Skills for Technology and Engineering Undergraduates: A Summary of the Validation Data. Journal of Technology Education, 28(1). https://scholar.lib.vt.edu/ejournals/JTE/v28n1/
title: Modified similarity flooding algorithm for automatic comparison of student and expert concept maps
description: The project programmed software using a similarity flooding algorithm (Melnik, Garcia-Molina, & Rahm, 2002), which 'provides a means of comparing two graphic items such as conceptual maps.' The team modified the original algorithm to include an automatic thesaurus for synonyms, relative versus full similarity, node weighting, and threshold values. Each modification significantly improved accuracy, validated so expert maps matched themselves at 100%. It generated the automatic feedback students received on their maps.
requirements: An encoded expert reference map is required for comparison, and the algorithm's modifications (thesaurus, relative similarity, node weighting, thresholds) must be configured for accurate matching
constraints: Validation of the algorithm is reported separately in Shahhosseini, Ye, Maughan, & Foster (2014), not fully in this article
target_learners: junior and senior undergraduate engineering, engineering technology, and related majors
target_learning_goals: diagnostic and problem-solving skills for technical problems
process mapping of diagnostic plans of action
examples: Student maps for the practice, electrical grid, and heat exchanger problems were electronically compared to encoded expert maps, with percentage accuracy returned as feedback
key_sources: Foster, W. T., Shahhosseini, A. M., & Maughan, G. (2016). Advancing Diagnostic Skills for Technology and Engineering Undergraduates: A Summary of the Validation Data. Journal of Technology Education, 28(1). https://scholar.lib.vt.edu/ejournals/JTE/v28n1/

article_title: Peer Tutoring as an Improvement Strategy for School Exploitation
citation: Guerrero Flores, D. I., Urdiales Ibarra, M. E., Villarreal Treviño, M. G., Castro Campos, C., & Loredo Tejeda, A. T. (2018). Peer Tutoring as an Improvement Strategy for School Exploitation. European Journal of Educational Research, 7(4), 953-961. https://doi.org/10.12973/eu-jer.7.4.953
title: Monitor tutor profiles and systematize the tutorial strategy to sustain peer tutoring effectiveness
description: Based on their results, the authors recommend that implementations of peer tutoring monitor the profile of tutors and systematize the tutorial strategy. They state it is necessary to have greater rigor and control of variables, such as timely training of tutors prior to implementation, and to focus and detail the particular tasks of both agents in the model. They also recommend monitoring the academic performance of high-performing students throughout the intervention to improve future choices of tutors.
requirements: Identification of tutor profiles and prior training of tutors
Detailed specification of the particular tasks of both tutors and tutees
constraints: The recommendation arises from the authors' stated need for greater rigor and control of variables in the present quasi-experimental implementation
target_learners: High school students acting as peer tutors and tutees in English learning units
target_learning_goals: Sustained effectiveness of peer tutoring on academic achievement
examples: The authors state that although results reflected a significant effect, it is necessary to monitor the profile of the tutors and systematize the tutorial strategy

article_title: An Analysis of the Effect of Mobile Learning on Lebanese Higher Education
citation: Khayrazad Kari Jabbour. (2014). An Analysis of the Effect of Mobile Learning on Lebanese Higher Education. Informatics in Education, 13(1), 1–15. https://informatica.vu.lt/journal/informatics-in-education
title: When integrating mobile devices in class, prepare a back-up plan and technical support arrangement for times the network will not support planned activities
description: The article reports that mobile-dependent lessons are vulnerable to network and 3G failures, so instructors should arrange a back-up plan and work with technical staff to keep the wireless system available. The teacher in this study worked collaboratively with the system manager, and the university had a back-up arrangement for times when mobile devices with 3G would not work quite right. The discussion states the teacher was compelled to prepare a back-up plan for those times when the network connection would not support the intended classroom activities.
requirements: Instructor preparation time to re-plan lessons and construct collaborative assignments around mobile technology
A back-up arrangement or plan for network or 3G failures
Coordination with the system manager so the wireless network is available in class
constraints: Off-task mobile use and distraction can disturb the class and require the teacher to redirect attention
Traditional lecture rooms with few power outlets and little space hinder group activities and device charging
target_learners: undergraduate higher education students
target_learning_goals: effective use of mobile technology as a learning tool in coursework
examples: The teacher worked collaboratively with the system manager to assure the wireless system network was available in class, and the university maintained a back-up arrangement for 3G failures
key_sources: Khayrazad Kari Jabbour. (2014). An Analysis of the Effect of Mobile Learning on Lebanese Higher Education. Informatics in Education, 13(1), 1–15. https://informatica.vu.lt/journal/informatics-in-education

article_title: The Effect of Mobile Learning on Students' Achievement and Conversational Skills
citation: Abdellah Ibrahim Mohammed Elfeky & Thouqan Saleem Yakoub Masadeh. (2016). The Effect of Mobile Learning on Students' Achievement and Conversational Skills. International Journal of Higher Education, Vol. 5, No. 3. https://doi.org/10.5430/ijhe.v5n3p20
title: Mobile phone-based educational website for the Strategies of Teaching and Learning course
description: A Blackboard-delivered mobile educational website developed by the researchers after analyzing E-learning instructional design models. The course content was prepared as PowerPoint lectures and split for small screens: "the web's content was split into smaller and shortened pieces to fit the mobile phones' monitors or screens." It offered a Content link plus links for discussions, groups, poster, and tools to encourage student-student and student-instructor interaction, and was compatible with Android and IOS devices used by participants.
requirements: Content must be split into shortened pieces fitting mobile screens
Compatibility with participants' mobile device operating systems via Blackboard
target_learners: English language major university students at Najran University
target_learning_goals: Academic achievement in Strategies of Teaching and Learning
English conversational skills
examples: Twelve lectures were uploaded to Blackboard and accessed via a Content link; discussions, groups, and blogs supported interaction over fourteen weeks.

article_title: The Effect of Mobile Learning on Students' Achievement and Conversational Skills
citation: Abdellah Ibrahim Mohammed Elfeky & Thouqan Saleem Yakoub Masadeh. (2016). The Effect of Mobile Learning on Students' Achievement and Conversational Skills. International Journal of Higher Education, Vol. 5, No. 3. https://doi.org/10.5430/ijhe.v5n3p20
title: Mobile learning as an extension of E-learning with its own terminology
description: The article defines Mobile Learning as "E-learning that uses mobile devices or learning connected to a mobile device" and characterizes it as an extension of E-learning combined with mobile computing. Drawing on Korucu & Alkan (2011) and Laouris & Eteokleous (2005), it contrasts the terminologies: mobile learning adopts terms like "spontaneous, intimate, situated, connected, informal, and lightweight," while E-learning uses "multimedia, interactive, hyperlinked, and media-rich environment," with Table 1 contrasting the two term sets dimension by dimension.
requirements: Technology use in educational environments must be based on dominant educational theories and approaches
target_learners: Higher education students and educators
target_learning_goals: Understanding the conceptual distinction between mobile learning and E-learning
examples: Table 1 contrasts paired terms such as distance learning versus situated learning and more formal versus informal.

article_title: Using a Sequential Multiple Assignment Randomized Trial (SMART) to Develop an Adaptive K-2 Literacy Intervention with Personalized Print Texts and App-Based Digital Activities
citation: James S. Kim, Catherine A. Asher, Mary Burkhauser, Laura Mesite, & Diana Leyva. (2019). Using a Sequential Multiple Assignment Randomized Trial (SMART) to Develop an Adaptive K–2 Literacy Intervention With Personalized Print Texts and App-Based Digital Activities. AERA Open. https://doi.org/10.1177/2332858419872701
title: MORE@Home literacy app with personalized digital activities
description: MORE@Home is a researcher-developed literacy app installed on parents' cell phones that paired each of 10 chosen print books with personalized reading activities. Activities were created at three levels of difficulty (low, medium, high) using children's MAP subtest scores, and included text-dependent and discussion questions, both literal and inferential, to stimulate parent–child conversation. Stage 2 added white hat gamification in which completed activities let students choose animals for a virtual zoo, plus text messaging supports for nonresponders.
requirements: Parents must download and use the app with their children; a family literacy event introduced parents to the app's goals and download code
constraints: Because the app is installed on parents' phones, parents must be motivated to download and use it; many never did
target_learners: kindergarten to Grade 2 children
target_learning_goals: word-level, sentence, and text-level reading skills and parent–child discussion about books
examples: App users read on average 4.4 books and completed 47 activities; the app was downloaded 134 times during the study period

article_title: Effectiveness of Using the iPad in Learning to Acquire the Mental and Performance Skills in Teaching Social Studies Curriculum
citation: Maadi Mahdi Alajmi & Hanan Abdullah Al-Hadiah. (2017). Effectiveness of using the iPad in Learning to Acquire the Mental and Performance Skills in Teaching Social Studies Curriculum. Journal of Curriculum and Teaching, 6(1). https://doi.org/10.5430/jct.v6n1p1
title: Mobile learning: education via portable electronic devices
description: The article frames the iPad as one form of mobile learning, which it defines, citing Qureshi and colleagues, as "the usage of the Electronic Instruments portable and movable such as Personal Digital Assistants(PDAs), Mobile Phones and Tablet Personal Computers in the Education". It lists device types (mobile phones, tablet PCs, laptops, PDAs) and attributes to mobile techniques advantages such as discussion, participation, cooperation with peers, and support for social structural learning. The iPad study is presented as an instance of this framework.
requirements: Portable, movable electronic devices used within the educational process
constraints: The article notes challenges including student distraction, difficulty writing long texts, and technological limits such as running multiple applications
target_learners: students across education phases using mobile devices
target_learning_goals: access to information sources, collaboration, and skill acquisition through mobile devices
examples: The study equipped an experimental classroom with iPads and wireless service so students could search and investigate required information in social studies

article_title: The Impact of Modeling Instruction within the Inverted Curriculum on Student Achievement in Science
citation: Dye, J., Cheatham, T., Rowell, G. H., Barlow, A. T., & Carlton, R. (2013). The Impact of Modeling Instruction within the Inverted Curriculum on Student Achievement in Science. Electronic Journal of Science Education, 17(2). https://ejse.southwestern.edu
title: Modeling instruction: a guided-inquiry pedagogy organized around collaborative model development and deployment cycles
description: Modeling instruction is described as a research-based, student-centered, inquiry-based pedagogy in which the teacher poses a research question and small groups collaboratively develop, debate and test a model, then apply it to new situations. Jackson et al.'s overview features two stages: "development and deployment". During development, groups use whiteboards with Socratic dialog and multiple representations; during deployment, students use the model to predict outcomes for new conditions, and the cycle concludes when a representative student defends the model to the class.
requirements: Teachers facilitate ongoing Socratic dialog, challenge misconceptions, define the real-world problem, guide model development and deployment, and assess student understanding
Teachers receive training in the methodology, such as the two-week workshops conducted by expert modelers described in the study
target_learners: high school science students in physics, chemistry, and biology
target_learning_goals: conceptual understanding of science through practicing scientific processes and discourse
examples: At CHS, teachers attended two two-week workshops using the Arizona State University curriculum, took on student and teacher roles in paradigm labs, and met weekly to ensure fidelity of modeling instruction
key_sources: Dye, J., Cheatham, T., Rowell, G. H., Barlow, A. T., & Carlton, R. (2013). The Impact of Modeling Instruction within the Inverted Curriculum on Student Achievement in Science. Electronic Journal of Science Education, 17(2). https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1188400

article_title: The Impact of Modeling Instruction within the Inverted Curriculum on Student Achievement in Science
citation: Dye, J., Cheatham, T., Rowell, G. H., Barlow, A. T., & Carlton, R. (2013). The Impact of Modeling Instruction within the Inverted Curriculum on Student Achievement in Science. Electronic Journal of Science Education, 17(2). https://ejse.southwestern.edu
title: Two-week modeling instruction teacher workshops with ongoing peer collaboration and observation for fidelity of implementation
description: The professional development element at CHS consisted of two, two-week summer workshops conducted by expert modelers using the Arizona State University curriculum, in which teachers were immersed in the methodology, taking on the roles of student and teacher while conducting paradigm labs. Support for fidelity included weekly teacher meetings, pairs of teachers in each subject meeting minimally 70 minutes each week, and three observations per year by the department chair and an administrator with written feedback.
requirements: Teachers attend workshops for their area of certification and refine strategies during a second summer of training
Ongoing collaboration and observation to ensure courses are taught using modeling strategies
target_learners: high school science teachers in physics, chemistry, and biology
target_learning_goals: fidelity of implementation of modeling instruction pedagogy
examples: CHS science teachers received training in summer 2009 and began implementing modeling instruction in chemistry in fall 2009, followed by biology and PWC in fall 2010

article_title: The Blended Learning Environment on the Foreign Language Learning Process: A Balance for Motivation and Achievement
citation: Isiguzel, B. (2014). The blended learning environment on the foreign language learning process: A balance for motivation and achievement. Turkish Online Journal of Distance Education-TOJDE, 15(3), Article 10. https://tojde.anadolu.edu.tr
title: Always take motivation into consideration in foreign language education
description: The article concludes that "Motivation in foreign language educatio n shall always be taken in consideration", describing motivation as a strong requirement of foreign language learning and a guarantee of long-term learning success when paired with an adequate learning environment. It links motivation and memory activities as inseparable notions in information processing.
requirements: An adequate learning environment supporting passage to the target language
target_learners: foreign language learners in higher education
target_learning_goals: sustained motivation for language learning
long-term learning success
examples: The study measured motivation with a 20-item Likert scale before and after the 10-week experimental process in both groups.

article_title: The Effect of Educational Modules Strategy on the Direct and Postponed Study's Achievement of Seventh Primary Grade Students in Science, in Comparison with the Conventional Approach
citation: Abeer Rashed Alelaimat, Khowla Abd Al_Raheem Ghoneem. (2012). The Effect of Educational Modules Strategy on the Direct and Postponed Study's Achievement of Seventh Primary Grade Students in Science, in Comparison with the Conventional Approach. Higher Education Studies, Vol. 2, No. 2. https://doi.org/10.5539/hes.v2n2p40
title: Module design pattern: sequenced subjects gated by an 85 percent mastery standard with pre- and post-tests
description: The article describes a reusable lesson/unit design in which learning content is divided into several subjects arranged in logical sequence (simple to complicated, known to unknown), each introduced by behavioral objectives and a pre-test, followed by self-evaluation questions with key answers, varied activities, and a post-test. Progression between subjects is mastery-gated: the standard "reached up to 85 percent to move from subject to the next", with three passing tests per subject graded in the teacher's presence.
requirements: behavioral objectives listed at the start of each lesson; pre-test and post-test with key answers; a study guide; varied activities and teaching utilities; an annex of references
constraints: mastery standard and test frequency were set according to the arbitrators' recommendation for this study's materials
target_learners: seventh-grade primary science students
target_learning_goals: mastery of scientific concepts in reproduction and organism classification
examples: The developed module included video material on organism reproduction and classification, hands-on activities such as examining the mint plant and looking for horizontal roots beneath the soil, and exercises with accompanied questions

article_title: The Impact of Problem-Based Learning on Iranian EFL Learners' Speaking Proficiency
citation: Loghman Ansarian, Ali Akbar Adlipour, Mehrnoush Akhavan Saber, Elmira Shafiei. (2016). The Impact of Problem-Based Learning on Iranian EFL Learners' Speaking Proficiency. Advances in Language and Literary Studies 7(3). https://doi.org/10.7575/aiac.alls.v.7n.3p.84
title: Modified Top Notch series with conversations omitted and problem-scenarios added for cognition-based PBL instruction
description: The experimental treatment material was the Top Notch series by John Saslow and Alan Ascher, modified by the researcher "to make it compatible with cognition-based teaching approach". The article states "The main difference was omission of conversations and adding problem-scenarios instead." The unmodified series, used in the control group, focuses on communication and contains standardized and natural conversations, grammar, pronunciation, and vocabulary sections.
requirements: Problem-scenarios designed so learners cannot decode the problem from its description
A defined tutorial process, built on Scott's (2004) model, piloted before data collection
constraints: The article states the teaching process designed for this study is in no way claimed to be perfect and should be enhanced by future researchers
target_learners: intermediate adult EFL learners aged 17-21 at a language institute
target_learning_goals: speaking proficiency across pronunciation, fluency and coherence, lexical resources, and grammatical accuracy
examples: Control-group learners used the unmodified Top Notch English series over the same twenty sessions

article_title: Developing Scientific Citizenship Identity Using Mobile Learning and Authentic Practice
citation: Duane E. Wallace & Alec M. Bodzin. (2017). Developing Scientific Citizenship Identity Using Mobile Learning and Authentic Practice. Electronic Journal of Science Education, 21(6). http://ejse.southwestern.edu
title: MobiLAP: mobile learning combined with authentic citizen science practice to foster scientific citizenship identity
description: MobiLAP is a learning approach that, as the article states, "integrates citizen science, mobile learning and authentic practice" to foster scientific citizenship in participants. Students use their own smartphones (a BYOD approach) with apps such as Leafsnap and Where Am I At to observe, record and submit real phenology data to a national citizen science project, acting like professional scientists on a legitimate research task. The approach builds on work by Gaydos and Squire (2012) and rests on identity theory and transformative learning accounts holding that engagement in authentic activity, plus reflection on it, can shift learners' perceptions, frames of reference and identities.
requirements: Access to mobile devices (73% of teens have smartphone access, per the article)
Training in the apps and observation protocols, which the literature recognizes as essential for citizen science data collection
A legitimate citizen science project to contribute data to
constraints: Tested only as a brief four-day intervention with one day of field data collection, limited by mandated curriculum time
Relied on convenience sampling from a single high school, limiting generalizability
Fall timing coincided with leaves changing and falling, complicating data collection
target_learners: ninth-grade high school biology students
target_learning_goals: scientific citizenship identity formation
STEM career and education interest
understanding of climate change through phenology observation
examples: Intervention students used their own iPhones with the Leafsnap and Where Am I At apps on a field trip to identify tree species, record phenophase data, and submit observations to Project BudBurst
key_sources: Duane E. Wallace & Alec M. Bodzin. (2017). Developing Scientific Citizenship Identity Using Mobile Learning and Authentic Practice. Electronic Journal of Science Education, 21(6). https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1187996

article_title: Mobile Learning in Foreign Language Learning: Podcasts and Lexicon Acquisition in the Elementary Instruction of Italian
citation: Unterrainer, Eva Maria. (2012). Mobile Learning in Foreign Language Learning: Podcasts and Lexicon Acquisition in the Elementary Instruction of Italian. In L. Bradley & S. Thouësny (Eds.), CALL: Using, Learning, Knowing, EUROCALL Conference, Gothenburg, Sweden, 22-25 August 2012, Proceedings. https://research-publishing.net
title: Mobile microlearning as a framework for vocabulary learning with small content units on mobile devices
description: The article combines microlearning and mobile learning into a framework for language learning: microlearning is "learning with micro-content", small individual units, understood as "special moments or episodes of learning while dealing with specific tasks or content, but engaging in small but conscious steps". Mobile learning in a narrow sense means handheld technologies providing anytime, anywhere access; more broadly it concerns the ability to acquire knowledge for successful action in changing situations and contexts. The study applies this framework by using podcasts as mobile (micro) learning for lexicon acquisition, emphasising vocabulary learning instead of teaching.
requirements: Mobile devices or podcast delivery enabling use beyond the classroom, and small, self-contained content units
constraints: The article notes microlearning is not simply equated with informal and lifelong learning, and that teaching is currently too focused, citing Nation (2011)
target_learners: Beginning learners of Italian as an L3 in Austrian secondary school (first year)
target_learning_goals: Foreign language vocabulary (lexicon) acquisition in Italian
examples: Students learn first-year Italian vocabulary with self-created German–Italian audio podcasts as mobile microlearning units

article_title: Developing Digital Competences Using an Educational Software. A Pedagogical Research
citation: Ioana Magdaş, Timea Bontea. (2011). Developing digital competences using an educational software. A pedagogical research. Acta Didactica Napocensia, Volume 4, Number 4, ISSN 2065-1430. https://www.moodle.ro
title: Moodle course pattern combining resources, interactive activities, communication tools and automated evaluation for skills teaching
description: The article's course design combines content resources with interactive, communicative and evaluative Moodle modules. As printed: "We used the option LABEL for add itional information, and RESOURCE for Word documents and PowerPoint presentations." Communication and collaboration used CHAT and FORUM, group feedback used CHOICE, collaborative project work used the WIKI option, and student work was evaluated with ASSIGNMENTS and WORKSHOPS, whose evaluation forms "offer many options for automatic evaluation". Tests, lessons and SCORM-interoperable modules enabled individualisation depending on options selected by students.
requirements: a Moodle installation with an assigned administrator and user classes with different access levels and permissions
target_learners: secondary and high-school students in technical education
target_learning_goals: digital competences; practical database application skills
examples: During the course the authors used the TESTS application for testing, LESON for lessons, and "Upload a single file" to check activities performed in Access

article_title: The Impact of Mobile Learning on Listening Anxiety and Listening Comprehension
citation: Mehrak Rahimi & Elham Soleymani. (2015). The Impact of Mobile Learning on Listening Anxiety and Listening Comprehension. English Language Teaching, 8(10). https://doi.org/10.5539/elt.v8n10p152
title: Mobile learning's unique features make listening tasks less threatening and more accomplishable
description: The article argues that beyond general computer-based learning benefits, mobile learning has distinctive features that make listening practice "less threatening and more accomplishable": portability, social interactivity, context sensitivity, connectivity, and individuality (customized scaffolding). These features, drawing on Klopfer & Squire as cited in Squire & Dikkers, are used to explain why mobile podcast listening lowered anxiety and raised comprehension relative to desktop practice.
requirements: Learners must have access to portable media player tools such as mobile phones, MP3 or MP4 players
constraints: The features are offered as the authors' interpretation of their findings, not as separately tested variables
target_learners: intermediate EFL learners
target_learning_goals: foreign language listening comprehension
reduction of listening anxiety
examples: Both groups completed the same 12 podcasts and course listening activities; only the device (portable vs desktop) differed

article_title: Effects of Modality and Redundancy Principles on the Learning and Attitude of a Computer-Based Music Theory Lesson among Jordanian Primary Pupils
citation: Osamah (Mohammad Ameen) Ahmad Aldalalah & Soon Fook Fong. (2010). Effects of Modality and Redundancy Principles on the Learning and Attitude of a Computer-Based Music Theory Lesson among Jordanian Primary Pupils. International Education Studies, 3(3). https://www.ccsenet.org/ies
title: Integrate the modality principle into music theory courseware by replacing onscreen text with narration accompanying images
description: The modality principle holds that pictures should be paired with synchronized spoken explanation rather than onscreen text, so that graphics use the visual channel and narration uses the auditory channel. The article reports that pupils using the AI mode learned music theory significantly better than pupils using the TI mode, and concludes that "the modality principle should be considered by the instructional designer when preparing multimedia music theory learning courseware".
requirements: Courseware must present graphical material with synchronized auditory narration rather than onscreen text
constraints: The article recommends particular attention for "disadvantaged-aptitude" pupils, described as those with external locus of control, high anxiety and low music intelligence
target_learners: third-grade primary pupils learning music theory
target_learning_goals: music theory: notation elements, scales, keys, intervals and rhythm
examples: The study developed a computer-based music theory lesson in three modes and found the audio-and-image mode produced the highest post-test mean (25.17) among 405 pupils

article_title: Mathematical Understanding and Proving Abilities: Experiment with Undergraduate Student by Using Modified Moore Learning Approach
citation: Rippi Maya, Utari Sumarmo. (2011). Mathematical Understanding and Proving Abilities: Experiment With Undergraduate Student By Using Modified Moore Learning Approach. IndoMS. J.M.E, Vol. 2 No. 2, pp. 231-250.
title: Modified Moore learning approach for advanced mathematics
description: A learning approach that motivates students to learn mathematical proving actively: students 'were motivated to think independently , start with a simple problem for improving a solution accompanied with its supporting reason and to communicate their ideas writtenly or orally'. Written communication occurs on a board or in article form; oral communication involves presenting and defending work in front of class with little lecturer guidance. The article implemented it in an advanced abstract algebra course to train self-regulated problem solving, composing relevant reasons, and convincing peers.
requirements: Implementation to no more than 24 students, or grouping students of varied prior mathematics ability when there are more
Students compose proofs themselves rather than copying lecturer's proofs passively
Adequate time, namely one semester, for advanced courses
constraints: In this study it was conducted during a half semester, which the authors say was too short for advanced proving tasks
Low prior-ability students needed revised materials with more explanation and exercises
target_learners: undergraduate mathematics students in advanced abstract algebra

mathematical proving ability
active learning habits and positive learning disposition
examples: In the experiment, MLA students were active in questioning, solving problems, and explaining their work in front of class, while conventional-class students preferred to listen to the lecturer's explanation

article_title: Psychological and Pedagogical Support for Students' Adaptation to Learning Activity in High Science School
citation: Vera P. Zeleeva, Svetlana S. Bykova, Silvia Varbanova. (2016). Psychological and Pedagogical Support for Students' Adaptation to Learning Activity in High Science School. International Journal of Environmental & Science Education, 11(3), 151-161.
title: Four-step lesson algorithm: motivation, lecture, game training, reflection
description: Classes held by tutors within the two courses followed a repeated four-step algorithm. As the article prints it: "motivation (goal - to generate interest in the topic under discussion); Lecture (objective - to inform the student); game training (goal - practical development of the material); Reflection (goal - fixing, the analysis of information received)". Each lesson in both courses lists talk, lecture/workshop, training workshop and reflection components with a stated proposed outcome.
requirements: Each lesson pairs an informational lecture with a practical game-training workshop and closes with reflection
target_learners: first-year university students in an adaptation-support program
target_learning_goals: practical development of course material
self-organization and planning skills
reflection on learning
examples: Lesson 1 of "Training activities technology" combined a tutor introduction, a School-University discussion, a lecture on peculiarities of high-school learning activity, a proactivity and self-organization workshop, and reflection.

article_title: Use of Video Feedback in the Training of Pre-Service Teachers
citation: Andrews, A., Bobo, L., & Spurlock, A. (2011). Use of video feedback in the training of pre-service teachers. Journal of Instructional Pedagogies. (no URL printed in the article text)
title: Modified Fishman Augmented Feedback Observation Guide for coding clinical teaching feedback
description: The study measured teacher feedback with "a slightly modified version of Augmented Feedback Observation Guide by Fishman", adding the subcategories auditory tactile, auditory visual, and no space. The tool codes feedback on Form, Direction, Time, Intent, General Referent and Specific Referent categories, and was originally designed for physical education motor-learning instruction but "was easily transferred for application with instruction of clinical skills". Validity was established through expert panel review and reliability showed 91.98% mean self-agreement, with 90% intra-observer agreement between investigators.
requirements: Trained observers coding each teaching behavior during videotaped sessions, with intra- and inter-observer agreement checked during the observation period to prevent drift
constraints: Originally designed to record augmented feedback by physical education teachers; the article reports its transfer to clinical skills instruction rather than validation in that setting beyond expert panel review
target_learners: pre-service clinical educators being observed during clinical skills teaching
target_learning_goals: measuring the amount, form, timing, intent and referent of augmented feedback provided during clinical instruction
examples: Researchers tallied observed feedback instances per category each week and entered them into SPSS for one-way ANOVA analysis

article_title: Focus on Student Success: Components for Effective Summer Bridge Programs
citation: Gonzalez Quiroz, A., & Garza, N. R. (2018). Focus on Student Success: Components for Effective Summer Bridge Programs. Journal of Hispanic Higher Education, 17(2), 101-111. https://doi.org/10.1177/1538192717753988
title: Model for Effective Summer Bridge Programs
description: A model developed by the authors in 2013 and enhanced each year from program findings, specifying four main components for summer bridge programs: academic preparation, emotional quotient, college experience, and leadership. The model holds that "learnable content must be engaging and culturally relevant to today's college student," and that each component's content must include connection to pop culture, physical and virtual interaction, consistent use of media, and gamification. It rests on a foundation of student-relevant content, early expectations for success, and cultural relevance to the population served.
requirements: Content must be engaging and culturally relevant to today's college student
Foundation of student-relevant content, early expectation for success, and cultural relevance to the population served
constraints: Developed and refined at a single predominately Hispanic (96%) 2-year community college
target_learners: First-time, full-time incoming community college students, predominantly Hispanic
target_learning_goals: College readiness in gatekeeper courses
Retention and transfer to a 4-year institution
examples: Four-hour preparatory mini-courses in English 1301, Math 1314, and History 1301 with mini-lectures, assignments, quizzes, and a final exam, plus workshops on study skills, delivered over 2 weeks before fall semester
