article_title: Effects of Multimedia-Based Graphic Novel Presentation on Critical Thinking among Students of Different Learning Approaches
citation: Hii, S. C., & Fong, S. F. (2013). Effects of Multimedia-Based Graphic Novel Presentation on Critical Thinking among Students of Different Learning Approaches. TOJET: The Turkish Online Journal of Educational Technology, 12(4). https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1080061
title: Presenting graphics with audio narration rather than on-screen text reduces extraneous cognitive load and improves learning outcomes (modality principle).
description: The modality principle claims that students learn more effectively from graphics and narration than from graphics and on-screen text. When graphics and words are both presented visually, the pictorial channel becomes overloaded while the verbal channel is unused. Converting written text to spoken narration allows processing in the verbal channel, balancing the two channels and avoiding cognitive overload. This study's finding that the GN mode significantly outperformed the GT and GTN modes provides empirical support for applying this principle in multimedia graphic novel history learning environments.
requirements: Multimedia presentation combining visual graphics with verbal content
Audio narration capability in the learning environment
constraints: Based on limited-capacity assumption of Mayer's cognitive theory of multimedia learning; applies when both pictorial and verbal channels have limited capacity
target_learners: Secondary school students of varying learning approaches
target_learning_goals: Improved comprehension and critical thinking in content-area learning
examples: The GN mode presented verbal content as simultaneous audio narration with graphics, while the GT mode used on-screen text next to graphics and the GTN mode used both narration and on-screen text
key_sources: Hii, S. C., & Fong, S. F. (2013). Effects of Multimedia-Based Graphic Novel Presentation on Critical Thinking among Students of Different Learning Approaches. TOJET: The Turkish Online Journal of Educational Technology, 12(4). https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1018032

article_title: Mobile Instant Messaging: Whatsapp and Its Potential to Develop Oral Skills
citation: Andújar-vaca, A., & Cruz-Martínez, M-S. (2017). Mobile Instant Messaging: Whatsapp and its Potential to Develop Oral Skills. Comunicar, 50. https://doi.org/10.3916/C50-2017-04
title: Mobile voice chat gives learners ubiquitous opportunities to negotiate meaning and evaluate their own performance through authentic interaction
description: The article argues that mobile learning offers an environment where learners "can ubiquitously negotiate meaning, reflect and evaluate on their own performance through authentic interaction and feedback", making voice-based MMC a powerful tool for second language proficiency. Interaction with peers supplies L2 input even when the teacher is absent, and students use spare time for practice, avoiding classroom time restrictions.
requirements: A mobile chat application with voice recording capability
Tasks that require real interaction rather than reproduction
constraints: Earlier limitations such as screen size and audio-visual quality are being minimized as mobile technology evolves, per the authors
target_learners: Second-language learners with smartphones
target_learning_goals: Second-language oral proficiency
learner autonomy
motivation and confidence
examples: The experimental group's daily WhatsApp interaction over six months, where students repaired mispronunciations through negotiation without explicit correction
key_sources: Andújar-vaca, A., & Cruz-Martínez, M-S. (2017). Mobile Instant Messaging: Whatsapp and its Potential to Develop Oral Skills. Comunicar, 50. https://doi.org/10.3916/C50-2017-04

article_title: Explicit Instructional Interactions: Observed Stability and Predictive Validity during Early Literacy and Beginning Mathematics Instruction
citation: Doabler, C. T., Nelson-Walker, N., Kosty, D., Baker, S. K., Smolkowski, K., & Fien, H. (2013). Explicit Instructional Interactions: Observed Stability and Predictive Validity During Early Literacy and Beginning Mathematics Instruction. SREE Fall 2013 Conference. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED545912
title: Modified COSTI observation instrument for explicit instructional interactions
description: The Classroom Observations of Student Teacher Interactions (COSTI) instrument, modified for these projects, "measures the frequency of explicit instructional interactions by specifically targeting six instructional interaction behaviors: two at the teacher level and four at the student level." Teacher behaviors are demonstrations and academic feedback; student behaviors include group responses, individual responses, errors, and other forms of student practice. All behaviors are coded continually and serially.
requirements: All classroom observations scheduled in advance and conducted during core instruction, with observers remaining for the duration of the instructional period
constraints: Observations were not scheduled according to specific math or reading content, or a particular instructional day
target_learners: First grade students
Kindergarten students
target_learning_goals: Early literacy
Beginning mathematics
examples: Used across three observation time points in both the ECRI and ELM randomized controlled trials

article_title: Convincing Science Teachers for Inquiry-Based Instruction: Guskey's Staff Development Model Revisited
citation: Zambak, V. S., Alston, D. M., Marshall, J. C., & Tyminski, A. M. (2017). Convincing Science Teachers for Inquiry-Based Instruction: Guskey's Staff Development Model Revisited. Science Educator, 25(2), 108-116. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1143566
title: A modified teacher change model emerging from this study's data
description: Regarding the results, a modified teacher change model can be drawn as shown in Figure 3, which presents a reciprocal relationship between the change in teachers' instructional practices and their students' achievement, and a one-way directional relationship between teachers' change in their instructional practices and their beliefs. The model emerging from the data did not indicate any links between variables in general, but they were evident when analyzing the sub-constructs.
requirements: The model requires analysis of sub-constructs (e.g., discourse, curriculum) rather than general variables to reveal relationships.
constraints: The strength of the claims made by this study is somewhat limited in terms of teacher change process and the sequence of proper teacher change through a PD program.
target_learners: in-service middle school science teachers
target_learning_goals: implementing inquiry-based instruction
examples: The study found a reciprocal relationship between the change in teachers' instructional practices and their students' achievement.

article_title: Comparison of Movement Notation (Laban) and Traditional Methodological Learning Success in Teaching Folk Dances
citation: Dilek Cantekin Elyağutu and Muhsin Hazar. (2017). Comparison of movement notation (Laban) and traditional methodological learning success in teaching folk dances. Educational Research and Reviews. https://doi.org/10.5897/ERR2016.3118
title: Use movement notation to reduce teacher dependency and enable self-paced repetition in dance teaching
description: The article's discussion recommends notation-based teaching because "Laban is a tool that removes teacher dependency, especially in the teaching of folk dances and all kinds of movements", letting students see and repeat movements as needed. Notation gives all learners access to the same content and quality of repetition, providing inspection and discipline compared with traditional demonstration.
requirements: Students must be literate in the notation system before independent use
constraints: Advantage did not hold for the dance section whose shifting nature affected both groups similarly

dance and physical education learners
target_learning_goals: independent movement learning
accurate reproduction of choreography
examples: The 14-week intervention taught the Harmandalı dance to conservatory students via notation motifs reinforced by dictation and deciphering

article_title: Bridging the Gap between Expert-Novice Differences: The Model-Based Feedback Approach
citation: Ifenthaler, D. (2010). Bridging the Gap between Expert-Novice Differences: The Model-Based Feedback Approach. Journal of Research on Technology in Education, 43(2), 103-117. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-009-9119-8
title: Model-Based Feedback Approach
description: A framework in which feedback is generated automatically from comparisons between a learner's externalized mental model (as a concept map or causal diagram) and an expert reference model. Two novel forms are introduced: cutaway feedback, which includes all propositions of the learner's model with semantically correct vertices highlighted, and discrepancy feedback, which includes only propositions with no semantic similarity to the expert model. The approach aims to restructure underlying representations and bridge expert-novice differences.
requirements: Requires a computer-based environment (HIMATT) capable of automatically generating standardized graphical re-representations on the fly
constraints: Feedback is based on comparison with a single expert reference representation
target_learners: university students
target_learning_goals: domain-specific conceptual understanding
expertise development

article_title: Results from a Study for Teaching Human Body Systems to Primary School Students Using Tablets
citation: Emmanuel Fokides and Aikaterini Mastrokoukou. (2018). Results from a Study for Teaching Human Body Systems to Primary School Students Using Tablets. Contemporary Educational Technology, 9(2), 154-170. https://doi.org/10.30935/cet.414808
title: Modified Bybee 5E instructional model adapted for tablet-based AR learning
description: The study's teaching method was "based on a slightly modified version (so as tablets could fit to the process) of Bybee's 5E". Its stages were: a short teacher introduction with engagement and exploration activities; use of the application for exploring and studying the material; application of new knowledge to everyday situations using worksheets; and evaluation by completing exercises in the application. Students worked in pairs with one tablet, were free to discuss and collaborate, and the teacher acted as a facilitator without giving away solutions.
requirements: Students work in pairs with one tablet per pair
The teacher acts as a facilitator rather than giving solutions
Enough time for students to work at their own pace (two teaching hours per session)
constraints: The method was modified from Bybee's 5E, which was not formed with tablets in mind
target_learners: primary school students, sixth grade
target_learning_goals: understanding the functions of the respiratory and circulatory systems
examples: Students in the tablets group completed four two-hour sessions following the modified 5E stages

article_title: Improving Outcomes for Refugee Children: A Case Study on the Impact of Montessori Education along the Thai-Burma Border
citation: Tobin, T., Boulmier, P., Zhu, W., Hancock, P., & Muennig, P. (2015). Improving outcomes for refugee children: A case study on the impact of Montessori education along the Thai-Burma border. The International Education Journal: Comparative Perspectives, 14(3). http://openjournals.library.usyd.edu.au/index.php/IEJ/index
title: Montessori education as a child-centred method suited to large-ratio refugee classrooms
description: The article describes Montessori as a child-centred educational method providing an alternative to traditional teacher-driven instruction. In this model, "students are able to direct their own learning and develop at their own pace, working with materials rather than in supervised groups or with direct teacher instruction." Because most children work alone, teachers have more time for one-on-one work even with large student-teacher ratios, allowing instruction to be tailored to each student's needs. The core components include educating the "whole child", promoting student choice and independence, positioning the teacher as a facilitator, and individualizing instruction.
requirements: Specifically designed Montessori materials and teachers positioned as facilitators rather than deliverers of direct instruction
constraints: The article notes other options such as the flipped classroom also exist, and the study focused on Montessori as implemented in one city in Thailand
target_learners: Displaced refugee children aged 3 to 6
target_learning_goals: Social, cognitive, and motor development; school readiness
examples: Two classrooms of 60 students each in Mae Sot, one converted to Montessori with child-directed learning and Montessori materials, the other taught in the traditional Thai style with teacher-driven instruction and repetition
key_sources: Tobin, T., Boulmier, P., Zhu, W., Hancock, P., & Muennig, P. (2015). Improving outcomes for refugee children: A case study on the impact of Montessori education along the Thai-Burma border. article_title: Modern English Drama and the Students' Fluency and Accuracy of Speaking
citation: Kian Pishkar, Ahmad Moinzadeh & Azizallah Dabaghi. (2017). Modern English Drama and the Students’ Fluency and Accuracy of Speaking. English Language Teaching, 10(8). https://doi.org/10.5539/elt.v10n8p69
title: Modern English drama texts (Death of a Salesman and Who's Afraid of Virginia Woolf) as instructional materials
description: The treatment materials were two modern English drama texts, Arthur Miller's Death of a Salesman and Albee's Who is Afraid of Virginia Woolf, taught over ten weeks to 18 treatment students. The texts "contain so many short phrases, colloquial words, English idioms, slangs and daily short dialogues which can motivate students to use them in their daily conversations". Students used familiar phrases learned from the texts in short sentences during treatment.
requirements: Texts must be prepared and conceived before the lesson; teachers must decide why they want to apply dramatic methods with a particular class
constraints: The texts contain little grammatical content and are based on informal oral communication, which the article links to students' accuracy not improving
target_learners: Upper-intermediate university EFL students
target_learning_goals: Speaking fluency and communicative competence

article_title: Growth in Secondary Teachers' Content Knowledge and Practice in Discrete Mathematics
citation: James A. Middleton, Mona Toncheff, Susan Haag. (2011). Growth in Secondary Teachers' Content Knowledge and Practice in Discrete Mathematics. Proceedings of the 33rd Annual Meeting of the North American Chapter of the International Group for the Psychology of Mathematics Education. https://www.pmena.org/pmena-proceedings/
title: Modeling MSP professional development program for discrete mathematics
description: A year-long, 135-contact-hour professional development program in which 42 teachers initially participated, built around a models and modeling perspective. It combined "two 40 -hour intensive summer workshops" with "9 additional 8-hour Saturday sessions", emphasized "modeling high cognitive demand tasks in problem -based-learning scenarios", and used simulation tools, probeware, data analysis, and graphical/visualization tools. Teachers organized into cross-school curriculum development teams designed and piloted a fourth-year discrete mathematics course, iterating lessons with videotaped practice and student work samples shared via a project Sharepoint site.
requirements: Teachers organized into curriculum development teams tasked with designing fourth-year curriculum structure and tasks for subsequent implementation
constraints: Retention of participants was an ongoing challenge; of 60 originally identified participants, 43 instructors participated
target_learners: Junior-Senior level high school mathematics teachers
target_learning_goals: Mathematical Knowledge for Teaching in discrete mathematics
Pedagogical content knowledge in mathematical modeling
examples: Monthly 8-hour PD sessions bookended by week-long summer workshops; iterative design cycles in which teachers developed, piloted, videotaped, and refined fourth-year discrete mathematics lessons

article_title: Using the MoodleReader as an Extensive Reading Tool and Its Effect on Iranian EFL Students' Incidental Vocabulary Learning
citation: Sepideh Alavi, Afsaneh Keyvanshekouh. (2012). Using the MoodleReader as an Extensive Reading Tool and its Effect on Iranian EFL Students' Incidental Vocabulary Learning. English Language Teaching, 5(6). http://dx.doi.org/10.5539/elt.v5n6p135
title: MoodleReader: an online database of over 1600 randomized quizzes on graded readers for extensive reading
description: The MoodleReader is a database of online quizzes on graded readers developed at Kyoto Sangyo University, Japan, created by Robb (2005) in response to shortcomings of the Accelerated Reader. It is "a database of over 1600 online qui zzes on graded readers" from series such as Oxford, Cambridge, Macmillan, Cengage/Heinle and Penguin. Learners read a book at their own level and choice of genre, then log in at anytime to take a quiz; questions are randomized so each student receives different question sets, and teachers can set time limits and control book levels.
requirements: Students need access to graded readers at their level and a MoodleReader course with quizzes for the chosen titles.
target_learners: ESL/EFL learners in extensive reading programs
target_learning_goals: Incidental vocabulary learning through extensive reading
examples: In this study, experimental students were required to enroll and take at least 12 quizzes over 3.5 months, each quiz consisting of 10 randomized questions (4 MC, 2 who-said, 3 T/F, 1 ordering).

description: The authors modified the Nursing-Mini-CEX for sophomores, revising teaching content to include "inquiry, physical examination, nursing diagnosis (nursing problems), communication skills, humanistic care, organizational effectiveness and overall evaluation." Each item is scored on a 9-point scale, with part one covering basic information and part three containing feedback information including teacher satisfaction and suggestions. citation: Wu Zongxi, Wang Mingyue, Luo Xueting, Liu Xiangqi, Yang Le, Gao Siyong, Zhang Sien, Zheng Guangsen. (2026). Structured Microskill Stepwise Progression for Undergraduate Tooth Extraction: A Randomized Mixed-Methods Study. International Dental Journal. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.identj.2026.111097
title: Modified Direct Observation of Procedural Skills (modified DOPS) scale for undergraduate tooth extraction
description: A 100-point procedural assessment scale adapted from the original DOPS framework for undergraduate tooth extraction training. It retains core domains including patient communication, preoperative preparation, aseptic technique, local anaesthesia, instrument handling, procedural execution, complication awareness, and postoperative instructions, with an additional domain for safe use of motorized rotary instruments. Content validity was reviewed by a six-member expert panel (I-CVI 0.83-1.00; S-CVI/Ave 0.92).
requirements: Assessment by two independent examiners blinded to group allocation, with the final score calculated as the mean of their ratings.
constraints: The scale was procedure-specific to tooth extraction.
target_learners: Fifth-year undergraduate dental students
target_learning_goals: Objective assessment of procedural competence in tooth extraction
examples: Inter-rater reliability for the total modified DOPS score was good (ICC = 0.86; 95% CI, 0.74-0.93).

citation: Baraza W., Staples G., Wells C., Barbier L., Tonga I., Singh P., Puttick M., Webster C. (2026). Artificially Intelligent Simulated Patients in Undergraduate Surgical Teaching: A Single Blinded Randomized Controlled Study. The Clinical Teacher. https://doi.org/10.1111/tct.70486
title: Model-agnostic AISP architecture combining speech-to-text, curated LLMs and generative voice within educator-defined pedagogical constraints
description: The article describes an explanatory architecture for AI simulated patients in which "SimConverse uses a model-agnostic approach and uses different AI models to create the simulated patient including user speech-to-text, curated large language models and realistic generative voice synthesis." Educator-authored pedagogical coding and case scripting define the patient's history, laboratory results and personality, and the AISP is constrained to stay within these designated settings during interactions. This framework lets educators design responsive platforms fulfilling specific curriculum requirements while allowing scenario complexity to increase as appropriate.
requirements: Educator-defined case scripting and pedagogical coding to constrain the simulated patient
constraints: The optimal approach to using LLMs and generative AI in interactive and dynamic learning contexts remains undefined, particularly in undergraduate medical education
target_learners: undergraduate medical students
target_learning_goals: history taking
clinical reasoning
communication skills
examples: The study's two AISP cases were scripted by educators and the software provider modified the scenario to facilitate the experimental assessment

The protocol uses a sequential multi-phase design: a preliminary competency framework, a first round with categorical maintain/remove/modify assessment, and a second round with binary agree/disagree responses. article_title: Artificial intelligence-assisted feedback in pharmacology education: a pilot evaluation of a custom generative model.
citation: Stephenson E, Morrigan K, Irfan A, Bascombe K, Okorie M. (2026). Artificial intelligence-assisted feedback in pharmacology education: a pilot evaluation of a custom generative model. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-026-09300-w
title: Deploy AI-generated formative feedback only within a moderated workflow with rubrics, references and ongoing human oversight
description: The article recommends that institutions considering implementation should invest in model calibration, training of faculty moderators and ongoing evaluation, and that safe rollout should "Consider use of rubrics, references, and ongoing human oversight". In the pilot, all AI-generated feedback was reviewed by faculty before release, and learners received only the moderated final version. This workflow combined speed advantages with the accuracy safeguards the authors judged essential.
requirements: Faculty moderation of all AI-generated feedback before release to students
A standardised rubric embedded in the model's operational instructions to guide scoring and feedback
Curated pharmacology reference materials provided to the model
constraints: The efficiency gains reported apply to a moderated workflow rather than autonomous AI deployment
The risk of hallucination persists, and regular retraining and monitoring are required
target_learners: Postgraduate Physician Associate MSc students in a UK medical programme
target_learning_goals: Formative pharmacology knowledge: drug mechanism of action, drug interactions, side effects and patient explanation
examples: In the pilot, all AI-generated feedback was reviewed by faculty members before release to students, and learners received only the moderated final version.

article_title: A MOOC-based and high-fidelity surgical simulation-integrated clinical internship mode in optometry teaching for ophthalmology graduate students.
citation: Yang K, Kanwen W, Jing C, Zidan G, Chenggong J, Xue L. (2026). A MOOC-based and high-fidelity surgical simulation-integrated clinical internship mode in optometry teaching for ophthalmology graduate students. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-026-09610-z
title: Structure blended clinical internships as a theory → simulation → practice pathway combining MOOC flexibility with simulation realism
description: The article's blended model organizes optometry internship teaching as a "theory → simulation → practice" learning pathway: students first learn theoretical content via MOOC self-study, then review high-fidelity surgical simulation demonstrations, and finally practice repeatedly with simulator feedback during classroom sessions. The authors state this combination "effectively bridges knowledge and practice" and "creates a reinforcing closed loop that promotes deep integration of knowledge and skills."
requirements: A dedicated online platform for MOOC video self-study and automated testing
Access to a high-fidelity ophthalmic surgical simulator with force-feedback and automated performance reports
Trained teachers who implement the full blended protocol
constraints: Evaluated in a single-center study with 54 ophthalmology graduate students; the authors state further multi-center and long-term studies are needed to confirm generalizability
target_learners: Ophthalmology graduate students undertaking optometry clinical rotations
target_learning_goals: Integration of optometry theory with clinical practice

title: Modified BOPPPS model: experiential anchoring of the Bridge-in phase guided by experiential learning and situated cognition theories
description: The article's modified BOPPPS model redefines the Bridge-in phase from a "theoretical bridge" to an "experiential anchor": ward visits (concrete clinical observation) and thoracoscopy simulation (embodied operational practice) serve as dual cognitive scaffolds. It embeds Kolb's learning cycle — "concrete experience → reflective observation → abstract conceptualization → active application" — within the BOPPPS framework, and invokes situated cognition theory on the grounds that "knowledge acquired in context is more readily transferable to clinical practice". The model aims to reshape students' cognitive schema from a linear theory-to-practice model to a three-dimensional "disease-anatomy-operation" framework, addressing decontextualized knowledge acquisition.

constraints: Evaluated only in thoracic surgery teaching for lung tumour-related content at a single center with a small sample and no long-term follow-up
Group allocation was by intact class, non-randomized, so unmeasured confounding cannot be fully excluded
target_learners: fifth-year clinical medicine undergraduate students
target_learning_goals: clinical imaging analysis ability
comprehensive clinical application ability
clinical reasoning bridging classroom learning and bedside practice
examples: The experimental group's 90-minute Bridge-in combined a 45-minute ward visit (briefing, bedside observation, instructor Q&A, intra-group exchange) with thoracoscopy simulation training of 15 minutes per student across three stations

title: Cyclic experiential cognitive chain replacing the linear BOPPPS sequence, building a three-dimensional disease-anatomy-operation schema
description: The article contrasts the traditional BOPPPS framework's linear sequence of "knowledge activation → objective setting → assessment → learning → summary" with the modified model's cyclic cognitive chain: "experiential anchoring (Bridge-in) → gap identification (Pre-assessment) → experience-based deepening (Participatory Learning) → application verification (Post-assessment) → schema refinement (Summary)". Each phase builds on the initial experiential input — for example, Participatory Learning via HIS/PACS scenario simulation becomes active integration of experiential insights with theoretical knowledge. The pattern fosters a three-dimensional "disease-anatomy-operation" cognitive schema rather than the traditional two-dimensional "disease-treatment" schema.
requirements: The Bridge-in phase must supply concrete experiential input (ward observation and embodied simulation) that all later phases build on
constraints: Developed and evaluated against thoracic surgery's profession-specific competency demands (imaging-anatomy correlation, surgical instrument proficiency)
target_learners: undergraduate clinical medicine students
target_learning_goals: clinical reasoning
knowledge transfer from classroom to clinical practice
examples: Table 6 contrasts the two models on Bridge-in function, cognitive framework, learning cycle, knowledge attribute, and core goal, reorienting the framework from knowledge transmission to competence construction

description: The study artifact is a three-round modified Delphi e-survey. Of 59 experts identified, "15 (25%) experts from 5 different countries participated in the round#2 of the Delphi method", with respondents kept anonymous to each other and consensus defined at ≥80% agreement.
requirements: Experts meeting inclusion criteria: having performed all listed procedures, ≥10 EES/skull-base publications in 5 years, and simulator-design or medical-education publications
constraints: Only 15 of 59 identified experts participated, which the authors link to the email recruitment method
target_learners: ENT surgeons and surgical educators
target_learning_goals: Quantifying perceived difficulty of surgical skills and procedures for curriculum design

article_title: Assessing moral competence in medical and psychology students: effects on anxiety and test duration in online versus paper-based testing.
citation: Zielina M, Pinkasová T, Dostál D, Ivanová K, Macháček M, Matějek J, Řebíková B, Kuchař J, Škoda J, Pospíšilová K, Volejníčková RM, Doležal A. (2025). title: Moral Competence Test (MCT) with C-score as the moral competence measure
description: The Moral Competence Test presents two moral dilemmas (a Worker's dilemma and a Doctor's dilemma), each followed by 12 arguments rated on a 9-point Likert scale. Its main outcome is the C-score, which "ranges from 1 to 100 and reflects the degree of consistency in applying moral principles across different arguments." Scores of 30 and above indicate high to very high moral competence, and a score above 20 is described as desirable for functioning in a free society. The study used the MCT to compare medical and psychology students across years and testing formats.
requirements: Respondents rate agreement with pro and contra arguments for two dilemmas on a 9-point scale
constraints: The article notes the MCT focuses primarily on moral judgment and does not include sensitivity, motivation, or behavior
target_learners: medical students
psychology students
target_learning_goals: assessing moral competence and moral judgment consistency
examples: In this study the MCT yielded a mean C-score of 25.72 (SD 15.12), with lower Doctor's dilemma subscores among medical students

title: Modified 9-item proctology video-assessment checklist adapted from LAP-VEGaS
description: A 9-item ordinal checklist for assessing the educational quality of proctology procedure videos, adapted from the LAP-VEGaS laparoscopic tool by three consultant colorectal surgeons. Laparoscopic access items were removed and "items such as patient positioning, case presentation and outcome reporting were retained and adapted for proctology". Each item is scored 0, 1 or 2, giving a maximum total of 18; higher totals indicate more complete educational content.
requirements: Face validation by colorectal surgeons with regular proctology practice; equally weighted items to ensure simplicity and reproducibility

article_title: Development of a digital peer-feedback tool for clinical skills training: a pilot study with second-year medical students.
citation: Yurdal Mustafa Onur & Kıncal Remzi Y. (2025). Development of a digital peer-feedback tool for clinical skills training: a pilot study with second-year medical students. Scientific Reports 15, 40807. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41598-025-24650-z
title: Moonen's 3-Space digital learning tool model as the design framework for Medifeeding
description: The article adopted "Moonen’s 3-Space digital learning tool model" as the guiding design framework for Medifeeding, structuring development into three areas. The pedagogical content area took Falchikov's peer feedback marking (PFM) model as its pedagogical element and structured the faculty's learning guides accordingly; the interaction area combined classical features (emojis, likes, text and voice comments) with the innovative feature of video comments; and the technological infrastructure area used "a rapid-prototyping, iterative software-development approach" culminating in release on both app stores.
requirements: Each of the three areas must be addressed in sequence: a pedagogical basis, an interaction design, and a technological infrastructure built through rapid prototyping and internal testing.
target_learners: Second-year (Term 2) medical students
target_learning_goals: Clinical skills training with structured peer feedback
examples: Medifeeding's development phase applied the model's three areas: Falchikov's PFM model as the pedagogical element, gamified interaction features including video comments, and iterative app development and release.

title: Modified Mini-CEX and DOPS scales with a 9-point three-level rating system for chairside assessment
description: The study adapted the internationally recognized Mini-CEX and DOPS instruments "to evaluate the teaching effectiveness in conjunction with oral clinical teaching." The modified scales "adopt a 9-point system divided into 3 levels: 1–3 points indicate failure to meet requirements; 4–6 points indicate meeting requirements; and 7–9 points indicate excellence." Mini-CEX covers seven domains from interviewing skills to overall clinical competence; DOPS covers procedural domains from indications to overall performance. Assessments lasted 30 minutes, scored by two calibrated non-teaching assessors blinded to allocation.

constraints: The study did not conduct a formal test of inter-rater reliability, which the authors state may compromise objective interpretation of results

clinical operational procedures

citation: Cevik Arif Alper; Abu-Zidan Fikri M. (2025). Open-access RUSH protocol course improves knowledge and perceived confidence among healthcare learners. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-025-07984-0
title: Use structured open-access online courses as a preparatory phase that saves time for advanced hands-on ultrasound practice
description: The article argues that a structured MOOC with formative assessments and multimedia can serve as the asynchronous foundation of a flipped-classroom model, so that in-person sessions focus on skill application. As the authors put it, "The online component can be used as a preparation phase which saves time for more advanced hands-on practice." The course demonstrated significant knowledge and confidence gains supporting this preparatory role.
requirements: Structured content with formative assessments and multimedia integration
Availability of subsequent hands-on practice to develop scanning proficiency
constraints: Online instruction is not a complete replacement for hands-on experience; trainees still require practical training to develop scanning proficiency
Long-term retention and real-world clinical application remain unassessed
target_learners: Medical students
Interns
Residents
Healthcare trainees in resource-limited settings
target_learning_goals: Point-of-care ultrasound protocol knowledge
Diagnostic reasoning in undifferentiated shock
examples: The iEM RUSH course ran from May 2020 to December 2023, delivering readings, videos, formative quizzes, and a 70%-threshold final exam entirely online before any hands-on practice

citation: Fan Na, Yin Yan-Ling, Zhang Sai-Na, Yan Rui, Han Shi-Fan. (2025). Developing a Competency Model for Mobile Nurses in Chinese Tertiary Hospitals: A Delphi-AHP Approach. Journal of Nursing Management. https://doi.org/10.1155/jonm/5561680
title: Competency framework for mobile nurses in tertiary hospitals (3 domains, 10 subdomains, 42 indicators)
description: A hierarchical competency index system for mobile nurses built via literature synthesis, semistructured interviews, and two-round Delphi-AHP consultation. Per the article, "the final competency model index system for mobile nurses in tertiary hospitals included 3 first-level indicators, 10 secondary indicators, and 42 tertiary indicators," spanning knowledge and skills, professionalism, and personality traits, with indicators such as hospital information system navigation (0.0757), physical fitness (0.0730), and professional ethics (0.0627). It is intended to inform recruitment, training, and performance evaluation.
requirements: Expert panel members with at least 10 years of experience in nursing management or mobile nursing, familiar with competency model development, participating in two consultation rounds
constraints: The expert panel was primarily recruited from Northeast China, which may restrict generalizability
The model lacks empirical validation; no evidence yet confirms practical impact on patient safety or workforce metrics

nursing managers
target_learning_goals: professional competency development for transient nursing roles
emergency response and cross-departmental coordination
examples: Used to propose tiered training: simulation-based serious games for junior nurses and crisis-leadership modules for senior nurses

Content and face validity were reviewed by a panel of ten expert professors, achieving a Content Validity Index of 95%. article_title: The impact of learning efficiency on teaching evaluation in urban-rural interactive classrooms: a moderated mediation model.
citation: Zhang Wanting, Sun Junhua, Yao Haichang. (2025). The impact of learning efficiency on teaching evaluation in urban-rural interactive classrooms: a moderated mediation model. BMC Psychology, 13. https://doi.org/10.1186/s40359-025-03313-8
title: Moderated mediation model of learning efficiency, classroom atmosphere, network environment, and grade level in remote teaching evaluation
description: The article proposes and validates a moderated mediation model in which classroom atmosphere mediates the effect of rural students' learning efficiency on teaching evaluation of urban-rural interactive classrooms, while network environment reliability and student grade level act as moderators. The authors report that "classroom atmosphere is the mediating variable, and Network environment and grade level are the moderating variables." The account is grounded in self-efficacy theory and Piaget's cognitive development theory, with grade level operating as a second-stage moderator of the indirect path.
requirements: Measurement of learning efficiency, classroom atmosphere, network environment, and teaching evaluation via validated questionnaires adapted to the rural interactive-classroom context
constraints: Developed and tested in the cultural and educational context of Chinese rural Hope Primary Schools, which the authors state may restrict broader applicability
Grade level was dichotomized into high and low groups for the moderation analysis
target_learners: Rural primary school students (grades 1–6) in Chinese Hope Primary Schools participating in urban-rural interactive classrooms
target_learning_goals: Improving teaching evaluation of remote interactive instruction
Understanding how learning efficiency, classroom atmosphere, and network conditions shape remote learning outcomes

citation: Ebina Koki, Abe Takashige, Hotta Kiyohiko, Lingbo Yan, Kamijo Chihiro, Higuchi Madoka, Kon Masafumi, Kikuchi Hiroshi, Miyata Haruka, Matsumoto Ryuji, Osawa Takahiro, Murai Sachiyo, Senoo Taku, Komizunai Shunsuke, Tsujita Teppei, Sase Kazuya, Chen Xiaoshuai, Konno Atsushi, Shinohara Nobuo. title: Mocap-based real-time surgical skill assessment system with ML classification, GOALS prediction, and SHAP-generated feedback
description: A wet-lab assessment system in which an optical motion-capture system (OptiTrack V120: Trio, 120 Hz) tracks forceps tip position and orientation, feeding kinematic parameters into two built-in ML models: a PCA-SVM three-tier classifier and a PCA-SVR GOALS score predictor. SHAP, an explainable AI method, generates automated feedback comments delineating "the positive and negative contributions of specific motion metrics to their performance evaluation". The interface displays a GOALS radar chart, classification result, SHAP comments and waterfall plot, principal component scores, and raw kinematic metrics.
requirements: Motion-capture markers affixed to surgical instruments and video recording of sessions for expert GOALS scoring
Training data from prior studies (n = 104) to construct the ML models before external testing
constraints: Validated only in porcine-organ wet-lab simulation tasks (dissection and suturing), not in actual surgery
The study did not verify the educational effects of the real-time feedback or its transfer to the operating room
target_learners: Urology trainees and medical students in laparoscopic simulation training
target_learning_goals: Laparoscopic psychomotor skill assessment and feedback
examples: Participants received automated skill evaluation immediately after training sessions, including radar charts, SHAP waterfall plots, and pre-registered feedback comment sets

article_title: Exploring the Interplay of Motivation, Self-Efficacy, Critical Thinking, and Self-Regulation in Predicting Academic Achievement Among University Students.
citation: Stavropoulou G, Daniilidou A, Nerantzaki K. (2025). Exploring the Interplay of Motivation, Self-Efficacy, Critical Thinking, and Self-Regulation in Predicting Academic Achievement Among University Students. F1000Research 14:344. https://doi.org/10.12688/f1000research.161821.1
title: Mediational path model linking motivation, self-efficacy, critical thinking, and self-regulation to academic achievement
description: The article proposes and tests a path model in which intrinsic and extrinsic motivation predict self-efficacy, which in turn predicts critical thinking and self-regulation, with critical thinking and self-regulation directly predicting academic achievement. As the article states, "Figure 1 shows the path model that includes direct and indirect effects, with self-efficacy, critical thinking and self-regulation acting as mediators." The model was estimated with path analysis in JASP on 250 university students and reached good fit on most printed indices.
requirements: Self-report measures of motivation, self-efficacy, critical thinking, and self-regulation (MSLQ subscales) plus a measure of academic achievement from the same learners
constraints: Cross-sectional data do not define causal relationships, per the article's own limitations
Convenience sample from education and psychology departments in a single cultural context limits generalizability
target_learners: university students in education and psychology programs
target_learning_goals: academic achievement
self-regulated learning
critical thinking
examples: The article fitted the model with JASP on data from 250 undergraduates at three Greek universities, reporting standardized path coefficients and fit indices

article_title: How nurses' moral competence can be supported: Findings from international focus groups with professionals.
citation: Wiisak, J., Suhonen, R., Galazzi, A., Gastmans, C., Keogh, B., Papastavrou, E. et al. (2025). How nurses' moral competence can be supported: Findings from international focus groups with professionals. International Nursing Review, 72. https://doi.org/10.1111/inr.13080
title: Approaches and tools to support nurses' moral competence in educational, emotional and practical fields
description: The informants identified practical approaches and tools in three fields (Table 3). In the educational field, "interprofessional education characterised by innovative teaching methods (e.g. simulation‐based teaching, case‐based teaching) as continuous or in internship education was suggested". In the emotional field, tools for communicating and processing emotions and spaces for sharing and reflecting were named, such as reflective diaries. In the practical field, an ethics toolkit with protocols, checklists, guidelines and job counselling, plus physical spaces, time and material resources for shared reflection, were suggested.
requirements: Tools such as the ethics toolkit would include ethical protocols, checklists, guidelines, and job counselling; educational approaches should include examples applied to practice.
constraints: Identified as suggestions by focus group informants; effectiveness of specific tools was not tested in this study.
target_learners: nursing students
registered nurses

processing emotions from ethical challenges
ethical practice
examples: A Cypriot informant described protocols and check-lists ensuring novice and experienced nurses work in the same way.
A Finnish informant noted the value of experiencing cases after failure to learn from them.

article_title: Dysphagia education in Addis Ababa, Ethiopia: student self-competency ratings during their dysphagia course.
citation: Smaoui S, Ganesan S, Williams T. (2025). Dysphagia education in Addis Ababa, Ethiopia: student self-competency ratings during their dysphagia course. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-025-07365-7
title: Modified DCVT with a 5-point agree/disagree Likert scale adapted for second-language English speakers
description: The Dysphagia Competency Verification Tool (DCVT), developed by an ASHA subcommittee to standardize evaluation of clinical competency in dysphagia, was modified for this study. The team changed the rating scale to a 5-point ordinal Likert format (strongly disagree to strongly agree) and lowered the reading level, stating this "allows for easier interpretation of these terms and subsequently a more accurate self-assessment of competency." Responses were dichotomized as Emergent (scores below 4) or Adequate (4 and above) for analysis.
requirements: Administered before and after dysphagia-related clinical exposure to capture change in self-perceived competency
constraints: Only two DCVT domains (General Skills and Direct Patient Care) were used because instrumental assessment such as VFSS and FEES is not accessible at Black Lion Hospital
target_learners: Graduate SLT master's students in Ethiopia
target_learning_goals: Self-assessment of dysphagia clinical competency in assessment and treatment
examples: Administered in April 2024 before clinical exposure and in May 2024 after clinical encounters with neurology patients at Black Lion Hospital
key_sources: Smaoui S, Ganesan S, Williams T. (2025). Dysphagia education in Addis Ababa, Ethiopia: student self-competency ratings during their dysphagia course. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-025-07365-7

article_title: Application and effectiveness of blended learning in medical imaging via the technology acceptance model.
citation: Sun Xiaofen, Wan Jianghua, Li Zhiqun, Tu Rong, Lin Juan, Li Xiaohua, Chen Jianqiang. (2025). Application and effectiveness of blended learning in medical imaging via the technology acceptance model. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-025-07293-6
title: 18-item modified TAM questionnaire for blended learning acceptance
description: A survey instrument with three five-point Likert items (1 = Strongly Disagree, 5 = Strongly Agree) for each of six constructs: PU, PEU, PIFs, EIFs, SS, and BI — 18 items total as printed in Table 1. It was developed from end-of-semester surveys of the 2019–2021 cohorts (n=130), a literature review, and expert review by professors in medical imaging, educational psychology, and statistics. In the study sample, standardized loadings exceeded 0.7 for all indicators except PIF2 (0.470), and all constructs showed CA and CR above 0.7 and AVE above 0.5.
requirements: Expert review to ensure validity and applicability of the questions
constraints: The authors acknowledge limitations in the questionnaire's specificity to medical imaging students' unique needs, noting a lack of specific inquiry into access to simulated medical imaging equipment
No formal pilot test was conducted prior to data collection
target_learners: Undergraduate medical imaging students
target_learning_goals: Measuring satisfaction and behavioral intention toward blended learning
examples: Item examples include 'Blended learning can improve learning efficiency' (PU) and 'You are willing to continue using this teaching method in the future' (BI)
key_sources: Sun Xiaofen, Wan Jianghua, Li Zhiqun, Tu Rong, Lin Juan, Li Xiaohua, Chen Jianqiang. (2025). Application and effectiveness of blended learning in medical imaging via the technology acceptance model. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-025-07293-6

article_title: Video based on the combination of animation and modules is effective in teaching suture technologies to novices without faculty involvement: a new surgical video course.
citation: Cheng Meng, Wang Xinle, Zhang Man, Li Sainan, Geng Cuizhi. (2025). Video based on the combination of animation and modules is effective in teaching suture technologies to novices without faculty involvement: a new surgical video course. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-025-06915-3
title: A surgical video curriculum combining modular demonstrations with animated simulations for 12 suturing techniques
description: The article describes a novel curriculum of three sets of tutorial videos covering 12 suturing techniques, each averaging 48 s (range 32-60 s). Each video blends "module-based stitching steps combined with animated simulations", pairing live demonstrations on a silicone skin model with animations whose "cross-sectional views in the animations closely mimic human tissue structures". It was evaluated with 60 preclinical medical students randomized to module-plus-animation, module-video, or traditional education groups.
requirements: Videos are structured by a progressive syllabus starting with easy-to-learn basic skills before more complex suturing methods built on those foundations
constraints: The study evaluated the curriculum on silicone skin models with surgically inclined volunteers, so transfer to clinical settings and generalizability to the whole student body remain uncertain per the authors' limitations
target_learners: preclinical medical students with no prior suture training
target_learning_goals: mastering 12 common suturing techniques including puncture sites, depth, needle angles, suture directions, and tissue hierarchies
examples: In April 2022, 60 preclinical medical students at Hebei Medical University were randomly assigned to three groups and completed a two-stage course: about 90 min of classroom video viewing with 4-12 min practice per stitch, then 80 min of independent practice performing each technique seven times
key_sources: Cheng Meng, Wang Xinle, Zhang Man, Li Sainan, Geng Cuizhi. (2025). Video based on the combination of animation and modules is effective in teaching suture technologies to novices without faculty involvement: a new surgical video course. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-025-06915-3

article_title: A Novel Training Model to Improve Diagnostic Accuracy of Cervical Fine-Needle Aspiration.
citation: Anschuetz Lukas, Tschopp Samuel, Trippel Mafalda, Huwendiek Sören, Trepp Roman, Caversaccio Marco, von Werdt Moritz, Borner Urs. (2025). A Novel Training Model to Improve Diagnostic Accuracy of Cervical Fine‐Needle Aspiration. Head & Neck. https://doi.org/10.1002/hed.28039
title: Incorporate low-cost model-based US-FNA training into medical education before trainees puncture patients
description: The article recommends that practical training on inexpensive simulation models precede clinical application of cervical US-FNA, because model practice raised both skills ratings and clinical diagnostic yield. It concludes: "We recommend that training on a model should be considered for all trainees in cervical US‐FNA prior to application on patients." The model's low cost (~$2 per unit) and 2-minute setup make systematic teaching feasible where supervised practice time is limited.
requirements: A model with tissue properties resembling human neck structures and targets that mimic cysts and lymph-node resistance, so practice transfers to clinical US-FNA
constraints: The clinical-yield evidence comes from an uncontrolled pre/post comparison and could partly reflect a Hawthorne effect; the authors call for a longer-term follow-up or control group
target_learners: otorhinolaryngology residents and other trainees in cervical US-FNA
target_learning_goals: ultrasound-guided fine-needle aspiration technique and diagnostic yield
examples: Fifteen residents completed three training sessions on the liver model with an instructional video, and their clinical diagnostic yield rose from 71% to 85%
key_sources: Anschuetz Lukas, Tschopp Samuel, Trippel Mafalda, Huwendiek Sören, Trepp Roman, Caversaccio Marco, von Werdt Moritz, Borner Urs. (2025). A Novel Training Model to Improve Diagnostic Accuracy of Cervical Fine‐Needle Aspiration. Head & Neck. https://doi.org/10.1002/hed.28039

article_title: HUMAn, a Real-Time Evolutive Patient Model for Major Incident Simulation: Development and Validation Study.
citation: Laurent M, Jaccard A, Suppan L, Erriquez E, Good X, Golay E, Jaccard D, Suppan M. (2025). HUMAn, a Real-Time Evolutive Patient Model for Major Incident Simulation: Development and Validation Study. JMIR Formative Research. https://doi.org/10.2196/66201
title: Modified user-centered design process with relevance, iterative development, and validation phases for building a physiological simulation model
description: The development process used a modified version of the user-centered design framework in which the six design-thinking modes plus the knowledge base mode were "sorted in 2 phases, the relevance phase and an iterative development phase", with a validation phase added. A 12-member multidisciplinary team including prehospital physicians, paramedics, a game designer, computer scientists, and an instructional designer was established, with end-users included early. Prototypes were progressively refined through brainswarming sessions and iterative testing by the development team.
requirements: A multidisciplinary design and development team including end-users (prehospital physicians and paramedics) established early in the process
Iterative cycles in which test-mode results feed back into knowledge base analysis and ideation
target_learners: design teams developing healthcare simulation and educational technology
target_learning_goals: developing and validating clinically realistic simulation tools for professional education
examples: The 12-member team included 3 prehospital senior physicians, 3 advanced paramedics, 1 medical student, 1 game designer, 3 computer scientists, and 1 instructional designer; 8 team members are coauthors of the article
key_sources: Laurent M, Jaccard A, Suppan L, Erriquez E, Good X, Golay E, Jaccard D, Suppan M. (2025). HUMAn, a Real-Time Evolutive Patient Model for Major Incident Simulation: Development and Validation Study. JMIR Formative Research. https://doi.org/10.2196/66201

article_title: Pupilometer efficacy in monitoring anxiety in undergraduate medical students during high-fidelity clinical simulation.
citation: Martín-Rodríguez Francisco et al. (2025). Pupilometer efficacy in monitoring anxiety in undergraduate medical students during high-fidelity clinical simulation. Scientific Reports. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41598-025-95290-6
title: Monitor anxiety during high-fidelity simulation because low-to-medium anxiety aids concentration while high anxiety impairs alertness, problem resolution, and decision-making
description: The article argues that measuring anxiety among simulation participants matters for learning outcomes: "Low-medium levels of anxiety are known to facilitate concentration and improve short-term results; similarly, high levels of anxiety are known to dampen alertness (for overstimulation), hinder problem resolution, and disrupt the decision-making process dramatically". It therefore supports routine anxiety monitoring, including objective physiological monitoring, as part of simulation-based education design.
requirements: A measurement instrument (questionnaire, biomarker, or pupillometry) applied before and after the simulation session
constraints: The supporting evidence base for the anxiety-performance relationship is cited background literature rather than tested in this trial
target_learners: undergraduate medical students
target_learning_goals: maintaining concentration and decision-making capacity during emergency and critical care simulation
examples: The trial measured STAI, vital signs, and pupillary response pre- and postsimulation to identify students with disabling anxiety
key_sources: Martín-Rodríguez Francisco et al. (2025). Pupilometer efficacy in monitoring anxiety in undergraduate medical students during high-fidelity clinical simulation. Scientific Reports. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41598-025-95290-6

article_title: Mental Practice to Maintain Procedural Competency of Faculty with Decreased Opportunities.
citation: Kong Kam Wa Terry T, Mema B. (2024). Mental Practice to Maintain Procedural Competency of Faculty with Decreased Opportunities. ATS Scholar. https://doi.org/10.34197/ats-scholar.2023-0150IN
title: Guillot and Collet's Motor Imagery Integrative Model (MIIM) as a framework for mental practice
description: The Motor Imagery Integrative Model (MIIM), devised by Guillot and Collet from the sports literature, is described as "a guiding framework for MP interventions" organized around three outcome domains: "1) motor learning and performance; 2) motivation, self-confidence, and anxiety; and 3) strategies and problem solving". The model holds that individuals use different types of mental practice for distinct goals, such as rehearsing tactical skills, regulating anxiety, improving motivation and self-confidence, and perfecting technical aspects of a motor skill. The authors adopted MIIM as the deductive coding lens for their faculty interview data.
requirements: MP interventions framed around the model target outcomes of motor learning and performance, motivation/self-confidence/anxiety, and strategies and problem solving
constraints: the model originates in the sports literature and is applied by the authors to medical procedural skills; the article reports MP definitions vary and the study applied "the most inclusive one" (Morris and colleagues' definition)
target_learners: physician faculty maintaining procedural skills
novice medical learners acquiring procedural skills
target_learning_goals: procedural skill maintenance and acquisition
anxiety regulation and self-confidence
procedural problem solving
examples: the study coded interview transcripts inductively and deductively using MIIM, exploring outcomes of performance, motivation, and problem solving
key_sources: Kong Kam Wa Terry T, Mema B. (2024). Mental Practice to Maintain Procedural Competency of Faculty with Decreased Opportunities. ATS Scholar. https://doi.org/10.34197/ats-scholar.2023-0150IN

article_title: Intention to use eLearning-based continuing professional development and its predictors among healthcare professionals in Amhara region referral hospitals, Ethiopia, 2023: using modified UTAUT-2 model.
citation: Kelkay Jenberu Mekurianew, Wubante Sisay Maru, Anteneh Deje Sendek, Takilo Mitiku Kassaw, Gebeyehu Chernet Desalegn, Alameraw Temesgen Ayenew, Gashu Kassahun Dessie. (2025). Intention to use eLearning-based continuing professional development and its predictors among healthcare professionals in Amhara region referral hospitals, Ethiopia, 2023: using modified UTAUT-2 model. BMC Health Services Research. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12913-025-12317-4
title: Modified UTAUT-2 model adding computer literacy to predict intention to use eLearning-based CPD
description: The study adapts the UTAUT-2 technology-acceptance framework, retaining performance expectancy, effort expectancy, social influence, facilitating condition, hedonic motivation, price value, and habit, and adding computer literacy as an eighth predictor of behavioral intention. Actual use was not measured because "there is no actual usage of the eLearning-based continuing professional development by healthcare professionals" in Ethiopia yet, so user behavior was dropped as a dependent variable. Experience was also dropped as a moderator because most participants were unfamiliar with eLearning-based CPD.
requirements: Requires measurement of the eight predictor constructs and intention via multi-item five-point Likert scales with reliability and validity checks (CFA, Cronbach's alpha, CR, AVE)
constraints: Applied where the technology is not yet implemented, so only intention, not actual use, is modeled; experience was excluded as a moderator due to participants' unfamiliarity with eLearning-based CPD
target_learners: Healthcare professionals in referral hospitals
target_learning_goals: Continuing professional development via eLearning
examples: The model was tested with SEM (AMOS 23) on 976 healthcare professionals, achieving fit indices the article labels excellent (e.g., CFI 0.975, RMSEA 0.031)
key_sources: Kelkay Jenberu Mekurianew, Wubante Sisay Maru, Anteneh Deje Sendek, Takilo Mitiku Kassaw, Gebeyehu Chernet Desalegn, Alameraw Temesgen Ayenew, Gashu Kassahun Dessie. (2025). article_title: Enhancing end-of-life care nursing competency: a nursing education quality improvement project in general medical wards.
citation: Lee Chen Na; Lee Guozhang; Aw Fung Chee; Zulkifle Nuraishah Binte; Tan Yih Shan; Amanulla Marianah; Chua Esther Hui Hui; Koh Wei Zhi; Lee Jolin Er Huan; Woong Natalie Liling. (2025). Enhancing end-of-life care nursing competency: a nursing education quality improvement project in general medical wards. BMJ Open Quality. https://doi.org/10.1136/bmjoq-2024-003228
title: Modified 20-item Palliative Care Quiz for assessing medical ward nurses' end-of-life care knowledge
description: A 20-item knowledge assessment adapted in 2022 from the Palliative Care Quiz for Nursing by Singapore General Hospital palliative care specialists (one palliative specialist and three advanced practice nurses). It assesses three domains: "assessment of terminally ill patients, pharmacological management and non-pharmacological management". Proficiency was defined as scoring 80% or higher, administered in hard copy within 20 minutes without electronic device support.
requirements: Administered under supervision within 20 minutes without electronic devices or external assistance
constraints: Adapted for medical ward nurses' context; proficiency threshold set at 80% or higher
target_learners: Registered nurses in general medical wards
target_learning_goals: Assessing palliative care knowledge across assessment, pharmacological and non-pharmacological EOL care domains
examples: Used as baseline needs assessment (15% pass rate among 40 nurses) and re-administered post-intervention (53% pass rate)

article_title: "MORAD ESCAPE", a novel research-based escape room approach for evaluating research competencies of health professions students.
citation: Mirshahi Arvin, Khanipour-Kencha Ali, Keyvanpour Sogol, Motlagh Maryam Karbasi. (2025). “MORAD ESCAPE”, a novel research-based escape room approach for evaluating research competencies of health professions students. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-025-06781-z
title: MORAD ESCAPE: a five-station research-based escape room for assessing research competencies
description: MORAD ESCAPE is a research-based escape room at Tehran University of Medical Sciences designed to assess research competencies of health professions students. The game "was structured across five stations, following a linear plot" so teams could not skip ahead, with puzzles unlocking clues rather than directly teaching content. Sessions lasted 90 minutes; 60 students in 12 groups of five participated voluntarily, and game masters monitored via cameras with two-way radios for hints.
requirements: A research competency checklist and game evaluation checklist; game masters; a scenario-aligned physical location; orientation meeting before play
constraints: Puzzles were not intended to serve direct educational purposes but to facilitate access to research-related data; participation was voluntary, which the authors note may have introduced selection bias
target_learners: health professions students at Tehran University of Medical Sciences
target_learning_goals: research competencies including literature searching, data extraction, methodology, and statistics interpretation
examples: Two pilot teams unfamiliar with the scenario trialled the game before implementation; the top three teams received research grants as prizes
key_sources: Mirshahi Arvin, Khanipour-Kencha Ali, Keyvanpour Sogol, Motlagh Maryam Karbasi. (2025). “MORAD ESCAPE”, a novel research-based escape room approach for evaluating research competencies of health professions students. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-025-06781-z

article_title: "MORAD ESCAPE", a novel research-based escape room approach for evaluating research competencies of health professions students.
citation: Mirshahi Arvin, Khanipour-Kencha Ali, Keyvanpour Sogol, Motlagh Maryam Karbasi. (2025). “MORAD ESCAPE”, a novel research-based escape room approach for evaluating research competencies of health professions students. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-025-06781-z
title: Validated research competency checklist and game evaluation checklist for escape room assessment
description: Two tools were developed for the escape room: a research competency checklist scored 0–500 at team level, covering literature searches, data extraction, methodology and study types, and statistics interpretation; and a game evaluation checklist with four dimensions (puzzles, research questions, scene-setting, scenario) on a five-point Likert scale. The game evaluation tool showed strong psychometrics: "The CVI for each item on the instrument was reported to be above 0.82" with S-CVI/Ave of 0.94 and Cronbach's alpha of 0.72.
requirements: Expert panel input (PhD holders in health professions education, research methodology teachers, professional escape room designers); face and content validity via Delphi rounds reaching 90% consensus
constraints: The checklist assessed competencies at team rather than individual level, which the authors note limited assessment of individual contributions
target_learners: health professions students
target_learning_goals: research competency assessment
game design evaluation
examples: Content validity used a two-round Delphi method with eight health professions education experts and two escape room designers, achieving 70% then 90% consensus

article_title: The use of specific coordination behaviours to manage information processing and task distribution in real and simulated trauma teamwork: an observational study.
citation: Fornander L, Garrido Granhagen M, Molin I, Laukkanen K, Björnström Karlsson K, Berggren P, Nilsson L. (2024). The use of specific coordination behaviours to manage information processing and task distribution in real and simulated trauma teamwork: an observational study. Scandinavian Journal of Trauma, Resuscitation and Emergency Medicine. https://doi.org/10.1186/s13049-024-01287-x
title: A modified CoMet-E classification system for trauma-team coordination behaviours adds confirmation and relational communication codes
description: The article modified the Coordination System for Medical Teams-Emergency, which "descriptively categorizes coordination behaviour", into a three-level system: main categories (information management, task management, relational communication, other communication, not codable), 19-20 coordination behaviours, and closed-loop communication coding of applicable utterances. "two new coordination behaviours were added to the system": "confirmation" and "relational communication", with a relational category added at level 1. Intercoder agreement reached Cohen's κ = 0.86 for main categories, κ = 0.68 for coordination behaviours, and κ = 0.8 for CLC.
requirements: Transcribed verbatim video material and trained coders calibrated against each other to achieve the reported Cohen's κ agreements of 0.86, 0.68 and 0.8 at levels 1, 2 and 3 respectively.
constraints: The article states the behaviours "request team member information", "give team member information", and "evaluate decision" were used at a minimum, which disqualified any conclusions drawn from those observations.
The system was modified to fit this single-centre material and research aim, limiting generalizability per the article's methodological considerations.
target_learners: Interprofessional trauma team members including physicians, nurses and assistant nurses
target_learning_goals: Describing and classifying coordination and communication behaviours during trauma resuscitation teamwork
examples: Coded 2476 real-life and 1728 simulated utterances, showing the modified system serviceable to describe utterances relative to coordination in both domains.
key_sources: Fornander L, Garrido Granhagen M, Molin I, Laukkanen K, Björnström Karlsson K, Berggren P, Nilsson L. (2024). The use of specific coordination behaviours to manage information processing and task distribution in real and simulated trauma teamwork: an observational study. Scandinavian Journal of Trauma, Resuscitation and Emergency Medicine. https://doi.org/10.1186/s13049-024-01287-x

article_title: Relationship between motivational climate, anxiety and average mark in pre-service physical education teachers: a cross-sectional study based on structural equation modelling approach.
citation: Melguizo-Ibáñez E, González-Valero G, Badicu G, Yagin FH, Alonso-Vargas JM, Ardigò LP, Puertas-Molero P. (2025). Relationship between motivational climate, anxiety and average mark in pre-service physical education teachers: a cross-sectional study based on structural equation modelling approach. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-025-06646-5
title: Motivational climate as a task/ego dual construct from Achievement Goals Theory
description: The article frames motivational climate within Achievement Goals Theory, defining it as "internal or external indicators from the environment that determine success or failure when undertaking a given task". It operates as a dual construct measured by the Perceived Motivational Climate in Sport Questionnaire-2, offering "data related to task climate and ego climate", with task climate comprising cooperative learning, effort/improvement and important role, and ego climate comprising punishment for errors, unequal recognition and member rivalry. The article also cites the 2 × 2 goal model subdividing goals into approach-mastery, avoidance-mastery, approach-performance and avoidance-performance.
requirements: Measured with validated instruments adapted to the population, here the PMCSQ-2 version of González-Cutre et al. and the Beck Anxiety Inventory
constraints: The construct is studied in the physical-sport and teacher-education context of the sample
target_learners: pre-service physical education teachers
university students in education and sport sciences
target_learning_goals: motivation towards learning tasks
anxiety regulation in academic and physical-sport settings
examples: The study modelled task and ego climate as two exogenous latent variables with observed indicators (cooperative learning, effort/improvement, important role; punishment for errors, unequal recognition, rivalry) in a structural equation model
key_sources: Melguizo-Ibáñez E, González-Valero G, Badicu G, Yagin FH, Alonso-Vargas JM, Ardigò LP, Puertas-Molero P. (2025). Relationship between motivational climate, anxiety and average mark in pre-service physical education teachers: a cross-sectional study based on structural equation modelling approach. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-025-06646-5

article_title: The effect of simulation-based training on problem-solving skills, critical thinking skills, and self-efficacy among nursing students in Vietnam: a before-and-after study.
citation: Oanh Tran Thi Hoang, Thuy Luu Thi, Huyen Ngo Thi Thu. (2024). The effect of simulation-based training on problem-solving skills, critical thinking skills, and self-efficacy among nursing students in Vietnam: a before-and-after study. Journal of Educational Evaluation for Health Professions. https://doi.org/10.3352/jeehp.2024.21.24
title: Moderate-fidelity simulation-based adult nursing preclinical course (8 sections over 4 weeks)
description: An 8-section simulation-based course on adult nursing delivered to second-year nursing students before clinical practice, using "moderate-fidelity simulated teaching approaches (using moderately realistic simulation models), based on the World Health Organization guidelines". Each section lasted 200 minutes, with 2 sections per week over 4 weeks, taught by simulation-trained instructors using standardized scenarios with pre- and post-scenario discussions and debriefing. The course was evaluated in a single-group pretest-posttest study of 173 students.

constraints: Moderate fidelity and the short 4-week duration are cited by the authors as possible reasons no critical thinking change was observed
target_learners: second-year full-time nursing students

problem-solving skills
self-efficacy
examples: Students engaged in diverse clinical scenarios covering various patient needs and care techniques, designed to vary in complexity

article_title: Research on the application of CBL combined with BOPPPS teaching mode in oral and maxillofacial surgery teaching: a randomized controlled study.
citation: Gao Ning, Fu Kun, Li Na, He Wei. (2024). Research on the application of CBL combined with BOPPPS teaching mode in oral and maxillofacial surgery teaching: a randomized controlled study. Scientific Reports. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41598-024-77432-4
title: Modified Mini-CEX scale for assessing clinical speculative thinking in oral and maxillofacial surgery postgraduates
description: The modified Mini-CEX scale is a five-item workplace assessment instrument used in this study to score students' clinical speculative thinking. Each item is worth 20 points, covering "clinical decision-making ability, communication and coordination ability, adaptive ability, treatment operation level, and medical history writing level". Students were assessed while independently receiving patients in the emergency department, observed by two attending physicians who were trained on the scale, did not participate in the teaching, and were blinded to grouping; each student was assessed five times and average scores were used.
requirements: Two trained attending physician raters blinded to grouping who do not participate in the teaching
Emergency-department patient encounters that students handle independently
Five assessments per student to obtain average scores
constraints: In this study the medical history writing level item did not detect a difference between teaching modes, and the authors note the sample size is small
target_learners: Medical postgraduate students assessed during clinical rotations
target_learning_goals: Clinical decision-making, communication and coordination, adaptive ability, treatment operation, and medical history writing
examples: Each master's student was assessed five times and the average score was taken as the final score
key_sources: Gao Ning, Fu Kun, Li Na, He Wei. (2024). Research on the application of CBL combined with BOPPPS teaching mode in oral and maxillofacial surgery teaching: a randomized controlled study. Scientific Reports. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41598-024-77432-4

article_title: A surgical instrument motion measurement system for skill evaluation in practical laparoscopic surgery training.
citation: Ebina Koki, Abe Takashige, Yan Lingbo, Hotta Kiyohiko, Shichinohe Toshiaki, Higuchi Madoka, Iwahara Naoya, Hosaka Yukino, Harada Shigeru, Kikuchi Hiroshi, Miyata Haruka, Matsumoto Ryuji, Osawa Takahiro, Kurashima Yo, Watanabe Masahiko, Kon Masafumi, Murai Sachiyo, Komizunai Shunsuke, Tsujita Teppei, Sase Kazuya, Chen Xiaoshuai, Senoo Taku, Shinohara Nobuo, Konno Atsushi. (2024). A surgical instrument motion measurement system for skill evaluation in practical laparoscopic surgery training. PLOS ONE. https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0305693
title: Post-processing pipeline for outlier removal and smoothing of MoCap measurement data
description: A data correction process developed for the measurement data, which "often include noise and outliers owing to misrecognition by the MoCap system." It combines threshold-based outlier removal using a partial measurement success rate over a 600-frame (5 s) moving window, ROI-based removal, and a second-order Kalman filter whose estimates flag outliers when the discrepancy exceeds five times the estimated standard deviation, followed by linear and Slerp interpolation and Savitzky–Golay smoothing (window 121, polynomial order 3).
requirements: Thresholds must be set: PMR below 25% removed, continuous-measurement threshold of 5 s, interpolated periods over 5 s or distances over 0.1 m excluded as unreliable
Kalman filter noise variances must be specified (system noise and observation noise), and Joseph's equation used to avoid covariance asymmetry
constraints: Interpolated values may deviate from actual instrument motion when interpolation is performed over a long period, so long interpolated values are excluded from skill analysis
target_learners: surgeons in laparoscopic surgery training
target_learning_goals: reliable kinematic indices for surgical skill evaluation
examples: Applied to the cadaver training data to obtain tip-position trajectories (Fig 10) and attitude angles (Fig 11), confirming outliers were eliminated and intraoperative instrument exchanges detected

title: Select students for extracurricular research programmes aimed at cultivating physician-scientists based on motivation rather than a GPA threshold
description: The article recommends shifting ERP selection from grades alone toward motivation, because intrinsic motivation for research, perceptions of research, and curiosity are prerequisites of future research involvement and were comparable across GPA groups. It argues "motivation should be given importance in selecting students for ERPs, allowing students with a GPA lower than seven to participate within such programmes as well". Selection should use a model in which GPA is not a threshold for entry.

Insight into applicants' motivation for research, e.g. via questionnaires or motivation letters.

Evidence comes from one cohort of 59 students at a single Dutch academic medical centre.

target_learning_goals: research involvement and development of future physician-scientists
examples: The LUMC Honours programme allowed every student to apply by self-selection without a GPA threshold for entering, enabling the comparison of the 29 ≥7 and 30 <7 students.

The authors note the approach was developed for 1:1 teaching but that students also welcome it for small group training, and that its implementation for procedural skill teaching is recommended.

constraints: The approach was developed for 1:1 teaching, though the article reports students also welcome it for small group training

citation: Nijenkamp, R., Nieuwenstein, M. R., de Jong, R., & Lorist, M. M. (2016). Do Resit Exams Promote Lower Investments of Study Time? Theory and Data from a Laboratory Study. PLoS ONE. https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0161708
title: A modified rational utility model of resit exams predicting reduced first-attempt study-time investment
description: The article modifies Kooreman's mathematical model of study-time investment by assuming that "knowledge of course materials will accumulate in an exponential fashion with increasing investments of study time" and modeling multiple-choice guessing statistically, producing an S-shaped passing-probability function rather than Kooreman's concave function. Combined with linearly increasing time costs, this yields expected-utility functions whose optimum shifts to lower study-time investment when a resit is available. The model predicts a roughly 20% reduction in optimal study time for a first attempt with resit access, less dramatic than Kooreman's original prediction.
requirements: Assumes students act rationally to maximize expected utility, trading off linear study-time costs against probabilistic passing benefits

constraints: The model was "effectively stripped of much of its relevant scope and functionality", omitting forgetting, grade ambitions, temporal discounting, and nonlinear cost functions
target_learners: higher education students
target_learning_goals: achieving passing-level mastery of course material on pass-or-fail exams

article_title: A Cost-Effectiveness Analysis of Blended Versus Face-to-Face Delivery of Evidence-Based Medicine to Medical Students.
citation: Maloney S, Nicklen P, Rivers G, Foo J, Ooi YY, Reeves S, Walsh K, Ilic D. (2015). A Cost-Effectiveness Analysis of Blended Versus Face-to-Face Delivery of Evidence-Based Medicine to Medical Students. Journal of Medical Internet Research. https://doi.org/10.2196/jmir.4346
title: Monash blended EBM program: classroom workshops, YouTube lectures, library guide, and self-directed mobile learning
description: This is the blended learning intervention evaluated in the randomized trial and its economic analysis. It integrated classroom, online, and mobile components: "The BL approach to teaching EBM integrated (1) classroom activities (lecture/tutorial) with (2) online and (3) mobile learning". Online activities comprised a YouTube channel of 11 lectures averaging 17 minutes and a Monash University library guide indexing databases, textbooks, and guidelines; mobile learning involved self-directed patient interactions on clinical placements. The format kept total face-to-face hours identical to the traditional approach.
requirements: Staff time to create the YouTube resources, tailor content, and design activities as a one-off transition investment; the library guide already existed, so only activity design was costed.
constraints: Mobile learning is completely student self-directed, with no costs factored into the cost model; the article notes wider applicability depends on the type of blended learning utilized, staffing expertise, and educational context.
target_learners: Third-year medical students (undergraduate and postgraduate) entering clinical training
target_learning_goals: Evidence-based medicine competency: asking clinical questions, acquiring and appraising evidence, and applying it to patients
examples: Students received a 4-hour introductory workshop, then small-group sessions with tutor-set topics investigated during the week and reported back in the next session.
